title: Transformer-Based Inpainting for Real-Time 3D Streaming in Sparse Multi-Camera Setups
generated_summary:
This paper presents a transformer-based, multi-view-aware inpainting method designed as a post-processing module for real-time 3D streaming pipelines using sparse multi-camera setups. The key contribution is leveraging original multi-view camera images as contextual information to fill incomplete textures and geometry artifacts that arise when synthesizing novel views from limited viewpoints.

The method employs a CNN encoder to extract hierarchical features from both the target novel view and context images (original camera views and past frames). These features are divided into overlapping patches and processed through transformer blocks using cross-attention, where input patches with missing content attend to context patches. A decomposed 3D rotary positional embedding (RoPE) encodes spatio-temporal relationships between patches, utilizing the geometry proxy for reprojection between views. A top-k attention-based patch filtering mechanism prunes irrelevant context patches after the first transformer block in each group, enabling a controllable trade-off between speed and quality for real-time performance. Encoded features from previous frames are cached to reduce redundant computation.

Evaluated on the DNARendering and RIFTCast datasets, the method significantly outperforms adapted state-of-the-art video inpainting baselines across PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and VFID metrics, while maintaining real-time inference capability. The approach generalizes well to unseen datasets without retraining. This work addresses a practical gap in 3D streaming pipelines, offering a representation-agnostic solution that enhances visual quality of novel view synthesis in resource-constrained, real-time settings.
original_abstract: High-quality 3D streaming from multiple cameras is crucial for immersive experiences in many AR/VR applications. The limited number of views - often due to real-time constraints - leads to missing information and incomplete surfaces in the rendered images. Existing approaches typically rely on simple heuristics for the hole filling, which can result in inconsistencies or visual artifacts. We propose to complete the missing textures using a novel, application-targeted inpainting method independent of the underlying representation as an image-based post-processing step after the novel view rendering. The method is designed as a standalone module compatible with any calibrated multi-camera system. For this we introduce a multi-view aware, transformer-based network architecture using spatio-temporal embeddings to ensure consistency across frames while preserving fine details. Additionally, our resolution-independent design allows adaptation to different camera setups, while an adaptive patch selection strategy balances inference speed and quality, allowing real-time performance. We evaluate our approach against state-of-the-art inpainting techniques under the same real-time constraints and demonstrate that our model achieves the best trade-off between quality and speed, outperforming competitors in both image and video-based metrics.

title: FaceCam: Portrait Video Camera Control via Scale-Aware Conditioning
generated_summary:
FaceCam introduces a portrait video camera-control system that addresses two key limitations of existing approaches: scale ambiguity in scene-agnostic camera representations and geometric distortions in reconstruction-based methods. The main contribution is a scale-aware camera conditioning scheme based on facial landmark correspondences in image space, which resolves monocular scale ambiguity by operating directly in pixel coordinates rather than relying on metric camera extrinsics.

The method encodes camera motion through 2D projections of 3D facial landmarks, providing an intuitive and mathematically sufficient representation of relative camera pose. For training data, the authors develop a pipeline combining multi-view studio captures from NeRSemble with in-the-wild videos, using synthetic camera motion (zoom and pan) and a multi-shot stitching technique that concatenates clips from different viewpoints. Despite training only on static camera captures and augmented monocular videos, the model generalizes to continuous camera trajectories at inference. The system builds upon the Wan video foundation model, fine-tuning attention and projection layers.

Experiments on the Ava-256 benchmark and in-the-wild portrait videos demonstrate that FaceCam achieves superior performance compared to ReCamMaster and TrajectoryCrafter in camera control accuracy, identity preservation, and visual quality. The approach maintains faithful facial expressions, head motion, and fine-grained details like hair dynamics across diverse camera trajectories, highlighting its practical applicability for real-world portrait video editing and production.
original_abstract: We introduce FaceCam, a system that generates video under customizable camera trajectories for monocular human portrait video input. Recent camera control approaches based on large video-generation models have shown promising progress but often exhibit geometric distortions and visual artifacts on portrait videos due to scale-ambiguous camera representations or 3D reconstruction errors. To overcome these limitations, we propose a face-tailored scale-aware representation for camera transformations that provides deterministic conditioning without relying on 3D priors. We train a video generation model on both multi-view studio captures and in-the-wild monocular videos, and introduce two camera-control data generation strategies: synthetic camera motion and multi-shot stitching, to exploit stationary training cameras while generalizing to dynamic, continuous camera trajectories at inference time. Experiments on Ava-256 dataset and diverse in-the-wild videos demonstrate that FaceCam achieves superior performance in camera controllability, visual quality, identity and motion preservation.

title: RoboPocket: Improve Robot Policies Instantly with Your Phone
generated_summary:
RoboPocket introduces a smartphone-based system that transforms handheld robotic data collection from a passive recording process into an active, computationally guided workflow, effectively democratizing robot policy learning. The key innovation is "Robot-Free Instant Policy Iteration," which eliminates the need for physical robot deployment during the policy improvement cycle. By streaming observations to an inference server and projecting the policy's predicted trajectory back onto the user's screen via Augmented Reality, users can visualize failure modes in real-time, collect targeted corrective demonstrations, and iteratively refine policies—all without accessing a physical robot.

The system integrates on-device visual feedback including SLAM stability indicators and kinematic feasibility checks, achieving 2.8mm average tracking accuracy, outperforming existing handheld interfaces. RoboPocket is validated across four challenging manipulation tasks: block sorting, seasoning pouring, towel folding, and bimanual snack bagging. Results demonstrate that instant policy iteration achieves up to 2× improvement in data efficiency compared to standard imitation learning baselines, breaking the diminishing returns of pure data scaling. In distributed experiments across four distinct environments, only 12 interactive corrections per user yielded dramatic performance improvements, with some scenes improving from 0.42 to 0.75 success rate.

The significance of RoboPocket lies in its potential to export expert-level robotics intuition into a consumer device, enabling scalable, distributed policy learning outside laboratory settings.
original_abstract: Scaling imitation learning is fundamentally constrained by the efficiency of data collection. While handheld interfaces have emerged as a scalable solution for in-the-wild data acquisition, they predominantly operate in an open-loop manner: operators blindly collect demonstrations without knowing the underlying policy's weaknesses, leading to inefficient coverage of critical state distributions. Conversely, interactive methods like DAgger effectively address covariate shift but rely on physical robot execution, which is costly and difficult to scale. To reconcile this trade-off, we introduce RoboPocket, a portable system that enables Robot-Free Instant Policy Iteration using single consumer smartphones. Its core innovation is a Remote Inference framework that visualizes the policy's predicted trajectory via Augmented Reality (AR) Visual Foresight. This immersive feedback allows collectors to proactively identify potential failures and focus data collection on the policy's weak regions without requiring a physical robot. Furthermore, we implement an asynchronous Online Finetuning pipeline that continuously updates the policy with incoming data, effectively closing the learning loop in minutes. Extensive experiments demonstrate that RoboPocket adheres to data scaling laws and doubles the data efficiency compared to offline scaling strategies, overcoming their long-standing efficiency bottleneck. Moreover, our instant iteration loop also boosts sample efficiency by up to 2$\times$ in distributed environments a small number of interactive corrections per person. Project page and videos: https://robo-pocket.github.io.

title: Accelerating Text-to-Video Generation with Calibrated Sparse Attention
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a training-free method called calibrated sparse attention for accelerating text-to-video generation in diffusion transformers. The key insight is that attention sparsity and repetition patterns, while varying significantly across layers, heads, and timesteps, remain largely consistent across different input prompts and noise initializations, enabling data-independent optimization.

The methodology involves a one-time offline calibration phase where attention maps are analyzed across a small set of prompts to identify two complementary patterns: block-level sparsity (where attention mass concentrates on few key blocks) and spatial repetition (where attention patterns repeat across spatial rows within frames). For each layer, head, and timestep combination, the algorithm produces calibrated binary block masks and flags for spatially repetitive heads. During inference, a custom FlashAttention3-based kernel uses precomputed skip lists to efficiently bypass unnecessary computations.

Evaluated on Wan 2.1 14B, Mochi 1, and a distilled few-step variant (LightX2V), the method achieves state-of-the-art attention sparsity and end-to-end latency improvements while maintaining generation quality comparable to dense attention baselines on VBench metrics. Notably, the approach requires minimal hyperparameter tuning across different models, resolutions, and diffusion configurations, without needing manual exclusion of specific layers or timesteps.

The significance lies in demonstrating that principled, automatic calibration of sparse attention patterns can deliver robust acceleration across diverse video generation settings, offering a practical path toward faster inference for increasingly large transformer-based generative models.
original_abstract: Recent diffusion models enable high-quality video generation, but suffer from slow runtimes. The large transformer-based backbones used in these models are bottlenecked by spatiotemporal attention. In this paper, we identify that a significant fraction of token-to-token connections consistently yield negligible scores across various inputs, and their patterns often repeat across queries. Thus, the attention computation in these cases can be skipped with little to no effect on the result. This observation continues to hold for connections among local token blocks. Motivated by this, we introduce CalibAtt, a training-free method that accelerates video generation via calibrated sparse attention. CalibAtt performs an offline calibration pass that identifies block-level sparsity and repetition patterns that are stable across inputs, and compiles these patterns into optimized attention operations for each layer, head, and diffusion timestep. At inference time, we compute the selected input-dependent connections densely, and skip the unselected ones in a hardware-efficient manner. Extensive experiments on Wan 2.1 14B, Mochi 1, and few-step distilled models at various resolutions show that CalibAtt achieves up to 1.58x end-to-end speedup, outperforming existing training-free methods while maintaining video generation quality and text-video alignment.

title: POET-X: Memory-efficient LLM Training by Scaling Orthogonal Transformation
generated_summary:
POET-X is a fast, scalable, and memory-efficient training algorithm that addresses the poor memory efficiency and slow runtime of the original POET (reParameterized Orthogonal Equivalence Training) algorithm for large language model training. While POET demonstrates strong training stability through its spectrum-preserving property, its intensive large-scale matrix multiplications make it impractical for large models.

The authors introduce several key optimizations: reformulating POET's weight-centric computation into an input-centric form inspired by matrix-free methods, eliminating unnecessary storage of intermediate activations; exploiting block-sparse structure of orthogonal matrices through parallel batch-wise computation; improving the Cayley-Neumann parameterization by storing only half of all skew-symmetric matrices; reducing total matrix multiplications through proper matrix rearrangement; and merging permutation operations into weight matrices. Custom CUDA and Triton kernels are developed for all computations.

These optimizations collectively achieve a 3× GPU memory reduction and 8× runtime speedup compared to original POET without sacrificing training stability. POET-X attains GPU memory efficiency comparable to parameter-efficient finetuning methods like LoRA while matching AdamW's runtime. Notably, POET-X enables pretraining of models up to 13 billion parameters on a single NVIDIA H100 GPU and consistently achieves better validation perplexity than AdamW across multiple Llama model sizes. This work effectively bridges the gap between POET's theoretical parameter efficiency and practical memory efficiency, making spectrum-preserving orthogonal training viable at scale.
original_abstract: Efficient and stable training of large language models (LLMs) remains a core challenge in modern machine learning systems. To address this challenge, Reparameterized Orthogonal Equivalence Training (POET), a spectrum-preserving framework that optimizes each weight matrix through orthogonal equivalence transformation, has been proposed. Although POET provides strong training stability, its original implementation incurs high memory consumption and computational overhead due to intensive matrix multiplications. To overcome these limitations, we introduce POET-X, a scalable and memory-efficient variant that performs orthogonal equivalence transformations with significantly reduced computational cost. POET-X maintains the generalization and stability benefits of POET while achieving substantial improvements in throughput and memory efficiency. In our experiments, POET-X enables the pretraining of billion-parameter LLMs on a single Nvidia H100 GPU, and in contrast, standard optimizers such as AdamW run out of memory under the same settings.

title: The Spike, the Sparse and the Sink: Anatomy of Massive Activations and Attention Sinks
generated_summary:
This paper provides a mechanistic account of why massive activations (extreme outlier values in hidden channels) and attention sinks (tokens attracting disproportionate attention mass) co-occur in decoder-only, pre-norm Transformers. Moving beyond prior descriptive observations, the authors advance three central claims supported by extensive analysis across multiple large language models and controlled ablation studies.

The methodology combines empirical analysis of pretrained models (including Llama 2, Qwen3, and others) with systematic architectural ablations examining normalization configurations, attention head dimensionality, context-length distributions, and feed-forward block designs. The authors trace the causal mechanisms through which specific design choices produce these phenomena.

Key findings reveal that normalization layers serve as the critical architectural bridge: massive activations interact with normalization to produce near-constant hidden representations that function as implicit global parameters, which attention sinks then exploit. Attention sinks themselves are driven by attention space dimensionality and training context-length distributions, serving as local modulators that bias certain heads toward short-range dependencies capturing local sentence structure. Crucially, the authors demonstrate that each phenomenon can be independently suppressed through alternative architectural choices—such as modifying normalization configuration—without degrading language-modeling performance.

These results are significant for practical LLM optimization, particularly for quantization, pruning, KV-cache management, and long-context inference, as they show the co-occurrence reflects incidental architectural interactions rather than functional necessity, opening clear paths for targeted mitigation strategies.
original_abstract: We study two recurring phenomena in Transformer language models: massive activations, in which a small number of tokens exhibit extreme outliers in a few channels, and attention sinks, in which certain tokens attract disproportionate attention mass regardless of semantic relevance. Prior work observes that these phenomena frequently co-occur and often involve the same tokens, but their functional roles and causal relationship remain unclear. Through systematic experiments, we show that the co-occurrence is largely an architectural artifact of modern Transformer design, and that the two phenomena serve related but distinct functions. Massive activations operate globally: they induce near-constant hidden representations that persist across layers, effectively functioning as implicit parameters of the model. Attention sinks operate locally: they modulate attention outputs across heads and bias individual heads toward short-range dependencies. We identify the pre-norm configuration as the key choice that enables the co-occurrence, and show that ablating it causes the two phenomena to decouple.

title: Safe-SAGE: Social-Semantic Adaptive Guidance for Safe Engagement through Laplace-Modulated Poisson Safety Functions
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Safe-SAGE, a framework that integrates social-semantic awareness into safety-critical control for legged robots navigating human-centered environments. The main contribution is bridging the gap between high-level semantic reasoning and real-time safety enforcement by extending Poisson safety functions (PSFs) and Laplace guidance fields (LGFs) with two key mechanisms: semantic flux modulation, which assigns class-dependent safety margins to different obstacle types, and social flow biasing through tangential boundary conditions that encode directional navigation norms such as passing conventions.

The methodology constructs a robot-centric occupancy grid from fused multi-sensor data, applies semantic segmentation via YOLOv11n with persistent object tracking, and solves vector Laplace and Poisson equations with class-aware boundary conditions to generate guidance and safety fields. These fields feed into a dual safety filter architecture comprising an MPC-based predictive planner and a high-frequency analytical safety filter, both operating on a reduced-order model. The authors provide formal forward invariance guarantees for the modified guidance field.

Hardware experiments on a Unitree Go2 quadruped and G1 humanoid robot across hallway, open area, and cafeteria scenarios demonstrate that the proposed modulation achieves larger human-robot margins and greater lateral offsets compared to nominal guidance fields lacking semantic differentiation. The framework is platform-agnostic and operates in real-time, representing a significant step toward deploying legged robots that respect both physical safety constraints and social navigation norms simultaneously.
original_abstract: Traditional safety-critical control methods, such as control barrier functions, suffer from semantic blindness, exhibiting the same behavior around obstacles regardless of contextual significance. This limitation leads to the uniform treatment of all obstacles, despite their differing semantic meanings. We present Safe-SAGE (Social-Semantic Adaptive Guidance for Safe Engagement), a unified framework that bridges the gap between high-level semantic understanding and low-level safety-critical control through a Poisson safety function (PSF) modulated using a Laplace guidance field. Our approach perceives the environment by fusing multi-sensor point clouds with vision-based instance segmentation and persistent object tracking to maintain up-to-date semantics beyond the camera's field of view. A multi-layer safety filter is then used to modulate system inputs to achieve safe navigation using this semantic understanding of the environment. This safety filter consists of both a model predictive control layer and a control barrier function layer. Both layers utilize the PSF and flux modulation of the guidance field to introduce varying levels of conservatism and multi-agent passing norms for different obstacles in the environment. Our framework enables legged robots to navigate semantically rich, dynamic environments with context-dependent safety margins while maintaining rigorous safety guarantees.

title: Cheap Thrills: Effective Amortized Optimization Using Inexpensive Labels
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a three-stage framework for amortized optimization that bridges supervised learning (SL) and self-supervised learning (SSL) by leveraging cheap, imperfect labels to warm-start training. The key insight is that for nonconvex constrained optimization problems, a surrogate model only needs to be initialized within the basin of attraction of a desirable solution rather than requiring expensive high-fidelity supervision.

The methodology consists of three stages: (1) generating inexpensive, approximate labels using methods such as iterative solvers with relaxed tolerances or simplified models, (2) pretraining the model via supervised regression on these imperfect labels to provide a warm start, and (3) fine-tuning with self-supervised learning that directly minimizes the task objective and constraint violations. The authors provide theoretical analysis showing that a modest number of cheap labels and pretraining epochs suffice to place the model in a favorable basin of attraction for subsequent SSL convergence.

Experiments across synthetic nonconvex optimization, optimal power flow for power grids, and stiff dynamical systems demonstrate that this approach consistently outperforms both pure SL and pure SSL baselines in terms of training stability, convergence speed, and final solution quality, while dramatically reducing offline computational costs. The framework also introduces a merit-based evaluation criterion combining objective quality and constraint satisfaction.

The significance lies in offering a simple, modular, and practically adoptable strategy that avoids both the expense of high-fidelity label generation and the instability of cold-start self-supervision, encouraging hybrid training approaches for learning-based optimization.
original_abstract: To scale the solution of optimization and simulation problems, prior work has explored machine-learning surrogates that inexpensively map problem parameters to corresponding solutions. Commonly used approaches, including supervised and self-supervised learning with either soft or hard feasibility enforcement, face inherent challenges such as reliance on expensive, high-quality labels or difficult optimization landscapes. To address their trade-offs, we propose a novel framework that first collects "cheap" imperfect labels, then performs supervised pretraining, and finally refines the model through self-supervised learning to improve overall performance. Our theoretical analysis and merit-based criterion show that labeled data need only place the model within a basin of attraction, confirming that only modest numbers of inexact labels and training epochs are required. We empirically validate our simple three-stage strategy across challenging domains, including nonconvex constrained optimization, power-grid operation, and stiff dynamical systems, and show that it yields faster convergence; improved accuracy, feasibility, and optimality; and up to 59x reductions in total offline cost.

title: Censored LLMs as a Natural Testbed for Secret Knowledge Elicitation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces censored Chinese open-weights LLMs—including Qwen, DeepSeek, and MiniMax models—as a naturally occurring testbed for evaluating honesty elicitation and lie detection techniques. Unlike prior work that relies on artificially constructed deceptive models, these models possess correct knowledge about politically sensitive topics (e.g., Tiananmen Square, Uyghur treatment) but are trained to suppress it, occasionally revealing truthful answers that confirm their underlying knowledge.

The authors construct a benchmark of 90 questions on censored topics paired with ground-truth facts from uncensored reference models. They evaluate a broad suite of honesty elicitation techniques on two Qwen3 models, including prompt engineering, few-shot prompting, prefill attacks, activation steering, and fine-tuning approaches. For lie detection, they assess self-classification by the censored model itself and linear activation probes trained on out-of-distribution truthfulness data.

Key findings show that sampling next-token completions without a chat template, few-shot prompting, and fine-tuning on generic honesty data are the most effective elicitation methods. These techniques successfully transfer to frontier models including DeepSeek-R1-0528 and Qwen3.5-397B. Remarkably, censored models can accurately classify their own false outputs, performing near an uncensored-model upper bound, while activation probes achieve comparable accuracy at lower cost.

The work is significant because it provides a realistic, non-synthetic benchmark for studying model dishonesty, offering the research community publicly available questions, code, and transcripts to advance secret knowledge auditing.
original_abstract: Large language models sometimes produce false or misleading responses. Two approaches to this problem are honesty elicitation -- modifying prompts or weights so that the model answers truthfully -- and lie detection -- classifying whether a given response is false. Prior work evaluates such methods on models specifically trained to lie or conceal information, but these artificial constructions may not resemble naturally-occurring dishonesty. We instead study open-weights LLMs from Chinese developers, which are trained to censor politically sensitive topics: Qwen3 models frequently produce falsehoods about subjects like Falun Gong or the Tiananmen protests while occasionally answering correctly, indicating they possess knowledge they are trained to suppress. Using this as a testbed, we evaluate a suite of elicitation and lie detection techniques. For honesty elicitation, sampling without a chat template, few-shot prompting, and fine-tuning on generic honesty data most reliably increase truthful responses. For lie detection, prompting the censored model to classify its own responses performs near an uncensored-model upper bound, and linear probes trained on unrelated data offer a cheaper alternative. The strongest honesty elicitation techniques also transfer to frontier open-weights models including DeepSeek R1. Notably, no technique fully eliminates false responses. We release all prompts, code, and transcripts.

title: cuRoboV2: Dynamics-Aware Motion Generation with Depth-Fused Distance Fields for High-DoF Robots
generated_summary:
cuRoboV2 presents a unified, GPU-native motion generation framework that addresses three fundamental barriers in robot autonomy: the gap between kinematic planning and dynamic feasibility, the trade-off between perceptual fidelity and reactive control speed, and the failure of existing methods to scale to high-degree-of-freedom (DoF) systems like humanoids.

The framework introduces three core algorithmic contributions. First, a B-spline optimization formulation enables dynamics-aware trajectory generation by optimizing control points that inherently enforce smoothness, allowing satisfaction of torque limits during both global planning and reactive control. Second, a GPU-native perception pipeline fuses depth images, meshes, and cuboids into a block-sparse TSDF, then generates a dense Euclidean Signed Distance Field (ESDF) covering the full workspace using a parallel banding algorithm, delivering collision queries up to 10× faster and with 8× less memory than existing approaches while achieving 99% collision recall. Third, scalable GPU-native building blocks for kinematics, inverse dynamics, and self-collision detection achieve up to 40× speedups, enabling convergence for robots ranging from 7-DoF arms to 48-DoF humanoids.

Key results demonstrate that the system enforces torque constraints that baselines skip—keeping trajectories executable under payload—while enabling reactive model predictive control with live depth fusion on real robots. The framework produces physically valid reference motions for humanoids that directly improve downstream locomotion policies, representing a significant advance toward unified, dynamics-aware autonomy across diverse robotic platforms.
original_abstract: Effective robot autonomy requires motion generation that is safe, feasible, and reactive. Current methods are fragmented: fast planners output physically unexecutable trajectories, reactive controllers struggle with high-fidelity perception, and existing solvers fail on high-DoF systems. We present cuRoboV2, a unified framework with three key innovations: (1) B-spline trajectory optimization that enforces smoothness and torque limits; (2) a GPU-native TSDF/ESDF perception pipeline that generates dense signed distance fields covering the full workspace, unlike existing methods that only provide distances within sparsely allocated blocks, up to 10x faster and in 8x less memory than the state-of-the-art at manipulation scale, with up to 99% collision recall; and (3) scalable GPU-native whole-body computation, namely topology-aware kinematics, differentiable inverse dynamics, and map-reduce self-collision, that achieves up to 61x speedup while also extending to high-DoF humanoids (where previous GPU implementations fail). On benchmarks, cuRoboV2 achieves 99.7% success under 3kg payload (where baselines achieve only 72--77%), 99.6% collision-free IK on a 48-DoF humanoid (where prior methods fail entirely), and 89.5% retargeting constraint satisfaction (vs. 61% for PyRoki); these collision-free motions yield locomotion policies with 21% lower tracking error than PyRoki and 12x lower cross-seed variance than mink. A ground-up codebase redesign for discoverability enabled LLM coding assistants to author up to 73% of new modules, including hand-optimized CUDA kernels, demonstrating that well-structured robotics code can unlock productive human--LLM collaboration. Together, these advances provide a unified, dynamics-aware motion generation stack that scales from single-arm manipulators to full humanoids.

title: NL2GDS: LLM-aided interface for Open Source Chip Design
generated_summary:
This paper introduces NL2GDS, the first framework that translates natural language hardware specifications directly into fabrication-ready GDSII chip layouts using an open-source design flow. The system bridges the gap between high-level design intent and physical implementation, aiming to democratize ASIC design by eliminating the need for specialized hardware description language (HDL) expertise and expensive proprietary tools.

NL2GDS employs a multi-agent LLM architecture incorporating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) and chain-of-thought reasoning to automatically generate synthesizable HDL code from plain language descriptions. The framework integrates HDL generation, error correction, verification, and design optimization into a fully automated cloud-based pipeline built on the open-source OpenLANE physical design flow with the Skywater 130nm process design kit.

Evaluated against ISCAS-85 and ISCAS-89 benchmark circuits, NL2GDS-generated designs outperform gate-level optimized benchmarks in nearly all power, performance, and area (PPA) metrics, achieving up to 54% area reduction, 35% delay reduction, and 70% power savings. The system also demonstrates rapid prototyping capability, generating and optimizing both combinational and pipelined 16×16 multiplier designs—including 98 optimization runs—in just one hour at a total cost of $1.12.

The significance of NL2GDS lies in its potential to dramatically lower barriers to ASIC design for researchers, educators, and small enterprises, enabling rapid architectural exploration and trade-off analysis without writing code, particularly benefiting edge-AI and IoT applications requiring efficient, rapidly deployed hardware.
original_abstract: The growing complexity of hardware design and the widening gap between high-level specifications and register-transfer level (RTL) implementation hinder rapid prototyping and system design. We introduce NL2GDS (Natural Language to Layout), a novel framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to translate natural language hardware descriptions into synthesizable RTL and complete GDSII layouts via the open-source OpenLane ASIC flow. NL2GDS employs a modular pipeline that captures informal design intent, generates HDL using multiple LLM engines and verifies them, and orchestrates automated synthesis and layout. Evaluations on ISCAS'85 and ISCAS'89 benchmark designs demonstrate up to 36% area reduction, 35% delay reduction, and 70% power savings compared to baseline designs, highlighting its potential to democratize ASIC design and accelerate hardware innovation.

title: Reasoning Theater: Disentangling Model Beliefs from Chain-of-Thought
generated_summary:
This paper investigates "performative reasoning" in large language models — instances where models generate chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens that appear to show ongoing deliberation despite having already internally committed to a final answer. The authors combine three complementary methods to track when models know their answers during reasoning: attention probes trained on internal activations, forced early answering through prompt truncation, and an external CoT monitor that reads only the generated text.

The key finding is a difficulty-dependent split in CoT faithfulness. On easier benchmarks like MMLU-Redux, attention probes can decode the model's final answer far earlier than the CoT monitor detects commitment, indicating that subsequent reasoning tokens are largely performative. On harder tasks like GPQA-Diamond, internal confidence and verbalized reasoning evolve more gradually in parallel, suggesting genuine test-time computation. Larger models exhibit more performative reasoning on easy tasks, while smaller models require more tokens to reach conclusions. Importantly, the authors find that reasoning inflection points — backtracking, "aha" moments, and reconsiderations — predominantly occur in responses with genuine internal uncertainty shifts, indicating these are not theatrical but reflect authentic belief updates.

The practical implications are significant: well-calibrated probes enable early exit strategies that save up to 80% of generated tokens on MMLU-Redux without sacrificing accuracy, and the findings caution against relying solely on CoT text for safety monitoring of reasoning models.
original_abstract: We provide evidence of performative chain-of-thought (CoT) in reasoning models, where a model becomes strongly confident in its final answer, but continues generating tokens without revealing its internal belief. Our analysis compares activation probing, early forced answering, and a CoT monitor across two large models (DeepSeek-R1 671B & GPT-OSS 120B) and find task difficulty-specific differences: The model's final answer is decodable from activations far earlier in CoT than a monitor is able to say, especially for easy recall-based MMLU questions. We contrast this with genuine reasoning in difficult multihop GPQA-Diamond questions. Despite this, inflection points (e.g., backtracking, 'aha' moments) occur almost exclusively in responses where probes show large belief shifts, suggesting these behaviors track genuine uncertainty rather than learned "reasoning theater." Finally, probe-guided early exit reduces tokens by up to 80% on MMLU and 30% on GPQA-Diamond with similar accuracy, positioning attention probing as an efficient tool for detecting performative reasoning and enabling adaptive computation.

title: Observing and Controlling Features in Vision-Language-Action Models
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a principled framework for observing and controlling the behavior of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models through their internal representations, formalizing the concepts of feature-observability and feature-controllability for generative models. The authors propose lightweight linear observer structures that extract behaviorally relevant features—such as robot states and actions—from transformer layer activations, motivated by the linear representation hypothesis. They complement this with a linear controller that computes minimal additive perturbations to internal representations, steering observed features toward desired target regions while preserving the naturalness of model outputs. These components are integrated into an online inference-time algorithm requiring no fine-tuning or retraining.

The framework is validated on two state-of-the-art VLA architectures (π₀.₅ and OpenVLA) across the Libero and BridgeData V2 benchmarks. Results demonstrate that robot actions and states are linearly decodable from internal representations and that targeted interventions reliably steer features including gripper state, end-effector height, and speed. Critically, the method achieves near-perfect constraint satisfaction while maintaining high closed-loop task success rates above 90%, with negligible computational overhead.

The significance of this work lies in bridging mechanistic interpretability techniques from large language models to embodied AI, enabling real-time behavioral alignment of VLAs with user preferences and safety constraints—a crucial requirement for reliable real-world robotic deployment.
original_abstract: Vision-Language-Action Models (VLAs) have shown remarkable progress towards embodied intelligence. While their architecture partially resembles that of Large Language Models (LLMs), VLAs exhibit higher complexity due to their multi-modal inputs/outputs and often hybrid nature of transformer and diffusion heads. This is part of the reason why insights from mechanistic interpretability in LLMs, which explain how the internal model representations relate to their output behavior, do not trivially transfer to VLA counterparts. In this work, we propose to close this gap by introducing and analyzing two main concepts: feature-observability and feature-controllability. In particular, we first study features that are linearly encoded in representation space, and show how they can be observed by means of a linear classifier. Then, we use a minimal linear intervention grounded in optimal control to accurately place internal representations and steer the VLA's output towards a desired region. Our results show that targeted, lightweight interventions can reliably steer a robot's behavior while preserving closed-loop capabilities. We demonstrate on different VLA architectures ($π_{0.5}$ and OpenVLA) through simulation experiments that VLAs possess interpretable internal structure amenable to online adaptation without fine-tuning, enabling real-time alignment with user preferences and task requirements.

title: Improved Decoding of Quantum Tanner Codes Using Generalized Check Nodes
generated_summary:
This paper proposes an improved iterative belief propagation (BP) decoding approach for quantum Tanner codes by exploiting their inherent local code structure through generalized check nodes. Quantum Tanner codes are constructed from square complexes where constraints at each vertex form generalized checks that are more complex than simple parity checks. The authors incorporate these natural groupings into the BP decoding framework, where each generalized check node is decoded using a maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoder during check node processing. This approach is combined with quaternary BP decoding with memory effects (MBP₄) and optional ordered statistics decoding (OSD) post-processing.

Key results demonstrate that the generalized MBP₄ decoder significantly outperforms conventional MBP₄ decoding for quantum Tanner codes on the depolarizing channel, both with and without OSD post-processing. Notably, OSD post-processing becomes unnecessary for approaching best performance with the generalized decoder, unlike the conventional approach. The method also outperforms the recently proposed Relay-BP decoder with seemingly lower overall complexity. However, when applied to other quantum LDPC code families such as generalized bicycle, bivariate bicycle, and hypergraph product codes, no noticeable gains are observed.

The authors provide theoretical backing through a cycle analysis of the Tanner graphs, deriving conditions guaranteeing no four-cycles for binary decoders and methods for counting four-cycles for quaternary decoders. These findings highlight that quantum Tanner codes possess structural properties that can be uniquely leveraged for superior decoding performance in the finite-length regime.
original_abstract: We study the decoding problem for quantum Tanner codes and propose to exploit the underlying local code structure by grouping check nodes into more powerful generalized check nodes for enhanced iterative belief propagation (BP) decoding by decoding the generalized checks using a maximum a posteriori (MAP) decoder as part of the check node processing of each decoding iteration. We mainly study the finite-length setting and show that the proposed enhanced generalized BP decoder for quantum Tanner codes significantly outperforms the standard quaternary BP decoder with memory effects, as well as the recently proposed Relay-BP decoder, even outperforming generalized bicycle (GB) codes with comparable parameters in some cases. For other classes of quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes, we propose a greedy algorithm to combine checks for generalized BP decoding. However, for GB codes, bivariate bicycle codes, hypergraph product codes, and lifted-product codes, there seems to be limited gain by combining simple checks into more powerful ones. To back up our findings, we also provide a theoretical cycle analysis for the considered qLDPC codes.

title: Towards Provably Unbiased LLM Judges via Bias-Bounded Evaluation

This ensures that, with high probability, the average-case bias remains below a specified threshold, rendering bias patterns indistinguishable from noise.

The authors evaluate BBE on the Arena-Hard-Auto benchmark using four judge models, including GPT-4o-mini, QwQ-32B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B, and GPT-3.5-Turbo. They measure sensitivity along two dimensions: formatting sensitivity (response presentation variations) and schematic adherence (alignment between per-criteria and overall judgments). Results demonstrate that BBE substantially reduces variance caused by bias-induced false confidence while preserving genuine comparative signal, achieving up to 81% correlation with original rankings for QwQ-32B and near-perfect correlation with GPT-4o-mini.

The significance of this work lies in its generality and formal guarantees. Rather than addressing biases individually, BBE provides mathematical bounds applicable to any measurable bias, including adversarially discovered ones. original_abstract: As AI models progress beyond simple chatbots into more complex workflows, we draw ever closer to the event horizon beyond which AI systems will be utilized in autonomous, self-maintaining feedback loops. Any autonomous AI system will depend on automated, verifiable rewards and feedback; in settings where ground truth is sparse or non-deterministic, one practical source of such rewards is an LLM-as-a-Judge. Although LLM judges continue to improve, the literature has yet to introduce systems capable of enforcing standards with strong guarantees, particularly when bias vectors are unknown or adversarially discovered. To remedy this issue, we propose average bias-boundedness (A-BB), an algorithmic framework which formally guarantees reductions of harm/impact as a result of any measurable bias in an LLM judge. Evaluating on Arena-Hard-Auto with four LLM judges, we achieve (tau=0.5, delta=0.01) bias-bounded guarantees while retaining 61-99% correlation with original rankings across formatting and schematic bias settings, with most judge-bias combinations exceeding 80%. The code to reproduce our findings is available at https://github.com/penfever/bias-bounded-evaluation.

title: Towards Multimodal Lifelong Understanding: A Dataset and Agentic Baseline

Extensive evaluation of state-of-the-art end-to-end Multimodal Large Language Models reveals a "Working Memory Bottleneck" — performance saturates and eventually degrades as more video data is provided, due to noise accumulation and computational overhead. To address this limitation, the authors propose the Recursive Multimodal Agent (ReMA), which augments MLLMs with dynamic memory management through three core mechanisms: visual perception tools for extracting temporally aligned descriptions, memory consolidation that merges overlapping observations to prevent memory explosion, and hierarchical two-stage retrieval for synthesizing answers across disjoint temporal events. Results demonstrate that ReMA significantly outperforms both end-to-end MLLMs and standard agentic baselines, with backbone reasoning capability (e.g., GPT-5 versus Qwen3-VL) substantially influencing performance. This work highlights that active memory management, rather than passive context extension, is essential for achieving true lifelong multimodal comprehension.
original_abstract: While datasets for video understanding have scaled to hour-long durations, they typically consist of densely concatenated clips that differ from natural, unscripted daily life. To bridge this gap, we introduce MM-Lifelong, a dataset designed for Multimodal Lifelong Understanding. Comprising 181.1 hours of footage, it is structured across Day, Week, and Month scales to capture varying temporal densities. Extensive evaluations reveal two critical failure modes in current paradigms: end-to-end MLLMs suffer from a Working Memory Bottleneck due to context saturation, while representative agentic baselines experience Global Localization Collapse when navigating sparse, month-long timelines. To address this, we propose the Recursive Multimodal Agent (ReMA), which employs dynamic memory management to iteratively update a recursive belief state, significantly outperforming existing methods. Finally, we establish dataset splits designed to isolate temporal and domain biases, providing a rigorous foundation for future research in supervised learning and out-of-distribution generalization.

title: SurvHTE-Bench: A Benchmark for Heterogeneous Treatment Effect Estimation in Survival Analysis

Notably, S-learners and matching-learners among survival meta-learners demonstrate particular robustness under severe assumption violations and high censoring rates. original_abstract: Estimating heterogeneous treatment effects (HTEs) from right-censored survival data is critical in high-stakes applications such as precision medicine and individualized policy-making. Yet, the survival analysis setting poses unique challenges for HTE estimation due to censoring, unobserved counterfactuals, and complex identification assumptions. Despite recent advances, from Causal Survival Forests to survival meta-learners and outcome imputation approaches, evaluation practices remain fragmented and inconsistent. We introduce SurvHTE-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark for HTE estimation with censored outcomes. The benchmark spans (i) a modular suite of synthetic datasets with known ground truth, systematically varying causal assumptions and survival dynamics, (ii) semi-synthetic datasets that pair real-world covariates with simulated treatments and outcomes, and (iii) real-world datasets from a twin study (with known ground truth) and from an HIV clinical trial. Across synthetic, semi-synthetic, and real-world settings, we provide the first rigorous comparison of survival HTE methods under diverse conditions and realistic assumption violations. SurvHTE-Bench establishes a foundation for fair, reproducible, and extensible evaluation of causal survival methods. The data and code of our benchmark are available at: https://github.com/Shahriarnz14/SurvHTE-Bench .

title: Finding Short Paths on Simple Polytopes
generated_summary:
This paper resolves several longstanding open questions about the computational complexity of finding shortest paths on simple polytopes, with direct implications for understanding the simplex method for linear programming. The main contributions are proving that computing shortest paths, shortest monotone paths, and combinatorial diameters of simple polytopes are all NP-hard problems.

The methodology centers on reducing from known hard problems to shortest path computations on fractional knapsack polytopes, which are simple. The authors leverage geometric insights about slicing hypercubes with hyperplanes to construct their hardness gadgets. For the diameter result, they develop a novel truncation-based polyhedral construction that, unlike previous approaches by Frieze and Teng, preserves simplicity of the polytope while reducing shortest path computation to diameter computation.

Key results include: (1) computing distances between vertices on simple polytopes is NP-hard, even when checking whether paths shorter than the Hirsch bound exist; (2) finding shortest monotone paths—directly corresponding to optimal simplex method execution—is NP-hard; and (3) computing the combinatorial diameter of simple polytopes is NP-hard, resolving a problem posed by Kaibel and Pfetsch in 2003. On the positive side, the authors show that short paths on rock extensions (special polytopes relevant to Smale's 9th problem) can be found in weakly polynomial time, establishing that a strongly polynomial simplex method exists if and only if strongly polynomial linear programming exists.

These results fundamentally clarify the computational barriers facing the simplex method.
original_abstract: We prove that computing a shortest monotone path to the optimum of a linear program over a simple polytope is NP-hard, thus resolving a 2022 open question of De Loera, Kafer, and Sanità. As a consequence, finding a shortest sequence of pivots to an optimal basis with the simplex method is NP-hard. In fact, we show this is NP-hard already for fractional knapsack polytopes. By applying an additional polyhedral construction, we show that computing the diameter of a simple polytope is NP-hard, resolving a 2003 open problem by Kaibel and Pfetsch. Finally, on the positive side we show that every polytope has a small, simple extended formulation for which a linear length path may be found between any pair of vertices in polynomial time building upon a result of Kaibel and Kukharenko.

title: Thermodynamic Response Functions in Singular Bayesian Models
generated_summary:
This paper proposes a thermodynamic framework for understanding Bayesian model evaluation in singular statistical models, where parameter non-identifiability causes classical asymptotic theory to fail. The central contribution is demonstrating that widely used Bayesian complexity measures—including the widely applicable information criterion (WAIC) and singular fluctuation—can be interpreted as thermodynamic response functions generated by posterior tempering, where an inverse temperature parameter continuously reweights the likelihood relative to the prior.

The authors formalize an "observable algebra" by quotienting out functions constant along non-identifiable parameter directions, separating parameterization artifacts from statistically meaningful quantities. Using a covariance identity relating temperature derivatives to posterior fluctuations, they define order parameters, susceptibilities, and complexity responses that form a hierarchical diagnostic framework. This approach is validated empirically on three canonical singular models: Gaussian mixture models (symmetry breaking), reduced-rank regression (algebraic singularity), and overparameterized neural networks (hidden-unit redundancy).

Across all three settings, the authors observe consistent qualitative behavior: order parameters smoothly track effective model complexity, susceptibilities exhibit sharp peaks near structural transitions in posterior geometry, and WAIC complexity aligns with regions of maximal fluctuation. These results demonstrate that information criteria correspond to response functions of the tempered posterior distribution. The framework provides finite-sample diagnostics complementary to asymptotic invariants from singular learning theory and suggests that statistical physics tools—particularly response theory—offer a principled organizational language for understanding modern overparameterized models.
original_abstract: Singular statistical models-including mixtures, matrix factorization, and neural networks-violate regular asymptotics due to parameter non-identifiability and degenerate Fisher geometry. Although singular learning theory characterizes marginal likelihood behavior through invariants such as the real log canonical threshold and singular fluctuation, these quantities remain difficult to interpret operationally. At the same time, widely used criteria such as WAIC and WBIC appear disconnected from underlying singular geometry. We show that posterior tempering induces a one-parameter deformation of the posterior distribution whose associated observables generate a hierarchy of thermodynamic response functions. A universal covariance identity links derivatives of tempered expectations to posterior fluctuations, placing WAIC, WBIC, and singular fluctuation within a unified response framework. Within this framework, classical quantities from singular learning theory acquire natural thermodynamic interpretations: RLCT governs the leading free-energy slope, singular fluctuation corresponds to curvature of the tempered free energy, and WAIC measures predictive fluctuation. We formalize an observable algebra that quotients out non-identifiable directions, allowing structurally meaningful order parameters to be constructed in singular models. Across canonical singular examples-including symmetric Gaussian mixtures, reduced-rank regression, and overparameterized neural networks-we empirically demonstrate phase-transition-like behavior under tempering. Order parameters collapse, susceptibilities peak, and complexity measures align with structural reorganization in posterior geometry. Our results suggest that thermodynamic response theory provides a natural organizing framework for interpreting complexity, predictive variability, and structural reorganization in singular Bayesian learning.

title: Towards 3D Scene Understanding of Gas Plumes in LWIR Hyperspectral Images Using Neural Radiance Fields
generated_summary:
This paper presents the first application of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) to longwave infrared (LWIR) hyperspectral imagery for 3D scene understanding and gas plume analysis. The authors propose several modifications to the Mip-NeRF architecture to improve performance with limited training views, which is critical since multi-view LWIR hyperspectral datasets are scarce in practice.

The methodology combines multi-channel density outputs, which allow the network to learn wavelength-dependent volumetric densities aligned with gas absorption physics, with geometry regularization from RegNeRF for sparse-view settings. A three-part spectral loss function is introduced, incorporating standard L2 loss, Spectral Angle Mapper (SAM) loss to preserve spectral shape, and a novel adaptive weighted L2 loss that dynamically emphasizes spectral channels with higher reconstruction errors, improving gas plume detection performance.

Using simulated LWIR hyperspectral data of a sulfur hexafluoride plume generated with the DIRSIG software suite, the authors demonstrate that their method achieves comparable image reconstruction quality to baseline Mip-NeRF while requiring 40–60% fewer training images. With 20 training images, the proposed method achieves a PSNR of 36.7 dB, matching Mip-NeRF's performance at 50 images. Gas plume detection using the Adaptive Coherence Estimator on NeRF-rendered views shows substantially improved true positive rates with minimal false positives.

This work establishes that NeRFs can create cohesive 3D representations of LWIR hyperspectral scenes while preserving radiometric information sufficient for gas plume detection, opening pathways for enhanced 3D gas plume analysis.
original_abstract: Hyperspectral images (HSI) have many applications, ranging from environmental monitoring to national security, and can be used for material detection and identification. Longwave infrared (LWIR) HSI can be used for gas plume detection and analysis. Oftentimes, only a few images of a scene of interest are available and are analyzed individually. The ability to combine information from multiple images into a single, cohesive representation could enhance analysis by providing more context on the scene's geometry and spectral properties. Neural radiance fields (NeRFs) create a latent neural representation of volumetric scene properties that enable novel-view rendering and geometry reconstruction, offering a promising avenue for hyperspectral 3D scene reconstruction. We explore the possibility of using NeRFs to create 3D scene reconstructions from LWIR HSI and demonstrate that the model can be used for the basic downstream analysis task of gas plume detection. The physics-based DIRSIG software suite was used to generate a synthetic multi-view LWIR HSI dataset of a simple facility with a strong sulfur hexafluoride gas plume. Our method, built on the standard Mip-NeRF architecture, combines state-of-the-art methods for hyperspectral NeRFs and sparse-view NeRFs, along with a novel adaptive weighted MSE loss. Our final NeRF method requires around 50% fewer training images than the standard Mip-NeRF and achieves an average PSNR of 39.8 dB with as few as 30 training images. Gas plume detection applied to NeRF-rendered test images using the adaptive coherence estimator achieves an average AUC of 0.821 when compared with detection masks generated from ground-truth test images.

title: Leveraging LLM Parametric Knowledge for Fact Checking without Retrieval
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the task of **fact-checking without retrieval**, where the factuality of atomic claims is assessed using only an LLM's internal parametric knowledge, without querying external databases or retrieval systems. This setting contrasts with dominant retrieval-based approaches like FActScore and SAFE, which depend on external evidence and face challenges related to latency, retrieval quality, and scalability.

The authors propose a comprehensive evaluation framework spanning nine datasets across five generalization dimensions: long-tail knowledge, claim source variation, multilingual claims, long-form generation, and cross-model claims. They benchmark 18 methods using three models (Llama 3.1, Ministral, and Phi-4) and introduce INTRA, a method that leverages interactions between internal hidden-state representations across layers and tokens to detect factual errors.

Key findings reveal that methods exploiting internal model representations consistently outperform logit-based uncertainty signals. INTRA achieves state-of-the-art average performance, outperforming the second-best method (Sheeps) by 2.7% in ROC-AUC across datasets for Llama 3.1 and by 1.3% across all models, while demonstrating strong robustness across diverse evaluation settings. The authors also identify that middle layers are particularly informative for factuality detection and that widely used rule-generated benchmarks may be saturated due to contamination.

This work establishes a foundation for lightweight, scalable claim verification and opens directions for integrating truthfulness signals directly into LLM generation processes, including as reward models for alignment training.
original_abstract: Trustworthiness is a core research challenge for agentic AI systems built on Large Language Models (LLMs). To enhance trust, natural language claims from diverse sources, including human-written text, web content, and model outputs, are commonly checked for factuality by retrieving external knowledge and using an LLM to verify the faithfulness of claims to the retrieved evidence. As a result, such methods are constrained by retrieval errors and external data availability, while leaving the models intrinsic fact-verification capabilities largely unused. We propose the task of fact-checking without retrieval, focusing on the verification of arbitrary natural language claims, independent of their source. To study this setting, we introduce a comprehensive evaluation framework focused on generalization, testing robustness to (i) long-tail knowledge, (ii) variation in claim sources, (iii) multilinguality, and (iv) long-form generation. Across 9 datasets, 18 methods and 3 models, our experiments indicate that logit-based approaches often underperform compared to those that leverage internal model representations. Building on this finding, we introduce INTRA, a method that exploits interactions between internal representations and achieves state-of-the-art performance with strong generalization. More broadly, our work establishes fact-checking without retrieval as a promising research direction that can complement retrieval-based frameworks, improve scalability, and enable the use of such systems as reward signals during training or as components integrated into the generation process.

title: Kraus Constrained Sequence Learning For Quantum Trajectories from Continuous Measurement
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a Kraus-structured output layer that enforces complete positivity and trace preservation (CPTP) constraints on neural network predictions for quantum trajectory estimation from continuous measurement records. The key idea is to parameterize the network's output as a Kraus map, ensuring that predicted quantum states remain physically valid by construction, regardless of the backbone architecture. This approach is evaluated as a drop-in layer across six sequence model families—GRU, LSTM, vanilla RNN, TCN, ESN, and Mamba—on a challenging non-stationary benchmark featuring abrupt orthogonal Hamiltonian switches with randomized parameters.

The results demonstrate that the Kraus layer provides consistent fidelity improvements across most architectures, effectively serving as a physics-informed regularizer. Gated recurrent networks (Kraus-GRU and Kraus-LSTM) achieve the highest performance, attributed to the structural alignment between gated recurrence and the Markovian, sequential nature of the underlying stochastic master equation. Their selective memory reset mechanisms enable rapid re-identification of new dynamics within 10–20 timesteps after regime switches, with minimal fidelity degradation. In contrast, architectures with smoothness priors (Mamba, Neural ODE) exhibit inertial lag of 50–100 timesteps post-switch, while fixed-dynamics models (ESN) and finite-receptive-field architectures (TCN) show more limited benefits.

This work provides a principled framework for incorporating quantum mechanical constraints into data-driven state estimation, enabling physically guaranteed trajectory predictions without requiring complete knowledge of the underlying system model.
original_abstract: Real-time reconstruction of conditional quantum states from continuous measurement records is a fundamental requirement for quantum feedback control, yet standard stochastic master equation (SME) solvers require exact model specification, known system parameters, and are sensitive to parameter mismatch. While neural sequence models can fit these stochastic dynamics, the unconstrained predictors can violate physicality such as positivity or trace constraints, leading to unstable rollouts and unphysical estimates. We propose a Kraus-structured output layer that converts the hidden representation of a generic sequence backbone into a completely positive trace preserving (CPTP) quantum operation, yielding physically valid state updates by construction. We instantiate this layer across diverse backbones, RNN, GRU, LSTM, TCN, ESN and Mamba; including Neural ODE as a comparative baseline, on stochastic trajectories characterized by parameter drift. Our evaluation reveals distinct trade-offs between gating mechanisms, linear recurrence, and global attention. Across all models, Kraus-LSTM achieves the strongest results, improving state estimation quality by 7% over its unconstrained counterpart while guaranteeing physically valid predictions in non-stationary regimes.

title: HALP: Detecting Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models without Generating a Single Token
generated_summary:
This paper introduces HALP (HALlucination Prediction via Pre-Generation Probing), a lightweight framework that detects hallucination risk in vision-language models (VLMs) before any output tokens are generated. Unlike existing approaches that require complete caption generation or decoding-time interventions, HALP performs a single forward pass over an image-query pair and extracts three types of internal representations: pooled visual features from the vision encoder, decoder states at the last vision token position across multiple layers, and decoder states at the final query token position at corresponding depths. Simple MLP probes trained on these representations estimate whether a model is likely to hallucinate based solely on pre-generative internal states.

The authors construct a 10,000-example benchmark spanning diverse hallucination stressors, including object presence, diagram and math reasoning, compositional knowledge, illusion-style traps, and targeted hallucination cases. Experiments across eight state-of-the-art open-source VLMs demonstrate that hallucination signals are reliably accessible before generation begins. Query-token representations near the top of the decoder prove most predictive, achieving AUROC scores of approximately 0.93 for Gemma-3, Phi-4-VL, and Molmo. Notably, the most informative representation locus varies by architecture—some models like Qwen-2.5-VL achieve strong detection from visual features alone, suggesting distinct failure pathways.

HALP offers a practical, low-cost solution for real-time hallucination risk assessment, enabling potential applications in early refusal mechanisms, adaptive routing, and confidence-aware generation without the computational burden of full decoding.
original_abstract: Hallucinations remain a persistent challenge for vision-language models (VLMs), which often describe nonexistent objects or fabricate facts. Existing detection methods typically operate after text generation, making intervention both costly and untimely. We investigate whether hallucination risk can instead be predicted before any token is generated by probing a model's internal representations in a single forward pass. Across a diverse set of vision-language tasks and eight modern VLMs, including Llama-3.2-Vision, Gemma-3, Phi-4-VL, and Qwen2.5-VL, we examine three families of internal representations: (i) visual-only features without multimodal fusion, (ii) vision-token representations within the text decoder, and (iii) query-token representations that integrate visual and textual information before generation. Probes trained on these representations achieve strong hallucination-detection performance without decoding, reaching up to 0.93 AUROC on Gemma-3-12B, Phi-4-VL 5.6B, and Molmo 7B. Late query-token states are the most predictive for most models, while visual or mid-layer features dominate in a few architectures (e.g., ~0.79 AUROC for Qwen2.5-VL-7B using visual-only features). These results demonstrate that (1) hallucination risk is detectable pre-generation, (2) the most informative layer and modality vary across architectures, and (3) lightweight probes have the potential to enable early abstention, selective routing, and adaptive decoding to improve both safety and efficiency.

title: EdgeDAM: Real-time Object Tracking for Mobile Devices
generated_summary:
EdgeDAM introduces a lightweight single-object tracking framework designed for real-time deployment on mobile and edge devices, addressing the fundamental trade-off between robustness under occlusion/distractor interference and computational efficiency. The key contribution is a bounding-box-level Distractor-Aware Memory (DAM) module featuring dual buffers: a Recent-Aware Memory (RAM) that stores geometrically verified target states through IoU and area-consistency gating, and a Distractor-Resolving Memory (DRM) that maintains stable appearance anchors for recovery after occlusion. Unlike segmentation-based approaches such as SAM2.1++, EdgeDAM requires no mask supervision, transformer inference, or cross-frame attention mechanisms.

The framework combines a category-agnostic single-class YOLOv11s detector with a CSRT correlation-filter tracker, employing confidence-driven switching and held-box recovery mechanisms to suppress distractor contamination during occlusion. The system is detector-agnostic, supporting any YOLO variant without architectural modifications.

Extensive evaluation across six benchmarks demonstrates strong performance: EdgeDAM achieves 0.926 quality on DiDi (+23.2% over SAM2.1++), 0.849 EAO on VOT2020, and 0.895 AUC on LaSOT, while running at 25 FPS on an iPhone 15 Pro Max. Ablation studies confirm that each component contributes independently, with a 10-10 RAM-DRM buffer configuration providing optimal accuracy-efficiency balance. EdgeDAM establishes a new operating point for edge-deployed tracking, demonstrating that explicit distractor reasoning can be achieved through lightweight geometric operations without heavy memory-based architectures.
original_abstract: Single-object tracking (SOT) on edge devices is a critical computer vision task, requiring accurate and continuous target localization across video frames under occlusion, distractor interference, and fast motion. However, recent state-of-the-art distractor-aware memory mechanisms are largely built on segmentation-based trackers and rely on mask prediction and attention-driven memory updates, which introduce substantial computational overhead and limit real-time deployment on resource-constrained hardware; meanwhile, lightweight trackers sustain high throughput but are prone to drift when visually similar distractors appear. To address these challenges, we propose EdgeDAM, a lightweight detection-guided tracking framework that reformulates distractor-aware memory for bounding-box tracking under strict edge constraints. EdgeDAM introduces two key strategies: (1) Dual-Buffer Distractor-Aware Memory (DAM), which integrates a Recent-Aware Memory to preserve temporally consistent target hypotheses and a Distractor-Resolving Memory to explicitly store hard negative candidates and penalize their re-selection during recovery; and (2) Confidence-Driven Switching with Held-Box Stabilization, where tracker reliability and temporal consistency criteria adaptively activate detection and memory-guided re-identification during occlusion, while a held-box mechanism temporarily freezes and expands the estimate to suppress distractor contamination. Extensive experiments on five benchmarks, including the distractor-focused DiDi dataset, demonstrate improved robustness under occlusion and fast motion while maintaining real-time performance on mobile devices, achieving 88.2% accuracy on DiDi and 25 FPS on an iPhone 15. Code will be released.

title: NCTB-QA: A Large-Scale Bangla Educational Question Answering Dataset and Benchmarking Performance
generated_summary:

The dataset addresses key limitations of existing Bangla QA resources by offering substantially greater scale, educational domain specificity, a balanced distribution of answerable and unanswerable questions, and adversarially designed unanswerable instances that require genuine contextual reasoning rather than superficial pattern matching.

NCTB-QA fills a critical gap in low-resource language NLP by providing a publicly available, educationally grounded benchmark that can advance Bangla reading comprehension research and support educational technology development for over 230 million Bangla speakers.
original_abstract: Reading comprehension systems for low-resource languages face significant challenges in handling unanswerable questions. These systems tend to produce unreliable responses when correct answers are absent from context. To solve this problem, we introduce NCTB-QA, a large-scale Bangla question answering dataset comprising 87,805 question-answer pairs extracted from 50 textbooks published by Bangladesh's National Curriculum and Textbook Board. Unlike existing Bangla datasets, NCTB-QA maintains a balanced distribution of answerable (57.25%) and unanswerable (42.75%) questions. NCTB-QA also includes adversarially designed instances containing plausible distractors. We benchmark three transformer-based models (BERT, RoBERTa, ELECTRA) and demonstrate substantial improvements through fine-tuning. BERT achieves 313% relative improvement in F1 score (0.150 to 0.620). Semantic answer quality measured by BERTScore also increases significantly across all models. Our results establish NCTB-QA as a challenging benchmark for Bangla educational question answering. This study demonstrates that domain-specific fine-tuning is critical for robust performance in low-resource settings.

title: Equilibrium for max-plus payoff
generated_summary:
This paper investigates non-cooperative games under uncertainty using a framework based on capacities (non-additive measures) and max-plus integrals, a type of fuzzy integral combining maximum and addition operations. The main contribution is the analysis of two distinct equilibrium concepts for games with max-plus payoff functions: Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies represented by capacities, and equilibrium under uncertainty in the sense of Dow and Werlang, where players select pure strategies while holding non-additive beliefs about opponents' actions.

The methodology employs tools from idempotent (max-plus) convexity theory and abstract fixed point theorems. For games with compact strategy spaces and continuous payoff functions, the author establishes existence results for both equilibrium notions. A key finding is that Nash equilibria in the full space of capacities always exist due to extremal elements, but the existence problem becomes nontrivial when restricted to possibility capacities. Using idempotent convexity structures, the author proves the existence of Nash min-equilibria in this restricted setting. For equilibrium under uncertainty, existence is demonstrated for games with possibility-valued beliefs, with equilibria representable via tensor products of individual possibility capacities.

The paper further clarifies the relationship between the two equilibrium concepts: while they do not generally coincide, equilibrium under uncertainty implies Nash equilibrium when players use possibility capacities. This work provides a natural bridge between capacity theory and idempotent analysis, extending equilibrium theory to qualitative decision-making settings where precise probabilistic information is unavailable.
original_abstract: We study equilibrium concepts in non-cooperative games under uncertainty where both beliefs and mixed strategies are represented by non-additive measures (capacities). In contrast to the classical Nash framework based on additive probabilities and linear convexity, we employ capacities and max-plus integrals to model qualitative and idempotent decision criteria. Two equilibrium notions are investigated: Nash equilibrium in mixed strategies expressed by capacities, and equilibrium under uncertainty in the sense of Dow and Werlang, where players choose pure strategies but evaluate payoffs with respect to non-additive beliefs. For games with compact strategy spaces and continuous payoffs, we establish existence results for both equilibrium concepts using abstract convexity techniques and a Kakutani-type fixed point theorem.

title: DEBISS: a Corpus of Individual, Semi-structured and Spoken Debates
