The methodology involves recording semi-structured debates on "Generative Artificial Intelligence and Its Impacts on Society," organized across 16 groups of 3-5 participants. Each session follows a standardized three-part format: initial stances, question-and-answer rounds, and final reflections. Audio transcription combines automatic speech-to-text processing using Azure's model with manual correction and speaker identification. The corpus is enriched with self-evaluation and peer assessment data collected through structured questionnaires.

The resulting dataset supports multiple NLP tasks and has spawned two derivative resources: DEBISS-Arg, annotated for argument mining with discourse units, argumentative components, and relation labels at micro and macro levels; and DEBISS-Eval, featuring expert evaluations from five linguist judges assessing debater quality across criteria including organization, argumentation, persuasion, and clarity. The corpus has also been applied to disfluency detection research using large language models.

DEBISS represents a significant contribution to open NLP resources for Brazilian Portuguese, offering multimodal data valuable for argument mining, debater quality analysis, speaker diarization, and speech processing research, while providing a replicable methodology for future debate corpus construction.
original_abstract: The process of debating is essential in our daily lives, whether in studying, work activities, simple everyday discussions, political debates on TV, or online discussions on social networks. The range of uses for debates is broad. Due to the diverse applications, structures, and formats of debates, developing corpora that account for these variations can be challenging, and the scarcity of debate corpora in the state of the art is notable. For this reason, the current research proposes the DEBISS corpus: a collection of spoken and individual debates with semi-structured features. With a broad range of NLP task annotations, such as speech-to-text, speaker diarization, argument mining, and debater quality assessment.

title: Beyond Scattered Acceptance: Fast and Coherent Inference for DLMs via Longest Stable Prefixes
generated_summary:
This paper identifies scattered token acceptance as a fundamental bottleneck in Diffusion Language Model (DLM) inference and proposes the Longest Stable Prefix (LSP) scheduler as a solution. The authors argue that conventional strategies, which commit tokens independently based on local confidence, create fragmented sequences that destroy KV cache locality and require costly repair cycles, undermining the parallel generation advantage of DLMs.

LSP is a training-free, model-agnostic scheduling paradigm that commits the longest contiguous, stable prefix of the active sequence in each iteration through three integrated mechanisms: a logit-margin stability diagnostic that assesses token confidence, adaptive thresholding that dynamically adjusts commitment size to achieve geometric decay of the active sequence, and structural boundary snapping that aligns commitment endpoints with natural delimiters such as punctuation or code symbols. A fallback rule guarantees at least one token is committed per step.

Evaluated on LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B across GSM8K, HumanEval, and MBPP benchmarks, LSP achieves up to 3.4× speedup over full-budget decoding while preserving or slightly improving generation quality. Ablation studies confirm each component's contribution, and analysis shows LSP reduces the token flip rate from 14.2% to 4.3%, demonstrating that freezing coherent prefixes stabilizes subsequent generation rather than constraining it. This work demonstrates that commitment topology, not just model architecture, is critical for realizing the efficiency potential of diffusion-based text generation.
original_abstract: Diffusion Language Models (DLMs) promise highly parallel text generation, yet their practical inference speed is often bottlenecked by suboptimal decoding schedulers. Standard approaches rely on 'scattered acceptance'-committing high confidence tokens at disjoint positions throughout the sequence. This approach inadvertently fractures the Key-Value (KV) cache, destroys memory locality, and forces the model into costly, repeated repairs across unstable token boundaries. To resolve this, we present the Longest Stable Prefix (LSP) scheduler, a training-free and model-agnostic inference paradigm based on monolithic prefix absorption. In each denoising step, LSP evaluates token stability via a single forward pass, dynamically identifies a contiguous left-aligned block of stable predictions, and snaps its boundary to natural linguistic or structural delimiters before an atomic commitment. This prefix-first topology yields dual benefits: systemically, it converts fragmented KV cache updates into efficient, contiguous appends; algorithmically, it preserves bidirectional lookahead over a geometrically shrinking active suffix, drastically reducing token flip rates and denoiser calls. Extensive evaluations on LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B demonstrate that LSP accelerates inference by up to 3.4x across rigorous benchmarks including mathematical reasoning, code generation, multilingual (CJK) tasks, and creative writing while matching or slightly improving output quality. By fundamentally restructuring the commitment topology, LSP bridges the gap between the theoretical parallelism of DLMs and practical hardware efficiency.

title: FlashAttention-4: Algorithm and Kernel Pipelining Co-Design for Asymmetric Hardware Scaling
generated_summary:
FlashAttention-4 introduces an algorithm-kernel co-design approach for efficient attention computation on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, addressing the fundamental challenge of asymmetric hardware scaling where tensor core throughput doubles over previous generations while other functional units—shared memory bandwidth, exponential units, and ALUs—scale more slowly, creating new computational bottlenecks.

The methodology centers on identifying and mitigating these shifted bottlenecks through several innovations. For the forward pass, the authors develop redesigned software pipelines exploiting Blackwell's fully asynchronous MMA operations and larger 128×128 tiles, implement software-emulated exponential functions via polynomial approximation to bypass exponential unit limitations, and introduce conditional softmax rescaling to skip unnecessary operations. For the backward pass, they leverage tensor memory to reduce shared memory traffic and employ Blackwell's 2-CTA MMA mode to halve atomic reductions. The entire implementation uses CuTe-DSL embedded in Python, achieving 20-30× faster compile times compared to C++ template approaches.

Benchmarks on the B200 GPU demonstrate that FlashAttention-4 achieves up to 1.3× speedup over cuDNN and 2.7× over Triton implementations in BF16, reaching approximately 1600 TFLOPS (71% of theoretical peak). The work also provides a deterministic execution mode with minimal overhead for reproducible training. This contribution is significant as the AI industry rapidly transitions to Blackwell-based datacenter systems, and the open-source release enables broad adoption across the research community.
original_abstract: Attention, as a core layer of the ubiquitous Transformer architecture, is the bottleneck for large language models and long-context applications. While FlashAttention-3 optimized attention for Hopper GPUs through asynchronous execution and warp specialization, it primarily targets the H100 architecture. The AI industry has rapidly transitioned to deploying Blackwell-based systems such as the B200 and GB200, which exhibit fundamentally different performance characteristics due to asymmetric hardware scaling: tensor core throughput doubles while other functional units (shared memory bandwidth, exponential units) scale more slowly or remain unchanged. We develop several techniques to address these shifting bottlenecks on Blackwell GPUs: (1) redesigned pipelines that exploit fully asynchronous MMA operations and larger tile sizes, (2) software-emulated exponential and conditional softmax rescaling that reduces non-matmul operations, and (3) leveraging tensor memory and the 2-CTA MMA mode to reduce shared memory traffic and atomic adds in the backward pass. We demonstrate that our method, FlashAttention-4, achieves up to 1.3$\times$ speedup over cuDNN 9.13 and 2.7$\times$ over Triton on B200 GPUs with BF16, reaching up to 1613 TFLOPs/s (71% utilization). Beyond algorithmic innovations, we implement FlashAttention-4 entirely in CuTe-DSL embedded in Python, achieving 20-30$\times$ faster compile times compared to traditional C++ template-based approaches while maintaining full expressivity.

title: Distributed Partial Information Puzzles: Examining Common Ground Construction Under Epistemic Asymmetry
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the Distributed Partial Information Puzzle (DPIP), a collaborative construction task designed to study common ground construction under epistemic asymmetry in multiparty, co-situated interactions. In the task, three directors each receive partial information about a goal structure and must collaboratively instruct a builder to construct a single structure consistent with all three views, requiring participants to negotiate and share privately-held information across multiple modalities.

The authors present a dataset of ten annotated DPIP interactions featuring speech transcriptions, gestures, and actions, along with cross-modal propositional annotations and belief state tracking. They develop an axiomatic common ground inference module grounded in dynamic epistemic logic, operating on three principles: seeing is believing, acting is believing, and saying is believing. These axioms incrementally construct shared belief sets as participants interact. The framework is evaluated alongside state-of-the-art LLMs (Qwen3-4B, LLaMA-3.2-3B, and GPT-5/GPT-5-mini) across four experimental conditions: predicting structure states from actions, from aligned multimodal annotations, from axiomatic common ground calculations, and predicting common ground from aligned annotations.

Results demonstrate that this task setting poses substantial challenges for current LLMs in modeling belief states, group dynamics, and task progress. The work establishes a challenging new benchmark for multimodal dialogue research, with implications for common ground tracking, theory of mind modeling in small groups, and spatiotemporal reasoning.
original_abstract: Establishing common ground, a shared set of beliefs and mutually recognized facts, is fundamental to collaboration, yet remains a challenge for current AI systems, especially in multimodal, multiparty settings, where the collaborators bring different information to the table. We introduce the Distributed Partial Information Puzzle (DPIP), a collaborative construction task that elicits rich multimodal communication under epistemic asymmetry. We present a multimodal dataset of these interactions, annotated and temporally aligned across speech, gesture, and action modalities to support reasoning over propositional content and belief dynamics. We then evaluate two paradigms for modeling common ground (CG): (1) state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), prompted to infer shared beliefs from multimodal updates, and (2) an axiomatic pipeline grounded in Dynamic Epistemic Logic (DEL) that incrementally performs the same task. Results on the annotated DPIP data indicate that it poses a challenge to modern LLMs' abilities to track both task progression and belief state.

title: RealWonder: Real-Time Physical Action-Conditioned Video Generation
generated_summary:
RealWonder introduces the first real-time streaming system for physical action-conditioned video generation, capable of accepting 3D physical actions such as forces, torques, robot manipulations, and camera controls as input. The key innovation lies in using physics simulation as an intermediate representation that bridges the gap between continuous physical actions and video generation models, thereby avoiding the difficult problems of tokenizing unbounded continuous actions and collecting paired action-video training data.

The system comprises three components: a 3D scene reconstruction module that lifts input images into simulatable representations, a physics simulator (Genesis) that computes action consequences as optical flow and coarse RGB previews, and a distilled flow-conditioned video generator that synthesizes photorealistic results. The video model is trained using LoRA modules on 200K flow-video pairs and further distilled for real-time performance using Self Forcing-style training, requiring approximately 128 A100 GPU-days of compute.

RealWonder achieves up to 13.2 FPS at 480×832 resolution on a single GPU, enabling interactive streaming generation across diverse materials including rigid objects, deformable bodies, fluids, and granular substances. Quantitative evaluations, including VBench metrics and a 400-participant user study, demonstrate significant advantages over baselines like PhysGaussian, CogVideoX-I2V, and Tora in action following, physical plausibility, and visual quality. Ablation studies confirm that both flow and RGB conditioning signals are essential. The system opens new possibilities for robotics simulation, motion planning, and AR/VR applications requiring real-time physical interaction feedback.
original_abstract: Current video generation models cannot simulate physical consequences of 3D actions like forces and robotic manipulations, as they lack structural understanding of how actions affect 3D scenes. We present RealWonder, the first real-time system for action-conditioned video generation from a single image. Our key insight is using physics simulation as an intermediate bridge: instead of directly encoding continuous actions, we translate them through physics simulation into visual representations (optical flow and RGB) that video models can process. RealWonder integrates three components: 3D reconstruction from single images, physics simulation, and a distilled video generator requiring only 4 diffusion steps. Our system achieves 13.2 FPS at 480x832 resolution, enabling interactive exploration of forces, robot actions, and camera controls on rigid objects, deformable bodies, fluids, and granular materials. We envision RealWonder opens new opportunities to apply video models in immersive experiences, AR/VR, and robot learning. Our code and model weights are publicly available in our project website: https://liuwei283.github.io/RealWonder/

title: Residual RL--MPC for Robust Microrobotic Cell Pushing Under Time-Varying Flow
generated_summary:
This paper presents ResRL+MPC, a contact-gated residual reinforcement learning architecture that augments model predictive control (MPC) for robust microrobotic cell pushing under time-varying Poiseuille flow in microfluidic environments. The key novelty is a hybrid controller where a Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) learned policy provides bounded velocity corrections only during confirmed robot–cell contact, while the nominal MPC handles the approach phase. This contact gating stabilizes training, prevents erratic exploration during sensitive contact acquisition, and preserves the interpretable structure of the baseline controller.

The methodology enforces a shared speed envelope across all compared methods—ResRL+MPC, pure MPC, and PID—ensuring that performance differences reflect decision quality rather than stronger actuation. The residual policy is trained on a compact clover curve with randomized initial conditions and time-varying flow, then evaluated on both seen (Clover) and unseen (Circle, Square) geometries. A residual-bound sweep reveals an authority–stability trade-off, with an intermediate bound of 15% of the speed envelope yielding optimal performance.

Across all three trajectory types under nonstationary disturbances, ResRL+MPC consistently improves success rate, progress ratio, and tracking accuracy compared to pure MPC and PID baselines. The learned corrections effectively suppress lateral drift spikes that cause baseline failures during sharp curvature changes. This work demonstrates that combining model-based structure with targeted data-driven adaptation offers a practical path toward robust autonomous micromanipulation, with planned future deployment on physical magnetic actuation systems.
original_abstract: Contact-rich micromanipulation in microfluidic flow is challenging because small disturbances can break pushing contact and induce large lateral drift. We study planar cell pushing with a magnetic rolling microrobot that tracks a waypoint-sampled reference curve under time-varying Poiseuille flow. We propose a hybrid controller that augments a nominal MPC with a learned residual policy trained by SAC. The policy outputs a bounded 2D velocity correction that is contact-gated, so residual actions are applied only during robot--cell contact, preserving reliable approach behavior and stabilizing learning. All methods share the same actuation interface and speed envelope for fair comparisons. Experiments show improved robustness and tracking accuracy over pure MPC and PID under nonstationary flow, with generalization from a clover training curve to unseen circle and square trajectories. A residual-bound sweep identifies an intermediate correction limit as the best trade-off, which we use in all benchmarks.

title: NaiLIA: Multimodal Nail Design Retrieval Based on Dense Intent Descriptions and Palette Queries
generated_summary:
NaiLIA is a multimodal retrieval model designed to search nail design images using dense intent descriptions and optional palette queries that specify desired colors. The work addresses the challenge that nail design descriptions are inherently multi-layered, encompassing visual attributes, themes, and impressions, while existing vision-language models exhibit biases toward photorealistic interpretations and fail to capture subtle color nuances.

The proposed model comprises three modules: the Intent-Palette Fusion Module, which structures descriptions into multi-layered components using LLMs and models relationships between textual intent and color palette queries; the Visual Design Fusion Module, which integrates unimodal visual features, multimodal aligned representations, and image-to-text intent structure representations generated by multimodal LLMs; and the Confidence-based Relaxed Alignment Module, which estimates confidence scores for unlabeled positive samples and incorporates them into a novel Confidence-based Relaxed Contrastive loss to avoid incorrectly penalizing similar but unlabeled images during training.

On the newly constructed NAIL-STAR benchmark, NaiLIA achieves a recall@1 of 56.4%, outperforming the best baseline (SigLIP) by 8.9 points. On Marqo Fashion200K, it achieves 74.6% recall@1, exceeding BLIP-2 by 9.4 points. Ablation studies confirm the contributions of each module, and the CRC loss demonstrates generalizability when applied to other architectures. This work is significant for beauty service platforms and broadly applicable to retrieval tasks involving fine-grained, multi-layered descriptions with numerous visually similar candidates.
original_abstract: We focus on the task of retrieving nail design images based on dense intent descriptions, which represent multi-layered user intent for nail designs. This is challenging because such descriptions specify unconstrained painted elements and pre-manufactured embellishments as well as visual characteristics, themes, and overall impressions. In addition to these descriptions, we assume that users provide palette queries by specifying zero or more colors via a color picker, enabling the expression of subtle and continuous color nuances. Existing vision-language foundation models often struggle to incorporate such descriptions and palettes. To address this, we propose NaiLIA, a multimodal retrieval method for nail design images, which comprehensively aligns with dense intent descriptions and palette queries during retrieval. Our approach introduces a relaxed loss based on confidence scores for unlabeled images that can align with the descriptions. To evaluate NaiLIA, we constructed a benchmark consisting of 10,625 images collected from people with diverse cultural backgrounds. The images were annotated with long and dense intent descriptions given by over 200 annotators. Experimental results demonstrate that NaiLIA outperforms standard methods.

title: Latent Wasserstein Adversarial Imitation Learning
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Latent Wasserstein Adversarial Imitation Learning (LWAIL), a method that addresses a fundamental limitation of Wasserstein-based adversarial imitation learning: the inadequacy of Euclidean distance as a ground metric for measuring distances between states. The Euclidean metric fails to capture environment dynamics, potentially misleading the learning process when states that are spatially close are dynamically unreachable from one another.

LWAIL employs a two-stage approach. First, in a pre-training stage, an Intention-Conditioned Value Function (ICVF) is trained using a small amount of unstructured, low-quality (e.g., random) state-only data to learn an embedding that captures dynamics-aware reachability between states. Second, during imitation learning, this frozen embedding serves as the ground metric within a standard Wasserstein adversarial imitation learning framework, where both the agent and discriminator operate in the learned latent space.

Evaluated on MuJoCo locomotion tasks and maze navigation environments from the D4RL benchmark, LWAIL achieves expert-level performance using only a single state-only expert trajectory. The method significantly outperforms numerous baselines, including classic imitation learning, Wasserstein-based, and learning-from-observations approaches. Ablation studies demonstrate robustness to environment noise, perturbed initial states, and varying data quality for ICVF pre-training.

The work provides a principled solution to the geometric limitations of prior Wasserstein occupancy matching methods, establishing that learning a dynamics-aware distance metric from minimal, low-quality data can substantially improve state-only imitation learning efficiency.
original_abstract: Imitation Learning (IL) enables agents to mimic expert behavior by learning from demonstrations. However, traditional IL methods require large amounts of medium-to-high-quality demonstrations as well as actions of expert demonstrations, both of which are often unavailable. To reduce this need, we propose Latent Wasserstein Adversarial Imitation Learning (LWAIL), a novel adversarial imitation learning framework that focuses on state-only distribution matching. It benefits from the Wasserstein distance computed in a dynamics-aware latent space. This dynamics-aware latent space differs from prior work and is obtained via a pre-training stage, where we train the Intention Conditioned Value Function (ICVF) to capture a dynamics-aware structure of the state space using a small set of randomly generated state-only data. We show that this enhances the policy's understanding of state transitions, enabling the learning process to use only one or a few state-only expert episodes to achieve expert-level performance. Through experiments on multiple MuJoCo environments, we demonstrate that our method outperforms prior Wasserstein-based IL methods and prior adversarial IL methods, achieving better results across various tasks.

title: O^3-LSM: Maximizing Disaggregated LSM Write Performance via Three-Layer Offloading
generated_summary:
This paper presents O³-LSM, a novel LSM-based key-value store architecture designed for disaggregated data centers that maximizes write performance through three-layer offloading: memtable offloading, flush offloading, and compaction offloading. While existing disaggregated LSM-KVS systems focus primarily on compaction offloading to disaggregated storage, they fail to address write slowdowns and stalls caused by limited write-buffer memory and slow flush operations at compute nodes.

O³-LSM introduces four key innovations to address these challenges. First, a DM-optimized memtable uses a contiguous, index-data separated layout enabling efficient transfer to disaggregated memory (DM) via RDMA without costly pointer reconstruction. Second, a collaborative flush offloading protocol with a contention-aware scheduler allows flush operations to execute on any DM-accessible node, avoiding expensive data readbacks. Third, asynchronous sharding partitions memtables into non-overlapping key-range shards, enabling parallel transfers and producing non-overlapping L0 SST files that eliminate serial L0 compaction bottlenecks. Fourth, cache-enhanced read delegation uses adaptive one-sided and two-sided RDMA operations to minimize read latency for DM-resident memtables.

Prototyped on RocksDB v8.2.0 and evaluated on CloudLab, O³-LSM achieves up to 4.5× write throughput improvement and 60% P99 latency reduction compared to state-of-the-art systems including Disagg-RocksDB, CaaS-LSM, and Nova-LSM. These results demonstrate that leveraging disaggregated memory as an extended write buffer with coordinated offloading significantly enhances LSM-KVS performance in disaggregated environments.
original_abstract: Log-Structured Merge-tree-based Key-Value Stores (LSM-KVS) have been optimized and redesigned for disaggregated storage via techniques such as compaction offloading to reduce the network I/Os between compute and storage. However, the constrained memory space and slow flush at the compute node severely limit the overall write throughput of existing optimizations. In this paper, we propose O3-LSM, a fundamental new LSM-KVS architecture, that leverages the shared Disaggregated Memory (DM) to support a three-layer offloading, i.e., memtable Offloading, flush Offloading, and the existing compaction Offloading. Compared to the existing disaggregated LSM-KVS with compaction offloading only, O3-LSM maximizes the write performance by addressing the above issues.   O3-LSM first leverages a novel DM-Optimized Memtable to achieve dynamic memtable offloading, which extends the write buffer while enabling fast, asynchronous, and parallel memtable transmission. Second, we propose Collaborative Flush Offloading that decouples the flush control plane from execution and supports memtable flush offloading at any node with dedicated scheduling and global optimizations. Third, O3-LSM is further improved with the Shard-Level Optimization, which partitions the memtable into shards based on disjoint key-ranges that can be transferred and flushed independently, unlocking parallelism across shards. Besides, to mitigate slow lookups in the disaggregated setting, O3-LSM also employs an adaptive Cache-Enhanced Read Delegation mechanism to combine a compact local cache with DM-assisted memtable delegated read. Our evaluation shows that O3-LSM achieves up to 4.5X write, 5.2X range query, and 1.8X point lookup throughput improvement, and up to 76% P99 latency reduction compared with Disaggregated-RocksDB, CaaS-LSM, and Nova-LSM.

title: Planning in 8 Tokens: A Compact Discrete Tokenizer for Latent World Model
generated_summary:
This paper introduces CompACT, a compact discrete tokenizer that compresses images into as few as 8 discrete tokens (approximately 128 bits) for efficient world model planning. The core insight is that effective planning requires semantic abstraction rather than photorealistic reconstruction, motivating extreme compression that preserves only decision-critical information.

The methodology employs a frozen pretrained vision encoder (DINOv3) whose semantic representations are distilled into compact tokens via cross-attention-based resampling with learnable queries, followed by finite scalar quantization. A generative decoder then reconstructs images by using these compact tokens as conditioning to unmask tokens from a pretrained VQGAN tokenizer, transforming intractable decompression into conditional generation. World models are trained directly in this compact discrete latent space using masked generative modeling.

Evaluated on goal-conditioned visual navigation (RECON dataset) and action-conditioned video prediction (RoboNet), CompACT achieves approximately 40× speedup in planning latency compared to the 784-token SD-VAE baseline while maintaining comparable planning accuracy. The 8-token model outperforms FlexTok at 64 tokens, and on RoboNet achieves 3× lower action prediction error than a 256-token baseline. Attention visualizations reveal that tokens naturally attend to semantically coherent, action-relevant scene elements like end-effectors and manipulation targets.

The work demonstrates that aggressive compression, when guided by pretrained semantic representations, can simultaneously improve both computational efficiency and planning performance, challenging the assumption that high-fidelity reconstruction is necessary for effective world models.
original_abstract: World models provide a powerful framework for simulating environment dynamics conditioned on actions or instructions, enabling downstream tasks such as action planning or policy learning. Recent approaches leverage world models as learned simulators, but its application to decision-time planning remains computationally prohibitive for real-time control. A key bottleneck lies in latent representations: conventional tokenizers encode each observation into hundreds of tokens, making planning both slow and resource-intensive. To address this, we propose CompACT, a discrete tokenizer that compresses each observation into as few as 8 tokens, drastically reducing computational cost while preserving essential information for planning. An action-conditioned world model that occupies CompACT tokenizer achieves competitive planning performance with orders-of-magnitude faster planning, offering a practical step toward real-world deployment of world models.

title: SAIL: Similarity-Aware Guidance and Inter-Caption Augmentation-based Learning for Weakly-Supervised Dense Video Captioning
generated_summary:
This paper introduces SAIL, a novel approach for Weakly-Supervised Dense Video Captioning (WSDVC) that addresses two key limitations of existing methods: the lack of semantic alignment between generated masks and corresponding events, and the sparsity of ground-truth annotations. Previous methods apply Gaussian masks to video features to implicitly localize events but produce temporally separated masks without ensuring they capture semantically relevant content, performing comparably to fixed, non-trainable mask baselines.

SAIL proposes two complementary strategies. First, a similarity-aware mask guidance mechanism leverages CLIP's cross-modal alignment to train masks via a margin ranking loss that maximizes cosine similarity between masked video features and corresponding caption embeddings while minimizing similarity to non-corresponding captions. Second, an LLM-based inter-caption augmentation strategy addresses annotation sparsity by generating synthetic captions for temporal gaps between consecutive ground-truth annotations using a large language model. These synthetic captions serve as auxiliary supervision through inter-event masks, providing denser alignment signals without introducing noise into the primary training objective.

Evaluated on ActivityNet Captions and YouCook2 benchmarks, SAIL achieves state-of-the-art results among weakly-supervised methods in both captioning and localization tasks, with a CIDEr score of 35.38 and F1 score of 57.00 on ActivityNet. Remarkably, it outperforms some fully-supervised methods despite not using temporal boundary annotations. The approach introduces negligible computational overhead, as the similarity-aware guidance requires only lightweight dot-product operations and the LLM augmentation is a one-time preprocessing step.
original_abstract: Weakly-Supervised Dense Video Captioning aims to localize and describe events in videos trained only on caption annotations, without temporal boundaries. Prior work introduced an implicit supervision paradigm based on Gaussian masking and complementary captioning. However, existing method focuses merely on generating non-overlapping masks without considering their semantic relationship to corresponding events, resulting in simplistic, uniformly distributed masks that fail to capture semantically meaningful regions. Moreover, relying solely on ground-truth captions leads to sub-optimal performance due to the inherent sparsity of existing datasets. In this work, we propose SAIL, which constructs semantically-aware masks through cross-modal alignment. Our similarity aware training objective guides masks to emphasize video regions with high similarity to their corresponding event captions. Furthermore, to guide more accurate mask generation under sparse annotation settings, we introduce an LLM-based augmentation strategy that generates synthetic captions to provide additional alignment signals. These synthetic captions are incorporated through an inter-mask mechanism, providing auxiliary guidance for precise temporal localization without degrading the main objective. Experiments on ActivityNet Captions and YouCook2 demonstrate state-of-the-art performance on both captioning and localization metrics.

title: On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning Compression
generated_summary:
This paper introduces **SAIL** (Self-distillation for reasoning compression), a method that reduces the verbosity of large reasoning models while simultaneously improving their accuracy. The key insight is that reasoning models already possess a latent ability to be concise when prompted, and this behavior can be internalized through on-policy self-distillation without requiring ground-truth answers, reward models, or difficulty estimators.

The method defines a teacher and student from the same model: the teacher receives a qualitative conciseness instruction prepended to its input, while the student does not. Training generates student rollouts and minimizes per-token reverse KL divergence between student and teacher distributions. The teacher weights are periodically synchronized with the student, creating progressively stronger compression targets. Reverse KL is critical—its mode-seeking property penalizes verbose tokens while preserving essential reasoning steps and maintaining entropy stability.

Evaluated on Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, SAIL achieves 57–59% token reduction on MATH-500 while improving accuracy by 9–16 percentage points (reaching ~86%). On AIME 2024, the 14B model gains 10 points with 41% compression. Compression naturally adapts to problem difficulty, with easier problems receiving more compression. General capabilities measured by MMLU remain fully preserved.

The significance is twofold: SAIL demonstrates that verbosity in reasoning models represents compounding error rather than productive deliberation, and it provides a simple, scalable compression approach applicable even in domains lacking ground-truth verification.
original_abstract: Reasoning models think out loud, but much of what they say is noise. We introduce OPSDC (On-Policy Self-Distillation for Reasoning Compression), a method that teaches models to reason more concisely by   distilling their own concise behavior back into themselves. The entire approach reduces to one idea: condition the same model on a "be concise" instruction to obtain teacher logits, and minimize per-token   reverse KL on the student's own rollouts. No ground-truth answers, no token budgets, no difficulty estimators. Just self-distillation. Yet this simplicity belies surprising sophistication: OPSDC automatically   compresses easy problems aggressively while preserving the deliberation needed for hard ones. On Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-14B, we achieve 57-59% token reduction on MATH-500 while improving accuracy by 9-16 points   absolute. On AIME 2024, the 14B model gains 10 points with 41% compression. The secret? Much of what reasoning models produce is not just redundant-it is actively harmful, compounding errors with every   unnecessary token.

title: Ensembling Language Models with Sequential Monte Carlo
generated_summary:
This paper introduces *f*-ensembles, a unified framework for composing multiple language models into ensemble distributions over strings using a family of aggregation functions based on generalized means. The authors propose a character-level (byte-level) Sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithm that sidesteps the vocabulary alignment problem inherent in combining models with different tokenizations and enables consistent sampling from the global ensemble distribution rather than biased local approximations.

The framework is evaluated across three structured text generation tasks—JSON schema conformance, word sorting (Big-Bench Hard), and text-to-SQL—using instruction-tuned models from the Llama, Qwen, and Phi families. The authors systematically compare four aggregation strategies spanning a consensus-coverage spectrum: minimum, product, sum (mixture), and maximum of experts, in both within-model prompt ensembling and cross-model ensembling settings.

Key findings reveal that consensus-seeking operators (product and minimum) consistently outperform coverage-seeking ones (sum and maximum), frequently exceeding the best individual base model's accuracy. Notably, standard probability averaging (sum ensemble) is theoretically and empirically shown to be bounded by the average of base model accuracies, explaining previously observed limitations. Furthermore, for consensus-seeking operators, better posterior approximations—achieved through more SMC particles—correlate positively with improved task performance, validating the importance of global rather than local ensemble sampling.

These results demonstrate that the choice of aggregation function matters significantly and that principled SMC-based inference can unlock synergistic gains from combining diverse language models.
original_abstract: Practitioners have access to an abundance of language models and prompting strategies for solving many language modeling tasks; yet prior work shows that modeling performance is highly sensitive to both choices. Classical machine learning ensembling techniques offer a principled approach: aggregate predictions from multiple sources to achieve better performance than any single one. However, applying ensembling to language models during decoding is challenging: naively aggregating next-token probabilities yields samples from a locally normalized, biased approximation of the generally intractable ensemble distribution over strings. In this work, we introduce a unified framework for composing $K$ language models into $f$-ensemble distributions for a wide range of functions $f\colon\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{K}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}$. To sample from these distributions, we propose a byte-level sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) algorithm that operates in a shared character space, enabling ensembles of models with mismatching vocabularies and consistent sampling in the limit. We evaluate a family of $f$-ensembles across prompt and model combinations for various structured text generation tasks, highlighting the benefits of alternative aggregation strategies over traditional probability averaging, and showing that better posterior approximations can yield better ensemble performance.

title: Spatially-aware Secondary License Sharing in mmWave Networks
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a spatially-aware secondary license sharing (SLS) framework for millimeter-wave (mmWave) networks, where primary operators lease unused spectrum to secondary users under interference-threshold constraints. The key novelty lies in incorporating antenna directionality, relative distance and orientation between primary and secondary links, and blockage states to determine secondary transmission opportunities—moving beyond simplified distance-based protection zones used in prior work.

The authors develop a stochastic geometry-based analytical framework modeling a mmWave network with a primary and secondary operator. title: Dissociating Direct Access from Inference in AI Introspection

original_abstract: Introspection is a foundational cognitive ability, but its mechanism is not well understood. Recent work has shown that AI models can introspect. title: ETH-Tight Complexity of Optimal Morse Matching on Bounded-Treewidth Complexes

original_abstract: The Optimal Morse Matching (OMM) problem asks for a discrete gradient vector field on a simplicial complex that minimizes the number of critical simplices. Parameterized by treewidth $k$, OMM has long been known to be solvable on triangulations of $3$-manifolds in $2^{O(k^2)} n^{O(1)}$ time and in FPT time for triangulations of arbitrary manifolds, but the exact dependence on $k$ has remained an open question. title: Bala-Join: An Adaptive Hash Join for Balancing Communication and Computation in Geo-Distributed SQL Databases

title: Generalized matching decoders for 2D topological translationally-invariant codes

original_abstract: Two-dimensional topological translationally-invariant (TTI) quantum codes, such as the toric code (TC) and bivariate bicycle (BB) codes, are promising candidates for fault-tolerant quantum computation. For such codes to be practically relevant, their decoders must successfully correct the most likely errors while remaining computationally efficient. For the TC, graph-matching decoders satisfy both requirements and, additionally, admit provable performance guarantees. Given the equivalence between TTI codes and (multiple copies of) the TC, one may then ask whether TTI codes also admit analogous graph-matching decoders. In this work, we develop a graph-matching approach to decoding general TTI codes. Intuitively, our approach coarse-grains the TTI code to obtain an effective description of the syndrome in terms of TC excitations, which can then be removed using graph-matching techniques. We prove that our decoders correct errors of weight up to a constant fraction of the code distance and achieve non-zero code-capacity thresholds. We further numerically study a variant optimized for practically relevant BB codes and observe performance comparable to that of the belief propagation with ordered statistics decoder. Our results indicate that graph-matching decoders are a viable approach to decoding BB codes and other TTI codes.

original_abstract: Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) remains a key challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP), especially when dealing with rare or domain-specific senses that are often misinterpreted. title: Judge Reliability Harness: Stress Testing the Reliability of LLM Judges

original_abstract: We present the Judge Reliability Harness, an open source library for constructing validation suites that test the reliability of LLM judges. title: Loop Closure via Maximal Cliques in 3D LiDAR-Based SLAM

original_abstract: Reliable loop closure detection remains a critical challenge in 3D LiDAR-based SLAM, especially under sensor noise, environmental ambiguity, and viewpoint variation conditions. RANSAC is often used in the context of loop closures for geometric model fitting in the presence of outliers. However, this approach may fail, leading to map inconsistency. We introduce a novel deterministic algorithm, CliReg, for loop closure validation that replaces RANSAC verification with a maximal clique search over a compatibility graph of feature correspondences. This formulation avoids random sampling and increases robustness in the presence of noise and outliers. We integrated our approach into a real- time pipeline employing binary 3D descriptors and a Hamming distance embedding binary search tree-based matching. We evaluated it on multiple real-world datasets featuring diverse LiDAR sensors. The results demonstrate that our proposed technique consistently achieves a lower pose error and more reliable loop closures than RANSAC, especially in sparse or ambiguous conditions. Additional experiments on 2D projection-based maps confirm its generality across spatial domains, making our approach a robust and efficient alternative for loop closure detection.

title: Harnessing Synthetic Data from Generative AI for Statistical Inference
generated_summary:

The authors organize motivations for synthetic data generation, survey major generative model classes (including GANs, VAEs, diffusion models, and large language models) with attention to their assumptions and appropriate use cases, and systematically compare paradigms for incorporating synthetic data into statistical workflows. Key findings emphasize that integrating statistical principles with generative AI is essential for trustworthy use of synthetic data, and that methodological guardrails can mitigate bias from imperfect generators. The work identifies open problems where new statistical theory is needed to fully leverage high-fidelity synthetic data for reliable scientific discovery.
original_abstract: The emergence of generative AI models has dramatically expanded the availability and use of synthetic data across scientific, industrial, and policy domains. While these developments open new possibilities for data analysis, they also raise fundamental statistical questions about when synthetic data can be used in a valid, reliable, and principled manner. This paper reviews the current landscape of synthetic data generation and use from a statistical perspective, with the goal of clarifying the assumptions under which synthetic data can meaningfully support downstream discovery, inference, and prediction. We survey major classes of modern generative models, their intended use cases, and the benefits they offer, while also highlighting their limitations and characteristic failure modes. We additionally examine common pitfalls that arise when synthetic data are treated as surrogates for real observations, including biases from model misspecification, attenuated uncertainty, and difficulties in generalization. Building on these insights, we discuss emerging frameworks for the principled use of synthetic data. We conclude with practical recommendations, open problems, and cautions intended to guide both method developers and applied researchers.

title: On the Necessity of Learnable Sheaf Laplacians
generated_summary:

The methodology involves benchmarking ISN against multiple SNN variants on five popular heterophilic graph datasets previously used to demonstrate sheaf-based improvements. Additionally, the authors introduce the Rayleigh quotient as a normalized measure for quantifying oversmoothing, enabling principled comparisons across different models and architectures.

The key finding is that the trivial sheaf Laplacian achieves competitive performance with learned sheaf constructions across all tested heterophily benchmarks, challenging the assumption that learning complex restriction maps is necessary for handling heterophily. Furthermore, using the Rayleigh quotient analysis, the authors demonstrate that the diffusion-based theoretical intuitions commonly invoked to motivate SNNs—namely that learned sheaf structures better prevent oversmoothing—are not empirically supported in trained networks.

These results carry significant implications for the sheaf neural network community, suggesting that the additional computational complexity of learning sheaf Laplacians may be unnecessary in practice. The work calls for a reevaluation of the theoretical frameworks used to explain SNN behavior and encourages the community to identify more rigorous justifications for sheaf-based architectures beyond oversmoothing and heterophily arguments.
original_abstract: Sheaf Neural Networks (SNNs) were introduced as an extension of Graph Convolutional Networks to address oversmoothing on heterophilous graphs by attaching a sheaf to the input graph and replacing the adjacency-based operator with a sheaf Laplacian defined by (learnable) restriction maps. Prior work motivates this design through theoretical properties of sheaf diffusion and the kernel of the sheaf Laplacian, suggesting that suitable non-identity restriction maps can avoid representations converging to constants across connected components. Since oversmoothing can also be mitigated through residual connections and normalization, we revisit a trivial sheaf construction to ask whether the additional complexity of learning restriction maps is necessary. We introduce an Identity Sheaf Network baseline, where all restriction maps are fixed to the identity, and use it to ablate the empirical improvements reported by sheaf-learning architectures. Across five popular heterophilic benchmarks, the identity baseline achieves comparable performance to a range of SNN variants. Finally, we introduce the Rayleigh quotient as a normalized measure for comparing oversmoothing across models and show that, in trained networks, the behavior predicted by the diffusion-based analysis of SNNs is not reflected empirically. In particular, Identity Sheaf Networks do not appear to suffer more significant oversmoothing than their SNN counterparts.

title: Fusion-CAM: Integrating Gradient and Region-Based Class Activation Maps for Robust Visual Explanations
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Fusion-CAM, a post-hoc explainability framework that integrates gradient-based and region-based Class Activation Map (CAM) methods to produce more robust and faithful visual explanations for deep convolutional neural networks. Fusion-CAM operates through a three-stage pipeline. First, the gradient-based map is denoised to suppress background noise and establish a precise baseline. Second, the denoised map is combined with the region-based map through confidence-weighted linear aggregation based on each map's contribution to the model's prediction. Third, a pixel-wise similarity-based fusion dynamically selects the blending strategy: pixels where both maps agree adopt maximum activation, while conflicting regions are proportionally blended.

Extensive experiments across ImageNet, PASCAL VOC, and plant disease datasets using VGG16, ResNet50, and MobileNet architectures demonstrate that Fusion-CAM consistently outperforms existing methods on standard metrics, achieving the lowest Average Drop, highest Average Increase in confidence, and optimal insertion-deletion AUC scores. Ablation studies confirm that each fusion stage contributes meaningfully to performance, and the framework generalizes beyond specific CAM variants. Fusion-CAM represents a flexible, architecture-agnostic approach to improving model interpretability, with potential extensions to emerging architectures like Vision Transformers.
original_abstract: Interpreting the decision-making process of deep convolutional neural networks remains a central challenge in achieving trustworthy and transparent artificial intelligence. Explainable AI (XAI) techniques, particularly Class Activation Map (CAM) methods, are widely adopted to visualize the input regions influencing model predictions. Gradient-based approaches (e.g. Grad-CAM) provide highly discriminative, fine-grained details by computing gradients of class activations but often yield noisy and incomplete maps that emphasize only the most salient regions rather than the complete objects. Region-based approaches (e.g. Score-CAM) aggregate information over larger areas, capturing broader object coverage at the cost of over-smoothing and reduced sensitivity to subtle features. We introduce Fusion-CAM, a novel framework that bridges this explanatory gap by unifying both paradigms through a dedicated fusion mechanism to produce robust and highly discriminative visual explanations. Our method first denoises gradient-based maps, yielding cleaner and more focused activations. It then combines the refined gradient map with region-based maps using contribution weights to enhance class coverage. Finally, we propose an adaptive similarity-based pixel-level fusion that evaluates the agreement between both paradigms and dynamically adjusts the fusion strength. This adaptive mechanism reinforces consistent activations while softly blending conflicting regions, resulting in richer, context-aware, and input-adaptive visual explanations. Extensive experiments on standard benchmarks show that Fusion-CAM consistently outperforms existing CAM variants in both qualitative visualization and quantitative evaluation, providing a robust and flexible tool for interpreting deep neural networks.

title: Accelerating Sampling-Based Control via Learned Linear Koopman Dynamics
generated_summary:

The methodology involves first training a deep neural network to learn lifting functions that map nonlinear system states into a higher-dimensional space where dynamics evolve approximately linearly. During MPPI rollouts, lifted states are propagated using the learned linear Koopman matrices rather than repeatedly evaluating the deep neural network, which is the key computational savings. The framework preserves MPPI's compatibility with nonconvex cost functions and stochastic sampling while naturally leveraging GPU parallelization.

The approach is validated on three systems: an inverted pendulum, a surface vehicle navigation task, and real-world experiments on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot. Results demonstrate that MPPI-DK achieves significant computational speedups compared to standard MPPI with true nonlinear dynamics—particularly beneficial at high control frequencies—while maintaining comparable tracking accuracy. The framework shows favorable trade-offs between computational efficiency and control performance, with GPU deployment yielding additional acceleration.

The significance lies in enabling real-time sampling-based control for complex robotic systems where computational resources are limited, bridging the gap between Koopman operator theory and practical sampling-based control.
original_abstract: This paper presents an efficient model predictive path integral (MPPI) control framework for systems with complex nonlinear dynamics. To improve the computational efficiency of classic MPPI while preserving control performance, we replace the nonlinear dynamics used for trajectory propagation with a learned linear deep Koopman operator (DKO) model, enabling faster rollout and more efficient trajectory sampling. The DKO dynamics are learned directly from interaction data, eliminating the need for analytical system models. The resulting controller, termed MPPI-DK, is evaluated in simulation on pendulum balancing and surface vehicle navigation tasks, and validated on hardware through reference-tracking experiments on a quadruped robot. Experimental results demonstrate that MPPI-DK achieves control performance close to MPPI with true dynamics while substantially reducing computational cost, enabling efficient real-time control on robotic platforms.

title: ORMOT: A Dataset and Framework for Omnidirectional Referring Multi-Object Tracking
generated_summary:
