The authors argue that omnidirectional imagery provides continuous spatial coverage, enabling better comprehension of long-horizon language descriptions involving actions, spatial relations, and group behaviors that span wide areas.

To support this task, the authors construct ORSet, a dataset built upon the JRDB benchmark containing 27 omnidirectional scenes, 848 language descriptions, and 3,401 annotated objects with bounding boxes and spatiotemporal trajectories. The dataset includes omnidirectional-specific descriptions such as boundary-crossing behaviors and extended motion paths unique to 360° environments.

The proposed framework, ORTrack, leverages large vision-language models (LVLMs) for open-vocabulary, language-guided detection and employs a two-stage cropping-based feature extraction strategy that captures both global contextual cues and fine-grained local details using CLIP encoders. Cross-frame association is performed through cosine similarity-based matching with the Hungarian algorithm, enabling robust identity preservation in equirectangular projections where IoU-based matching is unreliable.

Under zero-shot evaluation on ORSet, ORTrack with Qwen2.5-VL-7B achieves state-of-the-art performance, substantially outperforming existing open-source RMOT methods in HOTA (9.97 vs. 2.41), detection accuracy, and association accuracy. These results demonstrate strong zero-shot generalization capabilities for complex omnidirectional scenes, establishing an important baseline for future ORMOT research.
original_abstract: Multi-Object Tracking (MOT) is a fundamental task in computer vision, aiming to track targets across video frames. Existing MOT methods perform well in general visual scenes, but face significant challenges and limitations when extended to visual-language settings. To bridge this gap, the task of Referring Multi-Object Tracking (RMOT) has recently been proposed, which aims to track objects that correspond to language descriptions. However, current RMOT methods are primarily developed on datasets captured by conventional cameras, which suffer from limited field of view. This constraint often causes targets to move out of the frame, leading to fragmented tracking and loss of contextual information. In this work, we propose a novel task, called Omnidirectional Referring Multi-Object Tracking (ORMOT), which extends RMOT to omnidirectional imagery, aiming to overcome the field-of-view (FoV) limitation of conventional datasets and improve the model's ability to understand long-horizon language descriptions. To advance the ORMOT task, we construct ORSet, an Omnidirectional Referring Multi-Object Tracking dataset, which contains 27 diverse omnidirectional scenes, 848 language descriptions, and 3,401 annotated objects, providing rich visual, temporal, and language information. Furthermore, we propose ORTrack, a Large Vision-Language Model (LVLM)-driven framework tailored for Omnidirectional Referring Multi-Object Tracking. Extensive experiments on the ORSet dataset demonstrate the effectiveness of our ORTrack framework. The dataset and code will be open-sourced at https://github.com/chen-si-jia/ORMOT.

title: History-Deterministic Büchi Automata are Succinct
generated_summary:
This paper resolves a long-standing open question in automata theory by proving that history-deterministic (HD) Büchi automata can be strictly more succinct than deterministic Büchi automata. Specifically, the authors construct an HD Büchi automaton with 65 states and prove that every language-equivalent deterministic Büchi automaton requires at least 66 states, thereby answering the "HD-Büchi succinctness problem" that had remained open since it was first posed in 2013.

The methodology combines structural insights from multiple areas. The authors leverage the well-understood theory of HD coBüchi automata, particularly Abu Radi and Kupferman's characterization of minimality for HD coBüchi automata, to reason about the minimality of deterministic coBüchi automata recognizing the complement language. The construction is carefully designed so that most states are provably essential and cannot be eliminated. To complete the lower bound argument, the authors reduce a remaining subproblem to showing that no deterministic finite automaton with fewer than 5 states can separate two specific finite-word languages, which they verify using the SAT-based tool DFAMiner, making the proof computer-aided.

This result disproves a conjecture by Prakash that implied HD Büchi automata could always be determinized without increasing the number of states. The findings deepen understanding of the structural differences between HD and deterministic Büchi automata and have implications for applications in verification and synthesis, where automaton size is a critical bottleneck.
original_abstract: We describe a history-deterministic Büchi automaton that has strictly less states than every language-equivalent deterministic Büchi automaton. This solves a problem that had been open since the introduction of history-determinism and actively investigated for over a decade.   Our example automaton has 65 states, and proving its succinctness requires the combination of theoretical insights together with the aid of computers.

title: OpenFrontier: General Navigation with Visual-Language Grounded Frontiers
generated_summary:
OpenFrontier introduces a training-free navigation framework that grounds vision-language model (VLM) reasoning onto visual navigation frontiers for language-conditioned object-goal navigation. The key insight is that frontiers—boundaries between explored and unexplored space—serve as sparse, interpretable, and physically actionable anchors that bridge high-level semantic reasoning with metric navigation decisions.

The methodology operates primarily in the 2D image domain. Frontier clusters are detected directly from RGB observations without dense 3D reconstruction, then marked on the image using a set-of-marks prompting strategy. A VLM evaluates each frontier's relevance to the natural-language navigation goal in a single forward pass, producing semantic relevance scores that are combined with exploration-driven information gain to compute frontier utility. A global frontier management system maintains, updates, and selects frontier goals throughout navigation, balancing exploration with goal-directed exploitation. Open-vocabulary segmentation handles target detection, followed by VLM-based verification before final approach.

The framework demonstrates strong zero-shot generalization across multiple indoor navigation benchmarks, including both closed-set and open-set object-goal tasks, achieving competitive performance against baselines that rely on dense mapping or policy training. Real-world deployment on a mobile legged robot validates robust transfer to physical environments.

OpenFrontier's significance lies in demonstrating that effective system-level abstraction through frontier-based grounding, rather than increasingly complex models or training pipelines, enables scalable open-world navigation while remaining VLM-agnostic and requiring no fine-tuning.
original_abstract: Open-world navigation requires robots to make decisions in complex everyday environments while adapting to flexible task requirements. Conventional navigation approaches often rely on dense 3D reconstruction and hand-crafted goal metrics, which limits their generalization across tasks and environments. Recent advances in vision--language navigation (VLN) and vision--language--action (VLA) models enable end-to-end policies conditioned on natural language, but typically require interactive training, large-scale data collection, or task-specific fine-tuning with a mobile agent. We formulate navigation as a sparse subgoal identification and reaching problem and observe that providing visual anchoring targets for high-level semantic priors enables highly efficient goal-conditioned navigation. Based on this insight, we select navigation frontiers as semantic anchors and propose OpenFrontier, a training-free navigation framework that seamlessly integrates diverse vision--language prior models. OpenFrontier enables efficient navigation with a lightweight system design, without dense 3D mapping, policy training, or model fine-tuning. We evaluate OpenFrontier across multiple navigation benchmarks and demonstrate strong zero-shot performance, as well as effective real-world deployment on a mobile robot.

title: Robust Node Affinities via Jaccard-Biased Random Walks and Rank Aggregation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces TopKGraphs, a method for computing interpretable node-to-node affinity matrices in networks using Jaccard-biased random walks combined with robust rank aggregation. The core contribution is a framework that captures both local neighborhood overlap and multi-hop structural context while remaining parameter-light and interpretable.

The methodology anchors random walks at each start node, biasing transitions toward neighbors with high Jaccard similarity to the start node. Each walk produces a partial ranking of nodes based on first-visit order, and multiple independent walks are aggregated via Borda scoring to produce a consensus affinity measure. The authors provide theoretical justification by proving that, under mild assumptions, the Borda-aggregated rankings converge almost surely to the latent similarity ordering as the number of walks increases. This positions TopKGraphs as a rank-based estimator of latent structural similarity rather than a diffusion process, distinguishing it from PageRank or heat-kernel approaches.

Evaluation on synthetic benchmarks (stochastic block models and LFR graphs) and real-world networks (CORA citation network, protein-protein interaction networks, and kNN graphs from tabular data) demonstrates that TopKGraphs consistently matches or outperforms strong baselines in community detection and node classification, particularly in sparse, noisy, or weakly clustered settings. The method shows robust performance across varying walk parameters and achieves substantially faster computation than Node2Vec, offering a practical balance between accuracy, interpretability, and computational efficiency for graph-based machine learning tasks.
original_abstract: Estimating node similarity is a fundamental task in network analysis and graph-based machine learning, with applications in clustering, community detection, classification, and recommendation. We propose TopKGraphs, a method based on start-node-anchored random walks that bias transitions toward nodes with structurally similar neighborhoods, measured via Jaccard similarity. Rather than computing stationary distributions, walks are treated as stochastic neighborhood samplers, producing partial node rankings that are aggregated using robust rank aggregation to construct interpretable node-to-node affinity matrices. TopKGraphs provides a non-parametric, interpretable, and general-purpose representation of node similarity that can be applied in both network analysis and machine learning workflows. We evaluate the method on synthetic graphs (stochastic block models, Lancichinetti-Fortunato-Radicchi benchmark graphs), k-nearest-neighbor graphs from tabular datasets, and a curated high-confidence protein-protein interaction network. Across all scenarios, TopKGraphs achieves competitive or superior performance compared to standard similarity measures (Jaccard, Dice), a diffusion-based method (personalized PageRank), and an embedding-based approach (Node2Vec), demonstrating robustness in sparse, noisy, or heterogeneous networks. These results suggest that TopKGraphs is a versatile and interpretable tool for bridging simple local similarity measures with more complex embedding-based approaches, facilitating both data mining and network analysis applications.

title: Hierarchical Decoding for Discrete Speech Synthesis with Multi-Resolution Spoof Detection
generated_summary:
This paper introduces MSpoof-TTS, a training-free framework that improves discrete codec-based speech synthesis by integrating multi-resolution spoof detection into the decoding process without modifying the pretrained language model. The key insight is that distribution mismatches between ground-truth and synthesized codec tokens manifest across multiple temporal scales, causing perceptual degradation during autoregressive generation.

The methodology involves two main components. First, the authors train multi-resolution spoof detectors that operate directly on discrete codec token sequences at varying segment lengths and downsampling rates, using Conformer-based architectures to distinguish real from synthetic tokens. Second, they propose a hierarchical spoof-guided sampling framework that combines Entropy-Aware Sampling (an improved variant of repetition-aware sampling) with progressive discriminator pruning. During decoding, multiple candidate continuations are generated, evaluated by short-span detectors for early pruning, then extended and assessed by longer-span detectors, with final selection via multi-resolution rank aggregation.

Experiments on LibriTTS, LibriSpeech, and a challenging tongue-twister dataset (TwistList) demonstrate consistent improvements in perceptual quality metrics (NISQA, MOSNET) while maintaining competitive intelligibility and speaker similarity. Subjective evaluations confirm enhanced naturalness without degrading speaker identity. The framework's significance lies in demonstrating that spoof detection, traditionally used for post-hoc classification of synthetic speech, can be repurposed as an effective inference-time guidance mechanism for improving speech generation quality without costly retraining.
original_abstract: Neural codec language models enable high-quality discrete speech synthesis, yet their inference remains vulnerable to token-level artifacts and distributional drift that degrade perceptual realism. Rather than relying on preference optimization or retraining, we propose MSpoof-TTS, a training-free inference framework that improves zero-shot synthesis through multi-resolution spoof guidance. We introduce a Multi-Resolution Token-based Spoof Detection framework that evaluates codec sequences at different temporal granularities to detect locally inconsistent or unnatural patterns. We then integrate the spoof detectors into a hierarchical decoding strategy, progressively pruning low-quality candidates and re-ranking hypotheses. This discriminator-guided generation enhances robustness without modifying model parameters. Experiments validate the effectiveness of our framework for robust and high-quality codec-based speech generation.

title: Embedded Inter-Subject Variability in Adversarial Learning for Inertial Sensor-Based Human Activity Recognition
generated_summary:
This paper presents a novel adversarial deep learning framework for inertial sensor-based human activity recognition (HAR) that addresses the challenge of inter-subject variability—the fact that different individuals perform the same activity differently, creating a generalization gap when models encounter unseen users.

The key contribution is a new adversarial discrimination task that determines whether pairs of activity feature vectors originate from the same person performing the same activity or from different persons performing the same activity. By embedding both activity and user dimensions into the discrimination task, the framework learns subject-invariant feature representations that reduce distribution differences across individuals. The approach frames discrimination as binary classification, enhancing scalability compared to prior methods that require classes proportional to the number of users. The framework comprises four modules—a feature extractor, reconstructor, activity classifier, and discriminator—trained through a three-step process including pretraining and adversarial learning, with a novel combined loss function incorporating a non-saturating GAN loss.

Evaluated using Leave-One-Subject-Out cross-validation on three benchmark datasets (PAMAP2, MHEALTH, REALDISP), the framework consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods. Analyses demonstrate measurable reductions in inter-subject variability through decreased Wasserstein distances between training and test distributions. Ablation studies confirm that the proposed discrimination task outperforms alternative discrimination strategies within the same adversarial framework, supporting the development of more adaptable, user-agnostic HAR systems.
original_abstract: This paper addresses the problem of Human Activity Recognition (HAR) using data from wearable inertial sensors. An important challenge in HAR is the model's generalization capabilities to new unseen individuals due to inter-subject variability, i.e., the same activity is performed differently by different individuals. To address this problem, we propose a novel deep adversarial framework that integrates the concept of inter-subject variability in the adversarial task, thereby encouraging subject-invariant feature representations and enhancing the classification performance in the HAR problem. Our approach outperforms previous methods in three well-established HAR datasets using a leave-one-subject-out (LOSO) cross-validation. Further results indicate that our proposed adversarial task effectively reduces inter-subject variability among different users in the feature space, and it outperforms adversarial tasks from previous works when integrated into our framework. Code: https://github.com/FranciscoCalatrava/EmbeddedSubjectVariability.git

title: Learning Causal Structure of Time Series using Best Order Score Search
generated_summary:
This paper introduces TS-BOSS, a time series extension of the Best Order Score Search (BOSS) algorithm for causal discovery over multivariate time series data. The main contribution is adapting BOSS—a score-based method that performs permutation-based search over directed acyclic graphs using grow-shrink trees for efficient computation—to the time series setting, along with theoretical guarantees for its soundness.

The methodology extends BOSS to handle temporal dependencies by incorporating lagged causal relationships within the dynamic Bayesian network framework. TS-BOSS searches over permutations of variables to identify optimal causal orderings while accounting for both contemporaneous and lagged effects. The authors provide a key theoretical result extending existing sparsest permutation results to the time series setting under suitable stationarity assumptions, establishing that permutation-based causal discovery methods can be soundly applied to time series data.

Through simulation studies on synthetic data, the authors compare TS-BOSS against the constraint-based method PCMCI+. Key findings show that TS-BOSS outperforms PCMCI+ particularly in high auto-correlation regimes and generally maintains higher adjacency recall at comparable precision levels. An ablation study comparing TS-BOSS with an i.i.d. variant highlights the importance of properly accounting for temporal structure.

The significance of this work lies in establishing TS-BOSS as a competitive, scalable score-based alternative for time series causal discovery, complementing existing constraint-based approaches and demonstrating particular advantages in challenging autocorrelated settings common in real-world applications.
original_abstract: Causal structure learning from observational data is central to many scientific and policy domains, but the time series setting common to many disciplines poses several challenges due to temporal dependence. In this paper we focus on score-based causal discovery for multivariate time series and introduce TS-BOSS, a time series extension of the recently proposed Best Order Score Search (BOSS) (Andrews et al. 2023). TS-BOSS performs a permutation-based search over dynamic Bayesian network structures while leveraging grow-shrink trees to cache intermediate score computations, preserving the scalability and strong empirical performance of BOSS in the static setting. We provide theoretical guarantees establishing the soundness of TS-BOSS under suitable assumptions, and we present an intermediate result that extends classical subgraph minimality results for permutation-based methods to the dynamic (time series) setting. Our experiments on synthetic data show that TS-BOSS is especially effective in high auto-correlation regimes, where it consistently achieves higher adjacency recall at comparable precision than standard constraint-based methods. Overall, TS-BOSS offers a high-performing, scalable approach for time series causal discovery and our results provide a principled bridge for extending sparsity-based, permutation-driven causal learning theory to dynamic settings.

title: Progressive Residual Warmup for Language Model Pretraining
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Progressive Residual Warmup (ProRes), a simple and scalable technique for coordinating layerwise learning during Transformer pretraining. The core idea is that residual connections in stacked Transformer layers should be activated progressively from shallow to deep layers, respecting the observation that shallow layers tend to converge before deeper ones. ProRes assigns each layer's residual branch a time-dependent scaling factor that starts at zero and linearly increases to one during training, with deeper layers having longer warmup periods. This ensures shallow layers stabilize before deeper layers begin contributing, reducing conflicting learning signals and controlling update magnitudes during early training without sacrificing later expressivity.

The authors evaluate ProRes across decoder-only Transformers ranging from 71M to 7B parameters, testing multiple normalization schemes (Pre-LN, Post-LN, Sandwich-LN, DeepNorm), initialization methods, and model depths from 12 to 120 layers. ProRes consistently reduces perplexity across all configurations, with particularly strong gains for Post-LN architectures and deeper models. It yields an average 1.27% improvement on zero-shot reasoning benchmarks and substantially larger gains on out-of-distribution evaluation sets. Depth scaling experiments demonstrate that ProRes enables deeper models to achieve better performance while maintaining near-zero training instability spikes.

Schedule ablations confirm that the shallow-to-deep activation order is critical, as reverse or simultaneous activation degrades performance. The findings suggest that training-phase-aware residual scheduling is a practical and effective approach for improving Transformer optimization at scale.
original_abstract: Transformer architectures serve as the backbone for most modern Large Language Models, therefore their pretraining stability and convergence speed are of central concern. Motivated by the logical dependency of sequentially stacked layers, we propose Progressive Residual Warmup (ProRes) for language model pretraining. ProRes implements an "early layer learns first" philosophy by multiplying each layer's residual with a scalar that gradually warms up from 0 to 1, with deeper layers taking longer warmup steps. In this way, deeper layers wait for early layers to settle into a more stable regime before contributing to learning. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ProRes through pretraining experiments across various model scales, as well as normalization and initialization schemes. Comprehensive analysis shows that ProRes not only stabilizes pretraining but also introduces a unique optimization trajectory, leading to faster convergence, stronger generalization and better downstream performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/dandingsky/ProRes.

title: Shock Propagation and Macroeconomic Fluctuations
generated_summary:
This paper investigates how the temporal overlap of idiosyncratic productivity shocks affects aggregate volatility in production network economies. The main contribution is identifying a novel "time-averaging" channel: when new shocks arrive before the economy fully adjusts to previous ones, realized macroeconomic fluctuations are dampened relative to the standard static-equilibrium benchmark that assumes instantaneous adjustment.

The authors embed an i.i.d. productivity process into decentralized adjustment dynamics on a production network with Cobb-Douglas technologies. They develop a "wave" representation in which realized aggregate output is expressed as a superposition of partially propagated responses from past shock vintages, with propagation governed by iterates of the production network operator. This framework enables comparison between a static series (mapping each shock to its full equilibrium outcome) and a dynamic series (reflecting overlapping incomplete adjustments).

The key finding is that the macroeconomic significance of fat-tailed degree distributions—widely viewed as the primary driver of granular fluctuations—depends critically on the dominant transient eigenvalue of the production network. When network mixing is slow, intertemporal superposition of partially propagated waves washes out cross-sectional concentration, substantially reducing both aggregate volatility and tail risk. Notably, tail risk is dampened more sharply than volatility, since extreme outcomes require sustained alignment of waves across vintages that overlapping adjustment makes increasingly unlikely.

These results imply that assessing macroeconomic risk from firm-level shocks requires jointly considering network concentration and the speed of network mixing, not degree heterogeneity alone.
original_abstract: We study how idiosyncratic firm-level shocks generate aggregate volatility and tail risk when they propagate through a production network under overlapping adjustment: new productivity draws arrive before the economy reaches the static equilibrium associated with earlier draws. Each innovation generates a `productivity wave' that mixes and dissipates over time as it travels through the production network. Macroeconomic fluctuations emerge from the interference between these waves of different vintages. The interference between these waves is governed by the dominant transient eigenvalue of the production network, and therefore so is the macroeconomic fluctuations they generate. In such a dynamic regime, the tail of the degree distribution is a markedly weaker determinant of macro fluctuations than in the fully adjusted static benchmark. And the macroeconomic significance of the degree-heterogeneity of production networks cannot be known without knowing the rate at which the economy converges to equilibrium or equivalently the spectral properties of the production network. More concretely, once we permit the time-averaging of shocks, granular shocks may account for only a small fraction of the empirically observed aggregate volatility.

title: Radiation Hydrodynamics at Scale: Comparing MPI and Asynchronous Many-Task Runtimes with FleCSI
generated_summary:
This paper presents the first large-scale evaluation of the FleCSI framework across all its available parallelization backends—MPI, MPI+Kokkos, HPX, and Legion—using two computational fluid dynamics applications on up to 1024 nodes of the Chicoma supercomputer. The study aims to quantify the overhead introduced by asynchronous many-task runtimes (AMTRs) compared to traditional MPI-based parallelization and determine whether complex applications can benefit from asynchronous execution.

Two benchmark applications are employed: a red-black Gauss-Seidel Poisson solver, chosen as a communication-focused workload that exposes AMTR overhead, and HARD, a radiation hydrodynamics code representing a computationally intensive real-world application. Strong and weak scaling tests are conducted across all backends.

For the Poisson solver, pure MPI delivers the best performance, while AMTR backends show measurable overhead. The HPX backend suffers from inefficient collective communication implementations at scale. However, for the more complex HARD application, HPX achieves speedups of up to 1.28× over MPI+Kokkos on up to 32 nodes by leveraging asynchronous task scheduling to overlap computation and communication. In weak scaling, HPX demonstrates an average 1.12× speedup over MPI+Kokkos for the radiation hydrodynamics problem.

These results demonstrate that while AMTRs introduce overhead for simple workloads, computationally intensive applications can effectively hide this cost and benefit from asynchronous parallelism, validating the FleCSI framework's multi-backend approach for portable scientific computing.
original_abstract: Writing efficient distributed code remains a labor-intensive and complex endeavor. To simplify application development, the Flexible Computational Science Infrastructure (FleCSI) framework offers a user-oriented, high-level programming interface that is built upon a task-based runtime model. Internally, FleCSI integrates state-of-the-art parallelization backends, including MPI and the asynchronous many-task runtimes (AMTRs) Legion and HPX, enabling applications to fully leverage asynchronous parallelism. In this work, we benchmark two applications using FleCSI's three backends on up to 1024 nodes, intending to quantify the advantages and overheads introduced by the AMTR backends. As representative applications, we select a simple Poisson solver and the multidimensional radiation hydrodynamics code HARD. In the communication-focused Poisson solver benchmark, FleCSI achieves over 97% parallel efficiency using the MPI backend under weak scaling on up to 131072 cores, indicating that only minimal overhead is introduced by its abstraction layer. While the Legion backend exhibits notable overheads and scaling limitations, the HPX backend introduces only marginal overhead compared to MPI+Kokkos. However, the scalability of the HPX backend is currently limited due to the usage of non-optimized HPX collective operations. In the computation-focused radiation hydrodynamics benchmarks, the performance gap between the MPI and HPX backends fades. On fewer than 64 nodes, the HPX backend outperforms MPI+Kokkos, achieving an average speedup of 1.31 under weak scaling and up to 1.27 under strong scaling. For the hydrodynamics-only HARD benchmark, the HPX backend demonstrates superior performance on fewer than 32 nodes, achieving speedups of up to 1.20 relative to MPI and up to 1.64 relative to MPI+Kokkos.

title: PACE: A Personalized Adaptive Curriculum Engine for 9-1-1 Call-taker Training

The system maintains probabilistic beliefs as Beta distributions over skill nodes, enabling fine-grained competency tracking and decay-aware scheduling across multi-week training programs.

Evaluated using LLM-simulated trainee agents across four learner archetypes, PACE achieves up to 19.50% reduction in time-to-competence compared to the strongest baseline while maintaining superior terminal mastery. Fine-grained skill-level tracking proves essential, outperforming coarser granularities by substantial margins. In a co-pilot study with 21 domain experts at a partnering 9-1-1 center, PACE achieves 95.45% alignment with expert pedagogical decisions while reducing training turnaround time by 95.08%, from 11.58 minutes to 34 seconds. original_abstract: 9-1-1 call-taking training requires mastery of over a thousand interdependent skills, covering diverse incident types and protocol-specific nuances. A nationwide labor shortage is already straining training capacity, but effective instruction still demands that trainers tailor objectives to each trainee's evolving competencies. This personalization burden is one that current practice cannot scale. Partnering with Metro Nashville Department of Emergency Communications (MNDEC), we propose PACE (Personalized Adaptive Curriculum Engine), a co-pilot system that augments trainer decision-making by (1) maintaining probabilistic beliefs over trainee skill states, (2) modeling individual learning and forgetting dynamics, and (3) recommending training scenarios that balance acquisition of new competencies with retention of existing ones. PACE propagates evidence over a structured skill graph to accelerate diagnostic coverage and applies contextual bandits to select scenarios that target gaps the trainee is prepared to address. Empirical results show that PACE achieves 19.50% faster time-to-competence and 10.95% higher terminal mastery compared to state-of-the-art frameworks. Co-pilot studies with practicing training officers further demonstrate a 95.45% alignment rate between PACE's and experts' pedagogical judgments on real-world cases. Under estimation, PACE cuts turnaround time to merely 34 seconds from 11.58 minutes, up to 95.08% reduction.

title: Revisiting Graph Modification via Disk Scaling: From One Radius to Interval-Based Radii
generated_summary:
This paper generalizes a recently introduced "disk scaling" model for graph modification in unit disk graphs, where instead of assigning a single fixed radius to all modified disks, each rescaled disk can independently choose a radius within a given interval [r⁻, r⁺]. The central problem asks whether at most k disk radii in a unit disk graph can be modified to values within this interval so that the resulting disk graph belongs to a target graph class.

The authors first establish that the general problem is in XP with respect to k for any efficiently recognizable graph class. The key insight involves guessing the set of scaled disks and each scaled disk's furthest unscaled neighbor, then using linear programming to determine feasible radius assignments. For specific graph classes, they provide refined results: an FPT algorithm for cluster graphs parameterized by k, employing a branch-and-bound procedure that exploits geometric properties to bound the number of ambiguous adjacencies; and a polynomial-time algorithm for complete graphs by reducing to the known polynomial-time clique algorithm on unit disk graphs.

On the hardness side, the authors prove W[1]-hardness for obtaining connected graphs, showing that the general XP algorithm cannot always be improved to FPT. This result also demonstrates that complexity can differ drastically depending on whether disks are shrunk or expanded.

These results settle two open questions from prior work and demonstrate that the interval-based radius model, while more expressive, remains computationally tractable for important graph classes, with direct applications to sensor network optimization where transmission ranges can be individually adjusted.
original_abstract: For a fixed graph class $Π$, the goal of $Π$-Modification is to transform an input graph $G$ into a graph $H\inΠ$ using at most $k$ modifications. Vertex and edge deletions are common operations, and their (parameterized) complexity for various $Π$ is well-studied. Classic graph modification operations such as edge deletion do not consider the geometric nature of geometric graphs such as (unit) disk graphs. This led Fomin et al. [ITCS' 25] to initiate the study of disk scaling as a geometric graph modification operation for unit disk graphs: For a given radius $r$, each modified disk will be rescaled to radius $r$. In this paper, we generalize their model by allowing rescaled disks to choose a radius within a given interval $[r_{\min}, r_{\max}]$ and study the (parameterized) complexity (with respect to $k$) of the corresponding problem $Π$-Scaling. We show that $Π$-Scaling is in XP for every graph class $Π$ that can be recognized in polynomial time. Furthermore, we show that $Π$-Scaling: (1) is NP-hard and FPT for cluster graphs, (2) can be solved in polynomial time for complete graphs, and (3) is W[1]-hard for connected graphs. In particular, (1) and (2) answer open questions of Fomin et al. and (3) generalizes the hardness result for their variant where the set of scalable disks is restricted.

title: DiSCTT: Consensus-Guided Self-Curriculum for Efficient Test-Time Adaptation in Reasoning
generated_summary:
This paper introduces DiSCTT (Difficulty-aware Consensus-Guided Self-Curriculum Test-Time Adaptation), a framework that dynamically adapts large language models during inference by routing inputs to different optimization strategies based on estimated difficulty. The key insight is that effective test-time adaptation requires treating easy and hard reasoning problems differently rather than applying a uniform learning objective.

DiSCTT estimates instance difficulty by measuring agreement (consensus) among multiple independently sampled reasoning trajectories. High-consensus inputs, indicating low epistemic uncertainty, are optimized via supervised fine-tuning using majority-agreed solutions as pseudo-labels to consolidate reliable reasoning patterns. Low-consensus inputs are optimized via reinforcement learning with a novel correctness-gated, population-relative novelty reward that encourages meaningful exploration while maintaining stability. Critically, this difficulty-based routing is periodically recomputed as the model's competence evolves, creating a self-evolving curriculum that adapts throughout inference.

Across diverse mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks and multiple model scales, DiSCTT consistently outperforms uniform test-time adaptation baselines including standard self-training and test-time reinforcement learning approaches. The framework achieves higher accuracy with lower variance and substantially reduced computational cost, as reinforcement learning updates are concentrated only on genuinely uncertain instances.

These results demonstrate that difficulty-aware allocation of learning objectives is a fundamental structural principle for stable and efficient test-time adaptation, offering a scalable design pattern for adaptive reasoning in deployed language models.
original_abstract: Test-time adaptation offers a promising avenue for improving reasoning performance in large language models without additional supervision, but existing approaches often apply a uniform optimization objective across all inputs, leading to inefficient or unstable adaptation on heterogeneous reasoning problems. We propose DiSCTT, a difficulty-aware, consensus-guided self-curriculum framework that dynamically allocates test-time optimization strategies based on instance-level epistemic uncertainty estimated from agreement among sampled reasoning trajectories. Inputs with high consensus are consolidated via supervised fine-tuning using majority-agreed solutions as pseudo-labels, while low-consensus inputs are optimized via reinforcement learning with a consensus-regularized objective that encourages diversity under relevance constraints. Across a broad suite of mathematical and general reasoning benchmarks, DiSCTT consistently outperforms strong test-time adaptation baselines, achieving higher accuracy with reduced variance and substantially lower computation and wall-clock training times. These results demonstrate that explicitly accounting for instance difficulty and uncertainty enables more stable, efficient, and effective test-time adaptation for reasoning models.

title: Omni-Manip: Beyond-FOV Large-Workspace Humanoid Manipulation with Omnidirectional 3D Perception
generated_summary:
