The methodology centers on mounting a panoramic LiDAR sensor on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot to capture 360° point clouds, which are processed through a pyramid convolutional encoder enhanced with a novel Time-Aware Attention Pooling (TAP) mechanism. TAP aggregates point clouds over a temporal window with learned attention weights conditioned on temporal offsets, producing stable representations despite LiDAR sparsity and flickering. The encoded features condition a diffusion policy decoder that generates coordinated whole-body action sequences. A lightweight XR-based teleoperation system enables efficient collection of demonstration data involving full-body coordination.

Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that Omni-Manip achieves robust performance on tasks requiring out-of-view manipulation, where all RGB-D baselines fail completely due to perceptual limitations. The system also exhibits superior obstacle avoidance in cluttered environments and strong generalization across varying objects, lighting conditions, and scene clutter. Ablation studies confirm that both panoramic perception and temporal encoding are essential components. This work establishes omnidirectional 3D perception as a promising paradigm for deploying humanoid robots in unstructured real-world environments.
original_abstract: The deployment of humanoid robots for dexterous manipulation in unstructured environments remains challenging due to perceptual limitations that constrain the effective workspace. In scenarios where physical constraints prevent the robot from repositioning itself, maintaining omnidirectional awareness becomes far more critical than color or semantic information. While recent advances in visuomotor policy learning have improved manipulation capabilities, conventional RGB-D solutions suffer from narrow fields of view (FOV) and self-occlusion, requiring frequent base movements that introduce motion uncertainty and safety risks. Existing approaches to expanding perception, including active vision systems and third-view cameras, introduce mechanical complexity, calibration dependencies, and latency that hinder reliable real-time performance. In this work, We propose Omni-Manip, an end-to-end LiDAR-driven 3D visuomotor policy that enables robust manipulation in large workspaces. Our method processes panoramic point clouds through a Time-Aware Attention Pooling mechanism, efficiently encoding sparse 3D data while capturing temporal dependencies. This 360° perception allows the robot to interact with objects across wide areas without frequent repositioning. To support policy learning, we develop a whole-body teleoperation system for efficient data collection on full-body coordination. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world environments show that Omni-Manip achieves robust performance in large-workspace and cluttered scenarios, outperforming baselines that rely on egocentric depth cameras.

title: Exploring the potential and limitations of Model Merging for Multi-Domain Adaptation in ASR
generated_summary:
This paper systematically investigates model merging as an alternative to joint fine-tuning for multi-domain automatic speech recognition (ASR) adaptation. The authors benchmark eleven merging algorithms applied to Whisper Large v3-X models independently fine-tuned on ten European Portuguese (EP) domains, evaluating both in-domain accuracy and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization across diverse conditions including other Portuguese varieties, English, and multilingual test sets. To support this evaluation, the authors release a Whisper-compatible merging toolkit extending existing frameworks.

The study reveals a fundamental trade-off between target-domain specialization and cross-lingual robustness. While joint fine-tuning achieves the best EP accuracy, it substantially degrades performance on non-EP benchmarks, indicating catastrophic forgetting. In contrast, most merging approaches preserve or even improve OOD performance while narrowing the EP accuracy gap. Delta-subspace methods, particularly TSV-M, yield the strongest EP and closely related Portuguese variety results, while parameter-space methods like Model Stock and Karcher mean better preserve multilingual robustness. The authors propose BoostedTSV-M, which addresses rank collapse through singular-value boosting and improves numerical stability via Newton-Schulz orthogonalization, achieving the best overall EP performance among all merging methods with statistical significance over joint fine-tuning.

These findings demonstrate that model merging provides a practical, scalable approach to producing single deployable ASR models with strong target-domain accuracy and improved cross-domain generalization, without requiring access to all training data simultaneously.
original_abstract: Model merging is a scalable alternative to multi-task training that combines the capabilities of multiple specialised models into a single model. This is particularly attractive for large speech foundation models, which are typically adapted through domain-specific fine-tuning, resulting in multiple customised checkpoints, for which repeating full fine-tuning when new data becomes available is computationally prohibitive. In this work, we study model merging for multi-domain ASR and benchmark 11 merging algorithms for 10 European Portuguese domains, evaluating in-domain accuracy, robustness under distribution shift, as well as English and multilingual performance. We further propose BoostedTSV-M, a new merging algorithm based on TSV-M that mitigates rank collapse via singular-value boosting and improves numerical stability. Overall, our approach outperforms full fine-tuning on European Portuguese while preserving out-of-distribution generalisation in a single model.

title: InfoFlow KV: Information-Flow-Aware KV Recomputation for Long Context
generated_summary:
This paper introduces InfoFlow KV, a method that frames selective key-value (KV) cache recomputation for long-context inference as an information flow problem. In chunk-wise prefilling, where long contexts are split into independently processed chunks, positional encoding mismatches between chunk-local and global rotary position embeddings (RoPE) degrade model accuracy. Rather than recomputing all tokens under global positions, the authors propose selectively recomputing only those tokens most critical for transmitting information from context to generated answers.

The method selects recomputation targets using prompt-conditioned attention norms—aggregated attention weights from prompt tokens to context tokens—which jointly capture semantic relevance to the query and structural positioning within the causal attention graph. Crucially, the authors demonstrate that reliable token ranking requires computing these attention norms under inference-consistent global RoPE geometry rather than chunk-local positions, as mismatched positional configurations produce unstable and misleading importance estimates. An optional chunk reordering strategy places information-critical chunks closer to the prompt, further facilitating information propagation during decoding.

Experiments across three large language models and a vision-language model on multiple benchmarks show consistent improvements over existing methods like CacheBlend and EPIC, particularly on multi-hop reasoning tasks requiring cross-chunk evidence aggregation. The approach achieves these gains without modifying pretrained model weights, demonstrating that positional alignment in token selection is essential for efficient and accurate long-context inference in both unimodal and multimodal settings.
original_abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for long-context question answering is bottlenecked by inference-time prefilling over large retrieved contexts. A common strategy is to precompute key-value (KV) caches for individual documents and selectively recompute a small subset of tokens to restore global causal dependencies, but existing methods rely on heuristics or representation discrepancies without modeling whether selected tokens can effectively influence generation. We cast selective KV recomputation as an information flow problem and show that a simple attention-norm signal from the query reliably identifies tokens that are both semantically relevant and structurally positioned to propagate information, when computed under an inference-consistent RoPE geometry. We therefore reconstruct global positional assignments for retrieved chunks and introduce an information-flow-guided chunk reordering strategy. Experiments on LLM and VLM benchmarks demonstrate consistent gains over prior methods under comparable efficiency budgets.

title: Ailed: A Psyche-Driven Chess Engine with Dynamic Emotional Modulation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Ailed, a chess engine built around a "psyche model" that dynamically modulates move selection to simulate human-like emotional variability during play. The main contribution is an audio-inspired signal chain—comprising noise gate, dynamics compression/expansion, five-band equalizer, and saturation stages—that reshapes any engine's move probability distribution based on a single bounded psyche scalar, updated each move from five positional factors. This architecture-agnostic middleware transforms static move predictions into behaviorally dynamic play exhibiting stress-induced blundering, overconfident rigidity, and neutral balanced performance.

Across 12,414 games against Maia2-1100 using two probability sources (a minimal 23.7M-parameter model trained on 60K games and Maia2's own strong predictions), the signal chain produces consistent monotonic behavioral gradients. Top-move agreement spans 20–25 percentage points between stress and overconfident conditions regardless of underlying model strength. Stage-wise ablation identifies the dynamics stage as the dominant mechanism, accounting for most of the behavioral gradient, while EQ and saturation provide secondary amplification. Competitive scores for the strong-model configuration range from 30.1% under stress to 50.8% under overconfidence, with human baseline data from 7,748 Lichess games validating that the behavioral variation reflects psyche modulation rather than per-move quality differences.

The work demonstrates that formalizing emotional dynamics as structured signal processing can produce more engaging, human-like chess opponents, with potential applicability to any probabilistic game AI.
original_abstract: Chess engines passed human strength years ago, but they still don't play like humans. A grandmaster under clock pressure blunders in ways a club player on a hot streak never would. Conventional engines capture none of this.   This paper proposes a personality x psyche decomposition to produce behavioral variability in chess play, drawing on patterns observed in human games. Personality is static -- a preset that pins down the engine's character. Psyche is dynamic -- a bounded scalar ψ_t \in [-100, +100], recomputed from five positional factors after every move. These two components feed into an audio-inspired signal chain (noise gate, compressor/expander, five-band equalizer, saturation limiter) that reshapes move probability distributions on the fly. The chain doesn't care what engine sits behind it: any system that outputs move probabilities will do. It needs no search and carries no state beyond ψ_t.   I test the framework across 12,414 games against Maia2-1100, feeding it two probability sources that differ by ~2,800x in training data. Both show the same monotonic gradient in top-move agreement (~20-25 pp spread from stress to overconfidence), which tells us the behavioral variation comes from the signal chain, not from the model underneath. When the psyche runs overconfident, the chain mostly gets out of the way (66% agreement with vanilla Maia2). Under stress, the competitive score falls from 50.8% to 30.1%. The patterns are reminiscent of tilt and overconfidence as described in human play, but I should be upfront: this study includes no human-subject validation.

title: A Multilingual Human Annotated Corpus of Original and Easy-to-Read Texts to Support Access to Democratic Participatory Processes
generated_summary:
This paper presents the iDEM Corpus, a multilingual human-annotated resource of original and Easy-to-Read (E2R) texts in Spanish, Catalan, and Italian, designed to support accessibility in democratic participatory processes. The corpus addresses a critical gap in multilingual E2R resources, particularly for politically relevant domains, and represents the first annotated E2R corpus for Catalan along with substantial additions for Spanish and Italian.

The methodology follows a cross-lingual framework for human simplification and annotation. Trained E2R experts simplified texts to a level equivalent to A2 on the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages, following a curated annotation schema adapted to local standards. Crucially, the simplifiers annotated which specific simplification criteria they applied at each step, and these annotations are bundled with the corpus, providing transparency into the simplification process.

The corpus focuses on political, deliberative, and participatory content, reflecting the project's goal of reducing linguistic barriers that exclude people with reading difficulties—including persons with intellectual disabilities, low-literacy populations, and migrants—from democratic processes. The authors analyze the distribution of annotation tags, sentence segments, and word counts across languages.

The significance of this resource is twofold: it provides high-quality training and evaluation data for automated text simplification systems, particularly large language models requiring fine-tuning, and it advances linguistic accessibility research in an underserved but socially critical domain. The corpus is publicly available.
original_abstract: Being able to understand information is a key factor for a self-determined life and society. It is also very important for participating in democratic processes. The study of automatic text simplification is often limited by the availability of high quality material for the training and evaluation on automatic simplifiers. This is true for English, but more so for less resourced languages like Spanish, Catalan and Italian. In order to fill this gap, we present a corpus of original texts for these 3 languages, with high quality simplification produced by human experts in text simplification. It was developed within the iDEM project to assess the impact of Easy-to-Read (E2R) language for democratic participation. The original texts were compiled from domains related to this topic. The corpus includes different text types, selected based on relevance, copyright availability, and ethical standards. All texts were simplified to E2R level. The corpus is particularity valuable because it includes the first annotated corpus of its kind for the Catalan language. It also represents a noteworthy contribution for Spanish and Italian, offering high-quality, human-annotated language resources that are rarely available in these domains. The corpus will be made freely accessible to the public.

title: Building AI Coding Agents for the Terminal: Scaffolding, Harness, Context Engineering, and Lessons Learned
generated_summary:
This paper presents the first comprehensive technical report for an open-source, terminal-native, interactive AI coding agent. The system is designed as a compound AI system—a structured ensemble of agents and workflows rather than a monolithic model—where each cognitive workflow independently binds to a user-configured LLM, enabling fine-grained optimization of cost, latency, and capability.

The architecture is organized around two phases: scaffolding, which assembles the agent before execution (system prompt composition, tool schemas, subagent registration), and the harness, which orchestrates runtime tool dispatch, context management, and safety enforcement. Key technical contributions include an extended ReAct execution pipeline with explicit thinking phases separated from action, adaptive context compaction treating context as a finite budget rather than a buffer, event-driven system reminders that counteract instruction decay in long sessions, and a five-layer defense-in-depth safety architecture that makes dangerous operations structurally impossible through schema gating rather than runtime permission checks.

The paper distills five cross-cutting design tensions from iterative development: context as a budget, behavioral steering over long horizons, safety through architectural constraints, designing for approximate LLM outputs, and bounding unbounded resource growth. Practical lessons include lazy tool discovery reducing startup context costs from 40% to under 5%, fuzzy edit matching to absorb LLM imprecision, and calibrating context management from API-reported token counts rather than local estimates.

This work bridges a significant gap between closed-source industrial practice and open academic discourse in agentic coding systems.
original_abstract: The landscape of AI coding assistance is undergoing a fundamental shift from complex IDE plugins to versatile, terminal-native agents. Operating directly where developers manage source control, execute builds, and deploy environments, CLI-based agents offer unprecedented autonomy for long-horizon development tasks. In this paper, we present OPENDEV, an open-source, command-line coding agent engineered specifically for this new paradigm. Effective autonomous assistance requires strict safety controls and highly efficient context management to prevent context bloat and reasoning degradation. OPENDEV overcomes these challenges through a compound AI system architecture with workload-specialized model routing, a dual-agent architecture separating planning from execution, lazy tool discovery, and adaptive context compaction that progressively reduces older observations. Furthermore, it employs an automated memory system to accumulate project-specific knowledge across sessions and counteracts instruction fade-out through event-driven system reminders. By enforcing explicit reasoning phases and prioritizing context efficiency, OPENDEV provides a secure, extensible foundation for terminal-first AI assistance, offering a blueprint for robust autonomous software engineering.

title: Preserving Continuous Symmetry in Discrete Spaces: Geometric-Aware Quantization for SO(3)-Equivariant GNNs
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of applying low-bit quantization to SO(3)-equivariant graph neural networks without breaking their rotational symmetry properties. The authors identify that naive quantization of equivariant features on anisotropic Cartesian grids destroys the algebraic relationships required for equivariance, leading to violations of physical conservation laws in molecular dynamics simulations.

The proposed Geometric-Aware Quantization (GAQ) framework introduces three key innovations: magnitude-direction decoupled quantization (MDDQ), which separately quantizes vector norms and unit directions on the sphere S² to preserve rotational structure; a geometric straight-through estimator that projects gradients onto the tangent space of the spherical manifold during training; and cosine-normalized attention that stabilizes transformer attention computations under low-precision arithmetic. The framework also employs branch-separated quantization-aware training that handles invariant scalar and equivariant vector features with tailored strategies.

Evaluated on the rMD17 Azobenzene benchmark, the W4A8 quantized model achieves lower energy prediction error (9.31 meV) than the full-precision baseline (23.20 meV), suggesting quantization acts as a structural regularizer. The local equivariance error is suppressed to 0.15 meV/Å, compared to 5.23 meV/Å for naive quantization. Critically, the quantized model maintains stable energy conservation over 1 ns NVE simulations, while naively quantized models diverge within 100 ps. The approach achieves 2.39× inference speedup and 4× memory reduction, demonstrating that symmetry-preserving quantization enables scalable, physically faithful molecular simulations.
original_abstract: Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) are essential for physically consistent molecular simulations but suffer from high computational costs and memory bottlenecks, especially with high-order representations. While low-bit quantization offers a solution, applying it naively to rotation-sensitive features destroys the SO(3)-equivariant structure, leading to significant errors and violations of conservation laws. To address this issue, in this work, we propose a Geometric-Aware Quantization (GAQ) framework that compresses and accelerates equivariant models while rigorously preserving continuous symmetry in discrete spaces. Our approach introduces three key contributions: (1) a Magnitude-Direction Decoupled Quantization (MDDQ) scheme that separates invariant lengths from equivariant orientations to maintain geometric fidelity; (2) a symmetry-aware training strategy that treats scalar and vector features with distinct quantization schedules; and (3) a robust attention normalization mechanism to stabilize gradients in low-bit regimes. Experiments on the rMD17 benchmark demonstrate that our W4A8 models match the accuracy of FP32 baselines (9.31 meV vs. 23.20 meV) while reducing Local Equivariance Error (LEE) by over 30x compared to naive quantization. On consumer hardware, GAQ achieves 2.39x inference speedup and 4x memory reduction, enabling stable, energy-conserving molecular dynamics simulations for nanosecond timescales.

title: On the Statistical Optimality of Optimal Decision Trees
generated_summary:
This paper develops a comprehensive statistical theory for empirically optimal (ERM) decision trees under random design, addressing key gaps in existing theoretical analyses. The main contribution is establishing sharp oracle inequalities and minimax optimal convergence rates for non-dyadic ERM trees, explicitly characterizing the accuracy-interpretability trade-off as a function of the number of leaves.

The authors introduce a novel uniform concentration framework based on empirically localized Rademacher complexity that operates at the level of entire partitions rather than individual leaves, thereby avoiding restrictive structural assumptions such as bounded depth or minimum cell sizes. They also define the Piecewise Sparse Heterogeneous Anisotropic Besov (PSHAB) function space, which captures simultaneous sparsity, anisotropic smoothness, and spatial heterogeneity—properties that reflect the adaptive strengths of tree-based methods.

Key results demonstrate that ERM trees achieve minimax optimal generalization rates over PSHAB spaces for both regression and classification, with explicit dependence on the Besov integrability parameter emerging through the heterogeneity structure rather than sample size. The paper also provides the first explicit convergence rates for tree-based methods under heavy-tailed noise, revealing that performance degradation stems from variance inflation in leaf averaging rather than approximation deficits.

These findings provide rigorous theoretical justification for the empirical success of optimal decision trees, demonstrating their representational superiority for high-dimensional, heterogeneous data and offering a foundation that may extend to analyzing greedy algorithms like CART and Random Forests.
original_abstract: While globally optimal empirical risk minimization (ERM) decision trees have become computationally feasible and empirically successful, rigorous theoretical guarantees for their statistical performance remain limited. In this work, we develop a comprehensive statistical theory for ERM trees under random design in both high-dimensional regression and classification. We first establish sharp oracle inequalities that bound the excess risk of the ERM estimator relative to the best possible approximation achievable by any tree with at most $L$ leaves, thereby characterizing the interpretability-accuracy trade-off. We derive these results using a novel uniform concentration framework based on empirically localized Rademacher complexity. Furthermore, we derive minimax optimal rates over a novel function class: the piecewise sparse heterogeneous anisotropic Besov (PSHAB) space. This space explicitly captures three key structural features encountered in practice: sparsity, anisotropic smoothness, and spatial heterogeneity. While our main results are established under sub-Gaussianity, we also provide robust guarantees that hold under heavy-tailed noise settings. Together, these findings provide a principled foundation for the optimality of ERM trees and introduce empirical process tools broadly applicable to other highly adaptive, data-driven procedures.

title: Garment numbers of bi-colored point sets in the plane
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a systematic study of monochromatic four-point structures in bi-colored (bichromatic) point sets in the plane, motivated by longstanding open problems related to empty monochromatic convex quadrilaterals. The authors define five distinct structures formed by four monochromatic points—cravat, necklace, bowtie, skirt, and pant—and investigate the minimum number of points needed in a bichromatic point set to guarantee the existence of at least one empty monochromatic instance from a given combination of these structures.

The methodology combines computational search for lower bound constructions (point configurations that avoid certain structures) with theoretical proofs for upper bounds, employing inductive arguments and case analysis based on convex hull configurations. The authors systematically analyze multiple settings corresponding to different subsets of the five structures, establishing both new lower and upper bounds.

Key results include resolving the exact threshold for the pant-plus-bowtie setting, narrowing the gap between bounds in the pant-plus-necklace setting, and providing improved lower bounds for settings involving cravats combined with pants or skirts. The paper presents a comprehensive table summarizing known and new bounds across all considered combinations.

The significance of this work lies in providing a more fine-grained framework for understanding blocking configurations in bichromatic point sets, which relates to the broader open question of whether sufficiently large bichromatic point sets must contain empty monochromatic convex quadrilaterals. The authors identify finding upper bounds for settings without pants as the principal remaining challenge.
original_abstract: We consider colored variants of a class of geometric-combinatorial questions on $k$-gons and empty $k$-gons that have been started around 1935 by Erdős and Szekeres. In our setting we have $n$ points in general position in the plane, each one colored either red or blue. A structure on $k$ points is a geometric graph where the edges are spanned by (some of) these points and is called monochromatic if all $k$ points have the same color. Already for $k=4$ there exist interesting open problems. Most prominently, it is still open whether for any sufficiently large bichromatic set there always exists a convex empty, monochromatic quadrilateral. In order to shed more light on the underlying geometry we study the existence of five different monochromatic structures that all use exactly 4 points of a bichromatic point set. We provide several improved lower and upper bounds on the smallest $n$ such that every bichromatic set of at least $n$ points contains (some of) those monochromatic structures.

title: The effect of a toroidal opinion space on opinion bi-polarisation
generated_summary:
This paper systematically compares opinion dynamics on toroidal versus cubic opinion spaces, investigating how the implicit modeling assumption of opinion extremes affects collective behavior. Using a variant of the Axelrod model, the authors simulate 100 agents on a grid with three-dimensional opinions, examining baseline dynamics and two extensions: bounded confidence (limiting interaction between distant opinions) and personalized topical weights (agents weighting opinion dimensions differently).

The key finding is that while both spaces produce nearly identical dynamics in the baseline model—consistently reaching consensus—their behaviors diverge substantially under extensions. The toroidal opinion space, which removes the notion of extreme opinions, consistently supports greater opinion diversity in steady states. Under bounded confidence, the toroidal space shows earlier departure from consensus and more opinion fragmentation, whereas the cubic space exhibits higher probabilities of strict bi-polarization. Adding topical weights amplifies these differences: in the toroidal space, weights enable more disagreement, while in the cubic space they promote agreement. The toroidal model is also more sensitive to network rewiring.

The authors attribute these differences to the symmetric nature of the toroidal space, where all agents are equally affected by model extensions, unlike the cubic space where boundary effects create asymmetries. These results demonstrate that the choice of opinion space—often an unstated assumption—can substantially influence model outcomes and should be explicitly justified in opinion dynamics research.
original_abstract: Many models of opinion dynamics include measures of distance between opinions. Such models are susceptible to boundary effects where the choice of the topology of the opinion space may influence the dynamics. In this paper we study an opinion dynamics model following the seminal model by Axelrod, with the goal of understanding the effect of a toroidal opinion space. To do this we systematically compare two versions of the model: one with toroidal opinion space and one with cubic opinion space.   In their most basic form the two versions of our model result in similar dynamics (consensus is attained eventually). However, as we include bounded confidence and eventually per agent weighting of opinion elements the dynamics become quite contrasting. The toroidal opinion space consistently allows for a greater number of groups in steady state than the cubic opinion space model. Furthermore, the outcome of the dynamics in the toroidal opinion space model are more sensitive to the inclusion of extensions than in the cubic opinion space model.

title: Bayes with No Shame: Admissibility Geometries of Predictive Inference
generated_summary:
This paper establishes that statistical admissibility—the property of not being uniformly dominated by any competing procedure—is irreducibly criterion-relative across four major frameworks in predictive inference. The authors identify four distinct "admissibility geometries": Blackwell admissibility (classical risk dominance, where admissibility equals Bayes optimality via supporting hyperplane priors), anytime-valid admissibility (defined within e-processes via the nonnegative supermartingale property), marginal coverage validity (conformal prediction's exchangeability-based guarantee), and Cesàro-average admissibility (where defensive forecasters steer time-averaged risk to the boundary via fixed-point arguments).

The methodology is primarily geometric and constructive. The authors formalize each criterion within a common framework using convex risk sets and distinct partial orders on predictive procedures. Through canonical Bernoulli examples, they constructively prove separation theorems demonstrating that the four classes of admissible procedures are pairwise non-nested: a procedure optimal under one criterion may be inadmissible under another, and no single algorithm achieves optimality across all four geometries simultaneously.

Key results include the "no-shame" characterization (admissible rules under Blackwell risk are precisely Bayes-optimal rules), the demonstration that martingale coherence bridges Blackwell and anytime-valid geometries but fails to unify all four, and a constrained Bayes formulation that provides a unifying design principle where validity constraints determine the feasible set and Bayesian risk serves as the objective.

The significance lies in making explicit the structural incompatibility among optimality notions used across proper scoring rules, safe testing, conformal prediction, and online learning—resolving cross-talk between these active research programs.
original_abstract: Four distinct admissibility geometries govern sequential and distribution-free inference: Blackwell risk dominance over convex risk sets, anytime-valid admissibility within the nonnegative supermartingale cone, marginal coverage validity over exchangeable prediction sets, and Cesàro approachability (CAA) admissibility, which reaches the risk-set boundary via approachability-style arguments rather than explicit priors. We prove a criterion separation theorem: the four classes of admissible procedures are pairwise non-nested. Each geometry carries a different certificate of optimality: a supporting-hyperplane prior (Blackwell), a nonnegative supermartingale (anytime-valid), an exchangeability rank (coverage), or a Cesàro steering argument (CAA). Martingale coherence is necessary for Blackwell admissibility and necessary and sufficient for anytime-valid admissibility within e-processes, but is not sufficient for Blackwell admissibility and is not necessary for coverage validity or CAA-admissibility. All four criteria share a common optimization template (minimize Bayesian risk subject to a feasibility constraint), but the constraint sets operate over different spaces, partial orders, and performance metrics, making them geometrically incompatible. Admissibility is irreducibly criterion-relative.

title: CT-Enabled Patient-Specific Simulation and Contact-Aware Robotic Planning for Cochlear Implantation
generated_summary:
This paper presents a unified CT-to-simulation pipeline for contact-aware robotic cochlear implant insertion planning that couples patient-specific anatomy reconstruction with differentiable mechanical simulation and online path optimization. The main contribution is integrating three key components: a low-dimensional Cosserat-rod model of the electrode array capturing bending, torsion, shear, and distributed frictional contact; an analytic, differentiable parameterization of the scala-tympani lumen derived from CT imaging that enables efficient closest-point queries and smooth contact computations; and a continuous-time, contact-aware direction-update law under a remote-center-of-motion constraint at the cochlear entrance.

The methodology formulates insertion path optimization as a differentiated equilibrium-constraint problem, producing an online feedback-based direction adaptation strategy that regulates lateral contact forces while maintaining prescribed axial advancement. Contact forces are modeled using regularized Coulomb friction to ensure well-posed evolution across stick-slip transitions.

Simulation and benchtop experiments with varying insertion angles validate the framework, demonstrating that the optimized-path strategy reduces excessive lumen contact, delays buckling onset, and enables deeper electrode insertion compared to constant-path approaches. Optimized trajectories from multiple initial orientations converge to a global optimal insertion direction, showing robustness to initialization.

This work demonstrates how CT-derived patient-specific anatomy can directly enhance both simulation fidelity and robotic planning, advancing toward precise, autonomous, and safety-conscious cochlear implant procedures with potential for closed-loop intraoperative control.
original_abstract: Robotic cochlear-implant (CI) insertion requires precise prediction and regulation of contact forces to minimize intracochlear trauma and prevent failure modes such as locking and buckling. Aligned with the integration of advanced medical imaging and robotics for autonomous, precision interventions, this paper presents a unified CT-to-simulation pipeline for contact-aware insertion planning and validation. We develop a low-dimensional, differentiable Cosserat-rod model of the electrode array coupled with frictional contact and pseudo-dynamics regularization to ensure continuous stick-slip transitions. Patient-specific cochlear anatomy is reconstructed from CT imaging and encoded via an analytic parametrization of the scala-tympani lumen, enabling efficient and differentiable contact queries through closest-point projection. Based on a differentiated equilibrium-constraint formulation, we derive an online direction-update law under an RCM-like constraint that suppresses lateral insertion forces while maintaining axial advancement. Simulations and benchtop experiments validate deformation and force trends, demonstrating reduced locking/buckling risk and improved insertion depth. The study highlights how CT-based imaging enhances modeling, planning, and safety capabilities in robot-assisted inner-ear procedures.

title: Computational Complexity of Alignments
generated_summary:
This paper presents a systematic computational complexity analysis of the alignment problem in process mining, which measures how well observed process execution traces conform to normative process models specified as Petri nets. Alignments are the state-of-the-art technique in conformance checking, yet their computational hardness had not been thoroughly characterized across different model classes.

The authors establish complexity results for alignments across a hierarchy of Petri net classes using reductions, structural theory, and connections to reachability and membership problems. For safe Petri nets and sound workflow nets, the alignment problem is shown to be PSPACE-complete, matching the complexity of the reachability problem. For live, bounded, free-choice systems, the authors leverage the Shortest Sequence Theorem to prove that optimal alignments have polynomial length, placing the problem in NP. They then establish NP-completeness for this class and demonstrate a striking complexity gap: while reachability drops to polynomial time on several restricted classes (process trees, T-systems, acyclic systems), the alignment problem remains NP-complete. Only for live, safe S-systems do alignments become polynomial-time solvable, though relaxing either liveness or safeness restores NP-completeness.

These results are significant for process mining practice, as they identify which structural properties of process models fundamentally influence alignment complexity and guide the selection of appropriate algorithmic approaches. The findings confirm that high computational costs for conformance checking on general models are unavoidable while highlighting tractable special cases.
original_abstract: In process mining, alignments quantify the degree of deviation between an observed event trace and a business process model and constitute the most important conformance checking technique. We study the algorithmic complexity of computing alignments over important classes of Petri nets. First, we show that the alignment problem is PSPACE-complete on the class of safe Petri nets and also on the class of safe and sound workflow nets. For live, bounded, free-choice systems, we prove the existence of optimal alignments of polynomial length which positions the alignment problem in NP for this class. We further show that computing alignments is NP-complete even on basic subclasses such as process trees and T-systems. We establish NP-completeness on several related classes as well, including acyclic systems. Finally, we demonstrate that on live, safe S-systems the alignment problem is solvable in P and that both assumptions (liveness and safeness) are crucial for this result.

title: Dark3R: Learning Structure from Motion in the Dark
generated_summary:
Dark3R introduces an end-to-end framework for structure from motion (SfM) in extreme low-light conditions, where image signal-to-noise ratios fall well below 0 dB. The core contribution is adapting the strong geometric priors of 3D foundation models like MASt3R to the low-light regime through a teacher-student knowledge distillation strategy. The student model learns to predict dense feature maps from noisy raw images that align with feature maps produced by the teacher model on well-exposed counterparts, requiring no 3D supervision—only paired noisy-clean raw images, which can be captured or synthesized using a Poisson-Gaussian noise model.

To support training and evaluation, the authors introduce a novel dataset of approximately 42,000 multi-view, exposure-bracketed raw images with accurate 3D annotations across nearly 100 scenes. The predicted feature correspondences feed into MASt3R-SfM's global optimization and bundle adjustment pipeline for camera pose and depth recovery. Combined with a coarse-to-fine radiance field optimization scheme, the framework also enables novel view synthesis from extremely noisy inputs.

Experiments demonstrate that Dark3R maintains substantially better pose accuracy, depth consistency, and photometric reconstruction quality compared to state-of-the-art baselines as SNR decreases, with particularly pronounced advantages below 0 dB. The method generalizes across different camera sensors without retraining. This work opens passive 3D sensing to low-light environments previously inaccessible to existing reconstruction methods.
original_abstract: We introduce Dark3R, a framework for structure from motion in the dark that operates directly on raw images with signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) below $-4$ dB -- a regime where conventional feature- and learning-based methods break down. Our key insight is to adapt large-scale 3D foundation models to extreme low-light conditions through a teacher--student distillation process, enabling robust feature matching and camera pose estimation in low light. Dark3R requires no 3D supervision; it is trained solely on noisy--clean raw image pairs, which can be either captured directly or synthesized using a simple Poisson--Gaussian noise model applied to well-exposed raw images. To train and evaluate our approach, we introduce a new, exposure-bracketed dataset that includes $\sim$42,000 multi-view raw images with ground-truth 3D annotations, and we demonstrate that Dark3R achieves state-of-the-art structure from motion in the low-SNR regime. Further, we demonstrate state-of-the-art novel view synthesis in the dark using Dark3R's predicted poses and a coarse-to-fine radiance field optimization procedure.

title: FairFinGAN: Fairness-aware Synthetic Financial Data Generation
generated_summary:
This paper introduces FairFinGAN, a Wasserstein GAN-based framework for generating fairness-aware synthetic financial tabular data. The main contribution is a two-phase training strategy that incorporates fairness constraints into the generative process, producing synthetic datasets that mitigate bias with respect to protected attributes while preserving data utility.

The methodology employs a two-phase approach: the first phase trains the generator and critic through standard adversarial learning to produce realistic synthetic samples, while the second phase penalizes discrimination by incorporating fairness metrics—statistical parity (FairFinGAN-SP) or equalized odds (FairFinGAN-EOd)—computed via a pre-trained multi-layer perceptron classifier on generated samples as additional loss components. The generator is then iteratively updated to reduce these fairness violations.

Extensive experiments are conducted on five real-world financial datasets (Adult, Credit Card, Credit Scoring, Dutch Census, and German Credit) using four traditional classifiers and seven fairness measures. Results demonstrate that FairFinGAN achieves improved dataset-level statistical parity and generally obtains favorable trade-offs between fairness and predictive accuracy compared to baseline methods CTGAN and TabFairGAN. FairFinGAN-EOd tends to excel on equalized odds-related metrics, while FairFinGAN-SP performs better on statistical parity measures.

The significance of this work lies in its applicability to financial domains such as lending and credit scoring, where fairness-aware data generation can help reduce historical bias and align automated decision-making with regulatory requirements while maintaining predictive performance.
original_abstract: Financial datasets often suffer from bias that can lead to unfair decision-making in automated systems. In this work, we propose FairFinGAN, a WGAN-based framework designed to generate synthetic financial data while mitigating bias with respect to the protected attribute. Our approach incorporates fairness constraints directly into the training process through a classifier, ensuring that the synthetic data is both fair and preserves utility for downstream predictive tasks. We evaluate our proposed model on five real-world financial datasets and compare it with existing GAN-based data generation methods. Experimental results show that our approach achieves superior fairness metrics without significant loss in data utility, demonstrating its potential as a tool for bias-aware data generation in financial applications.

title: Riemannian Geometry of Optimal Rebalancing in Dynamic Weight Automated Market Makers
generated_summary:
This paper reveals the Riemannian geometric structure underlying optimal weight rebalancing in dynamic automated market makers, specifically Temporal Function Market Making (TFMM) pools that use geometric mean market makers. The authors demonstrate that the per-step arbitrage loss during weight rebalancing is a KL divergence between weight vectors, establishing the Fisher–Rao metric as the natural Riemannian structure on the weight simplex. Under this framework, the loss-minimizing interpolation corresponds to Spherical Linear Interpolation (SLERP) in Hellinger coordinates—geodesics on the positive orthant of the unit sphere.

A key theoretical result proves that the SLERP midpoint exactly equals the previously proposed (AM+GM)/normalise heuristic for any number of tokens, explaining why that heuristic captures nearly all improvement over linear interpolation despite lacking geometric justification. The authors establish that SLERP's sub-optimality relative to the exact KL-optimal trajectory scales as O(1/f⁴), where f is the number of interpolation steps. They also derive a trigonometric-function-free recursive bisection algorithm for computing exact SLERP trajectories at power-of-two step counts.

Numerical experiments validate these results, showing SLERP achieves near-perfect per-step loss uniformity (std/mean of 0.02%) and that brute-force optimization cannot improve upon SLERP meaningfully. Near simplex boundaries, where the Fisher–Rao metric diverges, SLERP's advantage over linear interpolation becomes particularly pronounced. These findings provide a unified information-geometric framework for understanding and optimizing rebalancing costs in multi-token AMM pools.
original_abstract: In Temporal Function Market Making (TFMM), a dynamic weight AMM pool rebalances from initial to final holdings by creating a series of arbitrage opportunities whose total cost depends on the weight trajectory taken. We show that the per-step arbitrage loss is the KL divergence between new and old weight vectors, meaning the Fisher--Rao metric is the natural Riemannian metric on the weight simplex. The loss-minimising interpolation under the leading-order expansion of this KL cost is SLERP (Spherical Linear Interpolation) in the Hellinger coordinates $η_i = \sqrt{w_i}$, i.e.\ a geodesic on the positive orthant of the unit sphere traversed at constant speed. The SLERP midpoint equals the (AM+GM)/normalise heuristic of prior work (Willetts & Harrington, 2024), so the heuristic lies on the geodesic. This identity holds for any number of tokens and any magnitude of weight change; using this link, all dyadic points on the geodesic can be reached by recursive AM-GM bisection without trigonometric functions. SLERP's relative sub-optimality on the full KL cost is proportional to the squared magnitude of the overall weight change and to $1/f^2$, where $f$ is the number of interpolation steps.

title: AttentiveLearn: Personalized Post-Lecture Support for Gaze-Aware Immersive Learning
generated_summary:
This paper introduces AttentiveLearn, a learning ecosystem that bridges immersive virtual reality lectures with personalized post-lecture support by leveraging eye-tracking attention data. The system comprises three components: a gaze-aware VR classroom that captures learners' eye-tracking data during lectures, a data processing pipeline that computes attention metrics, and a mobile learning assistant that delivers personalized quiz questions targeting content areas where individual learners exhibited lower attention.

The authors conducted a four-week between-subjects field study with 36 university students attending weekly VR lectures on Bayesian data analysis. The attentive group received personalized quizzes based on their gaze data, while the control group received randomly generated quizzes. The study collected survey data on motivation and engagement, intermediate and final exam scores, interaction logs, and semi-structured interviews.

Results demonstrate that attention-aware personalization significantly improved self-reported engagement, intrinsic goal orientation, self-efficacy, and perceived task value compared to the control group. The attentive group maintained stable intermediate exam performance across weeks, while the control group experienced significant score declines as content difficulty increased. However, no significant differences emerged in the final exam. Qualitative findings suggest that personalized quizzes helped learners identify attention gaps, set targeted review goals, and develop transferable learning strategies.

This work contributes empirical evidence for extending immersive learning beyond in-lecture interventions, demonstrating that attention-aware ex-situ personalization can meaningfully enhance motivation, engagement, and intermediate learning outcomes in real-world educational settings.
original_abstract: Immersive learning environments such as virtual classrooms in Virtual Reality (VR) offer learners unique learning experiences, yet providing effective learner support remains a challenge. While prior HCI research has explored in-lecture support for immersive learning, little research has been conducted to provide post-lecture support, despite being critical for sustained motivation, engagement, and learning outcomes. To address this, we present AttentiveLearn, a learning ecosystem that generates personalized quizzes on a mobile learning assistant based on learners' attention distribution inferred using eye-tracking in VR lectures. We evaluated the system in a four-week field study with 36 university students attending lectures on Bayesian data analysis. AttentiveLearn improved learners' reported motivation and engagement, without conclusive evidence of learning gains. Meanwhile, anecdotal evidence suggested improvements in attention for certain participants over time. Based on our findings of the field study, we provide empirical insights and design implications for personalized post-lecture support for immersive learning systems.

title: Designing for Adolescent Voice in Health Decisions: Embodied Conversational Agents for HPV Vaccination
generated_summary:
This paper presents ClaraEdu, a mobile Embodied Conversational Agent (ECA) intervention designed to give adolescents an active voice in HPV vaccination decisions alongside their parents. The main contribution is a "dual-path" architecture that simultaneously addresses both members of the parent-child dyad: parents interact with a simulated physician character (Dr. Clara), while adolescents can choose between the same physician-led educational experience or a gamified narrative path featuring character customization, forest exploration, and HPV-related riddles delivered through engaging storytelling mechanics.

The system was evaluated through a clinic-based pilot study with 21 parent-adolescent dyads. The study assessed satisfaction and attitudes toward the app and conversational agent, as well as exploratory measures of changes in HPV knowledge, attitudes, and vaccination intention from baseline to post-intervention. The planned randomized controlled trial was converted to a pilot evaluation due to abrupt termination of federal funding.

Results indicate that both parents and adolescents reported satisfaction and attitude scores significantly above neutral, supporting the first hypothesis. Exploratory efficacy findings suggest positive trends in HPV knowledge, attitudes, and vaccination intention, with the adolescent-facing tools appearing to enhance vaccination intention within the family unit.

The significance of this work lies in its novel approach to treating adolescents as active participants rather than passive recipients in health decisions, while respecting parental authority. The dual-audience ECA design addresses a gap in existing systems that rarely mediate the parent-child dyad simultaneously, offering a promising framework for shared clinical decision-making.
original_abstract: Adolescents are directly affected by preventive health decisions such as vaccination, yet their perspectives are rarely solicited or supported. Most digital interventions for Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination are designed exclusively for parents, implicitly treating adolescents as passive recipients rather than stakeholders with agency. We present the design and evaluation of a mobile intervention that gives adolescents a voice in HPV vaccination decisions alongside their parents. The system uses embodied conversational agents tailored to each audience: parents interact with an animated physician using education and motivational interviewing techniques, while adolescents can choose between an age-appropriate doctor or a narrative fantasy game that conveys HPV facts through play. We report findings from a clinic-based pilot study with 21 parent-adolescent dyads. Results indicate high satisfaction across both audiences, improved HPV knowledge, and increased intent to vaccinate. We discuss design implications for supporting adolescent participation, choice, and agency in decisions about their health.

title: GALACTIC: Global and Local Agnostic Counterfactuals for Time-series Clustering
generated_summary:
This paper introduces GALACTIC, a unified framework for generating both local and global counterfactual explanations for time-series clustering in a model-agnostic setting. The main contribution is bridging the gap between instance-level counterfactual reasoning and cluster-level explanatory summaries, enabling practitioners to understand why time series belong to specific clusters and what minimal changes would cause transitions between clusters.

At the local level, GALACTIC employs an importance-guided gradient search that restricts modifications to discriminative temporal regions identified through subgroup-level permutation analysis, producing sparse, shape-preserving counterfactuals. At the global level, the framework formulates the selection of representative perturbation patterns as an information-theoretic model selection problem using the Minimum Description Length (MDL) principle. This approach resolves the traditional multi-objective trade-off between coverage and complexity without requiring arbitrary parameter tuning. The authors prove that the MDL objective is a monotone submodular set function, enabling efficient greedy selection with provable approximation guarantees. An adaptive hierarchical refinement mechanism further adjusts the number of global counterfactuals based on the internal density and structural complexity of cluster subgroups.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that GALACTIC consistently outperforms adapted state-of-the-art baselines, producing sparser local counterfactuals and more concise global summaries with higher coverage while maintaining computational efficiency. The framework has significant implications for making time-series clustering actionable across domains including finance, neuroscience, and critical infrastructure, transforming opaque cluster assignments into interpretable, decision-supporting insights.
original_abstract: Time-series clustering is a fundamental tool for pattern discovery, yet existing explainability methods, primarily based on feature attribution or metadata, fail to identify the transitions that move an instance across cluster boundaries. While Counterfactual Explanations (CEs) identify the minimal temporal perturbations required to alter the prediction of a model, they have been mostly confined to supervised settings. This paper introduces GALACTIC, the first unified framework to bridge local and global counterfactual explainability for unsupervised time-series clustering. At instance level (local), GALACTIC generates perturbations via a cluster-aware optimization objective that respects the target and underlying cluster assignments. At cluster level (global), to mitigate cognitive load and enhance interpretability, we formulate a representative CE selection problem. We propose a Minimum Description Length (MDL) objective to extract a non-redundant summary of global explanations that characterize the transitions between clusters. We prove that our MDL objective is supermodular, which allows the corresponding MDL reduction to be framed as a monotone submodular set function. This enables an efficient greedy selection algorithm with provable $(1-1/e)$ approximation guarantees. Extensive experimental evaluation on the UCR Archive demonstrates that GALACTIC produces significantly sparser local CEs and more concise global summaries than state-of-the-art baselines adapted for our problem, offering the first unified approach for interpreting clustered time-series through counterfactuals.

title: How important are the genes to explain the outcome - the asymmetric Shapley value as an honest importance metric for high-dimensional features
generated_summary:
This paper proposes asymmetric Shapley values as a framework for quantifying the importance of high-dimensional genomic features alongside low-dimensional clinical variables in prediction models, accounting for causal ordering between features. The main contribution addresses two shortcomings of conventional leave-one-feature-out approaches: their failure to handle correlations between feature groups and their disregard for temporal or causal ordering, particularly the mediating role of disease state between genes and outcomes.

The authors develop several methodological extensions, including grouped asymmetric Shapley values for high-dimensional features, subset-based asymmetric weights for efficient computation, an importance sampling approximation for many features, and a dimension reduction approach for modeling conditional dependencies in mixed-dimensional settings. They also propose two inference methods using local Shapley values to test global feature importance. The framework is applied to predicting progression-free survival in colorectal cancer patients, combining gene expression data from 500 genes with clinical variables.

Key results demonstrate that asymmetric Shapley values substantially increase the perceived importance of genomic features compared to both symmetric Shapley values and the naive leave-one-feature-out approach, which showed only modest performance decline when genes were removed. The asymmetric version more effectively captures the mediation effect of tumor stage on the gene-outcome relationship, particularly for patients with advanced disease.

This framework provides a principled, interpretable decomposition of predictive performance metrics like C-index across features of varying dimensionality while respecting known directional relationships.
original_abstract: In clinical prediction settings the importance of a high-dimensional feature like genomics is often assessed by evaluating the change in predictive performance when adding it to a set of traditional clinical variables. This approach is questionable, because it does not account for collinearity nor known directionality of dependencies between variables. We suggest to use asymmetric Shapley values as a more suitable alternative to quantify feature importance in the context of a mixed-dimensional prediction model. We focus on a setting that is particularly relevant in clinical prediction: disease state as a mediating variable for genomic effects, with additional confounders for which the direction of effects may be unknown. We derive efficient algorithms to compute local and global asymmetric Shapley values for this setting. The former are shown to be very useful for inference, whereas the latter provide interpretation by decomposing any predictive performance metric into contributions of the features. Throughout, we illustrate our framework by a leading example: the prediction of progression-free survival for colorectal cancer patients.

title: Frequency-Aware Error-Bounded Caching for Accelerating Diffusion Transformers
generated_summary:
This paper introduces SpectralCache, a caching framework for accelerating Diffusion Transformer (DiT) inference that exploits three previously unrecognized axes of non-uniformity in the denoising process: temporal, depth, and feature heterogeneity. The authors demonstrate that existing caching methods treat denoising as uniform, applying identical thresholds across all timesteps, blocks, and feature dimensions, which limits their effectiveness.

SpectralCache addresses these limitations through three tightly coupled components. Timestep-Aware Dynamic Scheduling (TADS) modulates caching thresholds using a cosine bell schedule, enabling aggressive caching during tolerant middle timesteps while protecting sensitive early and late phases. Cumulative Error Budgets (CEB) limit consecutive cached timesteps to prevent error-amplifying cascades through the residual stream. Frequency-Decomposed Caching (FDC) partitions hidden states into frequency bands with asymmetric thresholds, capturing heterogeneous temporal dynamics across feature dimensions.

Evaluated on FLUX.1-schnell at 512×512 resolution, SpectralCache achieves 1.46× speedup while maintaining near-identical quality to the uncached baseline (LPIPS 0.058, SSIM 0.953), outperforming TeaCache by 16% in speed with less than 1% difference in perceptual quality metrics. Ablation studies confirm that each component provides meaningful contributions, with TADS and CEB together yielding the best quality preservation while FDC adds frequency-aware gating benefits.

The framework demonstrates that exploiting structural non-uniformities in diffusion inference enables superior quality-speed tradeoffs, with planned extensions to video diffusion transformers and composition with orthogonal acceleration techniques.
original_abstract: Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) have emerged as the dominant architecture for high-quality image and video generation, yet their iterative denoising process incurs substantial computational cost during inference. Existing caching methods accelerate DiTs by reusing intermediate computations across timesteps, but they share a common limitation: treating the denoising process as uniform across time,depth, and feature dimensions. In this work, we identify three orthogonal axes of non-uniformity in DiT denoising: (1) temporal -- sensitivity to caching errors varies dramatically across the denoising trajectory; (2) depth -- consecutive caching decisions lead to cascading approximation errors; and (3) feature -- different components of the hidden state exhibit heterogeneous temporal dynamics. Based on these observations, we propose SpectralCache, a unified caching framework comprising Timestep-Aware Dynamic Scheduling (TADS), Cumulative Error Budgets (CEB), and Frequency-Decomposed Caching (FDC). original_abstract: Continuum parallel robots (CPR) combine rigid actuation mechanisms with multiple elastic rods in a closed-loop topology, making forward statics challenging when rigid--continuum junctions are enforced by explicit kinematic constraints. A fourth-order Magnus approximation yields an explicit and geometrically consistent mapping between element end poses and the strain. title: SLICE: Speech Enhancement via Layer-wise Injection of Conditioning Embeddings

original_abstract: Acoustic scattering by vehicle surfaces can have significant effects on overall noise levels. After showing linear stability for rotating circles, we prove the existence of rotating waves by combining a bifurcation-theoretical approach together with critical point theory. Finally, by exploiting the Hamiltonian structure, we show that whenever volume and barycenter are fixed to be the same as those of rotating circle, this solution is also conditionally energetically stable. original_abstract: Simulating the dynamics of molecular excitons in complex nanophotonic environments requires integrating rigorous electromagnetic simulations with accurate treatments of open quantum system dynamics. In this work, we develop MQED-QD (Macroscopic Quantum Electrodynamics for Quantum Dynamics), a robust computational package for simulating exciton dynamics in arbitrary dielectric and plasmonic environments. Based on the MQED framework, the package offers a unified workflow for constructing the dyadic Green's functions from classical electromagnetic solvers, parametrizing quantum master equations, and propagating the time evolution to determine the molecular subsystem's dynamical properties. To demonstrate the package's capabilities, we simulate exciton transport within a one-dimensional molecular chain near a silver nanostructure, including benchmarking against planar surfaces and exploring the influence of silver nanorods. Our results reveal that surface plasmon polaritons on nanorods dramatically enhance long-range dipole-dipole interactions, accelerating exciton delocalization and yielding higher participation ratios compared to planar geometries. By elucidating accurate molecular exciton dynamics in conjunction with nanophotonics and plasmonics, MQED-QD provides a powerful, open-source package that facilitates the rational design of nanoscale architectures.

title: Benchmarking mixed quantum-classical dynamics for collective electronic strong coupling

Here, we benchmark mixed quantum-classical approaches, Ehrenfest dynamics and Fewest-Switches Surface Hopping (FSSH), for simulating nonadiabatic dynamics of electronically strongly coupled carbon monoxide molecules. Their predictions are compared against numerically exact quantum dynamics simulations performed with the multi-configuration time-dependent Hartree (MCTDH) method, which treats both electronic and nuclear degrees of freedom quantum mechanically. We find that the semi-classical approaches reproduce the qualitative features of the full quantum dynamics. Quantitative agreement is best achieved with FSSH when a decoherence correction is included. title: Detection of C3 in Titan with VLT-ESPRESSO

title: Cubic magneto-optic Kerr effect in Co(111) thin films

Here, the change in polarization upon reflection from the magnetized sample is mainly regarded as being linearly proportional to the magnetization $\mathbf{M}$ (LinMOKE). This CMOKE manifests itself as an anisotropic contribution to the MOKE signal (with regard to the crystallographic orientation) measured in longitudinal or transversal configuration in full magnetic saturation. While LinMOKE (odd in $\mathbf{M}$) and QMOKE (even in $\mathbf{M}$) can easily be separated by methods based on magnetization parity, this no longer holds true for LinMOKE and CMOKE (odd in $\mathbf{M}$). While the QMOKE is almost vanishing in Co(111) using light with wavelengths of 635\,nm and 406\,nm, the CMOKE contributions reach up to about 30\% of the LinMOKE contribution at an AoI of 45 degrees and become even more dominant towards normal AoI, which emphasizes the importance of higher-order MOKE effects in magneto-optic experiments.

title: Impact of scissors-correction schemes on second-harmonic generation in ultraviolet nonlinear-optical crystals

Scheme-N yields systematically 15\%--25\% larger magnitudes than scheme-L, although for several tensor components scheme-L agrees better with available experimental benchmarks. title: Pulse-duration-sensitive high harmonics and attosecond locally-chiral light from a chiral topological Weyl semimetal

Here, we theoretically reveal that the driving pulse duration can play a major role in extending HHG to higher photon energies by promoting higher conduction band excitations. The effect is present in a conventional semiconductor as Si, restricted in a large-gap insulator as MgO, and most prominent in RhSi, a prototypical chiral Weyl semimetal presenting numerous band crossings. Further, we elucidate the HHG selection rules in RhSi required for the synthesis of attosecond locally chiral light. The chiral crystal structure enables the generation of a local 3D electric field exhibiting an asymmetric instantaneous torsion on attosecond timescales. A pronounced circular dichroism emerges when the driving helicity is either aligned with or opposite to the crystal handedness. Our findings motivate future experiments in chiral Weyl semimetals to track high-energy band crossings and in-situ locally chiral light, paving the way for chiral compact light sources and light-wave driven topological electronics.

title: Comparison of data-driven symmetry-preserving closure models for large-eddy simulation

original_abstract: Symmetries are fundamental to both turbulence and differential equations. The large-eddy simulation (LES) equations inherit these symmetries provided the LES closure respects them. Classical LES closures based on eddy viscosity or scale similarity preserve many of the original symmetries by design. In this work, we compare approaches for constructing symmetry-preserving data-driven LES closures, including tensor-basis neural networks (TBNNs) and group-convolutional neural networks, alongside unconstrained convolutional networks. All three data-driven closures outperform classical models in both the functional sense (producing the right amount of dissipation) and the structural sense (stress tensor prediction). While unconstrained networks achieve comparable prediction accuracy, symmetry-preserving models produce more physically consistent velocity-gradient statistics, suggesting that enforcing symmetries improves the quality of the learned closure beyond what aggregate error metrics such as relative tensor prediction errors capture.

title: The Angular Localization Function (ALF): a practical tool to measure solvent angular order with Molecular Density Functional Theory

Mathematically, ALF is defined as the Kullback-Leibler divergence between the isotropic orientation distribution and the actual distribution, connecting it to the first-order orientational entropy contribution within the ideal part of the free energy functional.

ALF is computed within the framework of Molecular Density Functional Theory (MDFT), which provides the full six-dimensional solvent density field at significantly lower computational cost than molecular dynamics simulations, while maintaining high spatial and angular resolution. The authors demonstrate ALF's utility on three systems solvated in water: a single water molecule, an octanol molecule, and three neutral clay minerals (talc, fluorotalc, and pyrophyllite). These applications reveal that ALF provides complementary insights to conventional metrics such as number density and dipolar polarization. Notably, ALF identifies regions of strong orientational anisotropy near hydrogen-bonding sites and within hexagonal cavities at clay surfaces, even in low-density regions where traditional density-based analyses prove insufficient.

ALF represents a practical visualization and analysis tool for understanding complex solvation structures, particularly relevant for studying solid-liquid interfaces, biological solvation environments, and systems where orientational ordering plays a critical role.
original_abstract: Molecular density functional theory is a powerful technique for efficiently computing the spatially and orientationally dependent equilibrium density of a molecular solvent around an arbitrary solute. This density encodes the detailed solvent structure, but contains so much information that it is difficult to interpret comprehensively. Although spatial dependence is frequently analyzed through orientationally integrated number density, angular information remains poorly exploited. The present work addresses this gap by introducing a function that provides a local measure of the angular order: the Angular Localization Function (ALF), derived from the ideal free energy functional, which quantifies the entropy. We discuss the connections between ALF and well known statistical functions. We illustrate the utility of ALF by discussing the solvent structure for three systems immersed in water: water as a solute, an octanol molecule, and three clay minerals (talc, fluorotalc and pyrophyllite) with small differences in their structure leading to subtle effects on their interactions with water. ALF provides information complementary to quantities such as the average polarization or charge density to characterize the local orientational distribution of solvent molecules around solutes and next to surfaces. It also offers a convenient visualization tool akin to the Electronic Localization Function (ELF) used to analyze bonding in quantum chemistry.

title: Why Projection-Based DMRG-in-DFT Cannot Be Exact, Even with the Exact Exchange-Correlation Functional
generated_summary:
This paper establishes the theoretical foundations of projection-based wavefunction-in-DFT embedding and demonstrates that such schemes cannot be formally exact, even with access to the exact exchange-correlation functional. The authors construct an exact energy functional for a multideterminantal wavefunction embedded in a Kohn-Sham environment and show that, analogous to orbital-free embedding, it contains an unknown kinetic-energy functional. The standard projection-based formulation renders this functional nonvariational, precluding formal exactness.

The methodology combines density matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations for strongly correlated active regions with DFT descriptions of the environment within a projection-based framework. The authors analyze sources of error using model systems, including linear hydrogen chains and propionitrile, benchmarking DMRG-in-DFT results against full DMRG calculations across bond dissociation coordinates.

Key findings reveal that the nonadditive exchange-correlation energy is the principal error source in approximate projection-based DMRG-in-DFT. Crucially, the fractional-spin error of approximate exchange-correlation functionals is not the dominant source of inaccuracy in dissociating systems. The use of pair-density functional theory, which is free of fractional-spin error and ostensibly better suited for strongly correlated systems, actually produces larger errors than conventional functionals like PBE. Errors diminish when density overlap between subsystems is reduced, either by enlarging the active region or increasing inter-fragment distances.

These results have significant implications for the design and interpretation of embedding methods targeting strongly correlated systems, clarifying fundamental limitations of the projection-based WF-in-DFT approach.
original_abstract: We establish the theoretical foundations for embedding a correlated wave function in an environment formed by Kohn-Sham orbitals. We show that introducing an approximation which equates two, in principle distinct, kinetic-energy functionals yields an embedding functional identical to the projection-based wavefunction-in-DFT formulation of Miller and co-workers. We demonstrate that this functional is inherently nonvariational: its minimum is not guaranteed to coincide with the exact ground-state energy and remains bounded from above by it. Building on this formal framework, we analyze the dominant sources of error in projection-based DMRG-in-DFT embedding with approximate exchange-correlation (xc) functionals. Using molecules with dissociating covalent bonds as a diagnostic example, we demonstrate that the primary source of error is the nonadditive exchange-correlation energy describing the nonclassical coupling between the active subsystem and its environment. Eliminating the fractional-spin error by employing a pair-density xc functional (PDFT) instead of a semilocal GGA does not remedy this deficiency, because the inaccuracy stems from self-interaction effects at the subsystem-environment interface.

title: Wealth Tax Neutrality as Drift-Shift Symmetry: A Statistical Physics Formulation
generated_summary:
