The central insight is that the geometric Brownian motion underlying standard finance models is mathematically equivalent to a Langevin equation with multiplicative noise, allowing the evolution of wealth distributions across investors to be analyzed using stochastic dynamics tools.

The authors demonstrate that a proportional wealth tax is neutral—meaning it does not distort investment decisions or portfolio allocations—if and only if it enters the Fokker–Planck equation as a uniform, state-independent shift of the drift coefficient, which they term "drift-shift symmetry." This formulation makes the symmetry content of neutrality transparent and mathematically precise. Each violation of neutrality (book-value assessment, liquidity frictions, dividend extraction, investor migration, and market impact) maps to a specific, classifiable symmetry-breaking mechanism that deforms the wealth distribution in distinct ways, providing an exhaustive taxonomy of distortions.

Key results include the demonstration that this symmetry is robust to non-Gaussian returns and stochastic volatility, and that relaxation toward new steady-state distributions after tax changes occurs on timescales exceeding typical electoral cycles. The framework naturally accommodates questions about wealth distribution evolution, steady states, and the interplay between individual dynamics and aggregate outcomes that lie beyond representative-agent asset pricing, offering a unified language for economists and physicists studying wealth taxation.
original_abstract: We reformulate the neutral wealth tax framework of Froeseth (2026) in the language of stochastic dynamics and statistical physics. Individual wealth under geometric Brownian motion satisfies a Langevin equation with multiplicative noise; the probability density of wealth across a population then evolves according to a Fokker-Planck equation. A proportional wealth tax at market value enters as a uniform reduction of the drift coefficient, preserving the diffusion structure and all relative probability currents. This drift-shift symmetry is the physical content of tax neutrality. Each channel through which neutrality breaks down in practice, book-value assessment, liquidity frictions, forced dividend extraction, migration, and market impact, corresponds to a specific violation of this symmetry: a state-dependent, asset-dependent, or flow-dependent modification of the Fokker-Planck equation. The framework clarifies when wealth taxation is a benign rescaling of the dynamics and when it introduces genuinely new physics.

title: Probing vacuum birefringence in an Ultrastrong Laser Field via High-energy Gamma-ray Polarimetry
generated_summary:

The key innovation is a "self-probing" architecture where a single ultrastrong laser pulse serves a dual role: it generates multi-GeV circularly polarized gamma-ray photons via nonlinear Compton scattering from a relativistic electron beam and simultaneously acts as the birefringent medium through which these photons propagate. This eliminates the synchronization, alignment, and beam-transport challenges that have hindered conventional pump-probe experiments.

Using comprehensive Monte Carlo simulations with a 3 GeV longitudinally polarized electron beam colliding with a petawatt-class laser pulse, the authors observe an average refractive index difference of approximately 10⁻¹² for selected photons, accumulating a phase delay of about 10⁻² radians over micron-scale interaction lengths. This represents a signal enhancement of nearly ten orders of magnitude compared to traditional optical experiments. The study identifies an optimal operational window around specific laser intensity and electron energy parameters that maximizes the birefringent signal while minimizing competing vacuum dichroism effects. The authors demonstrate that a statistically significant 5σ detection is feasible with as few as two laser shots using existing multi-petawatt laser and accelerator facilities, presenting a practical pathway toward the first definitive laboratory confirmation of this long-sought QED phenomenon.
original_abstract: Vacuum birefringence (VB), a fundamental prediction of nonlinear quantum electrodynamics (QED), has eluded direct laboratory detection due to its extreme weakness. We propose a compact, "self-probing" scheme where a GeV electron beam collides head-on with a petawatt laser pulse. Circularly polarized gamma-ray photons, generated via nonlinear Compton scattering in the same pulse, then probe the birefringent vacuum it induces. This integrated design bypasses the stringent synchronization and beam transport requirements of traditional pump-probe setups. Our nonperturbative strong-field QED simulations reveal a clear VB signature: conversion of circular to linear polarization, with the induced Stokes parameter $S_1$ reaching ~0.019 within the selected angular range. This corresponds to a refractive index difference $Δn = 1.829 \times 10^{-4}$ over micron-scale paths, directly measurable as a high-contrast "X-shape" asymmetry in $e^+e^-$ pair distributions. The scheme provides a feasible path to first laboratory VB detection with current laser and accelerator technologies.

title: Extensions to the Wealth Tax Neutrality Framework
generated_summary:
This paper extends a wealth tax neutrality framework to investigate the conditions under which proportional wealth taxes remain neutral with respect to portfolio choice, asset pricing, and equilibrium outcomes, and identifies the channels through which real-world implementations depart from neutrality. The authors employ analytical methods spanning stochastic volatility models (including the Heston model), general Markov diffusions, and Epstein–Zin recursive utility, alongside calibrations to existing tax systems, particularly Norway's.

The key findings establish that portfolio neutrality is preserved under considerably broader conditions than previously shown, including stochastic volatility and Epstein–Zin preferences, provided investors exhibit constant relative risk aversion (CRRA). The operative condition is the homogeneity of preferences: non-homothetic preferences such as HARA utility break neutrality by making effective risk aversion wealth-dependent. Four channels of non-neutrality in implemented wealth taxes are identified even under CRRA: non-uniform assessment across asset classes, general equilibrium price effects amplified through demand multipliers in inelastic markets, progressive threshold structures that create tax shields encouraging risk-taking near exemption boundaries, and endogenous labor supply distortions. Tax-induced migration is formalized as an extreme participation response at progressive thresholds, illustrated through Norway's post-2022 experience.

The framework is applied to evaluate the Saez–Zucman global minimum wealth tax and France's national minimum tax, demonstrating how design choices activate different non-neutrality channels. The paper provides testable empirical predictions and highlights important open questions for optimal wealth tax design.
original_abstract: Froeseth (2026) shows that a proportional wealth tax on market values is neutral with respect to portfolio choice, Sharpe ratios, and equilibrium prices under CRRA preferences and geometric Brownian motion. This paper investigates the robustness of that result along two dimensions. First, we extend the neutrality frontier: portfolio neutrality, including all intertemporal hedging demands, is preserved under stochastic volatility (Heston and general Markov diffusions) and Epstein-Zin recursive utility, but breaks under non-homothetic preferences such as HARA. Second, we identify four channels through which implemented wealth taxes depart from neutrality even under CRRA: non-uniform assessment across asset classes, general equilibrium price effects in inelastic markets, progressive threshold structures, and endogenous labour supply. Each channel is formalised and, where possible, calibrated to the Norwegian wealth tax system. The progressive threshold introduces a tax shield that increases risk-taking near the exemption boundary, an effect opposite in sign to the HARA distortion, and, at the extreme, generates a participation margin at which investors exit the tax jurisdiction entirely. We formalise this tax-induced migration as the extreme response at the progressive threshold and examine the Norwegian post-2022 experience as a case study. The full framework is applied to evaluate the Saez-Zucman proposal for a global minimum wealth tax on billionaires and the related French proposal for a national minimum tax above EUR 100 million.

title: Asset Returns, Portfolio Choice, and Proportional Wealth Taxation
generated_summary:
This paper develops a comprehensive framework for analyzing the effects of a proportional wealth tax on asset returns, portfolio choice, and asset pricing. The central contribution is demonstrating that a proportional wealth tax levied uniformly on all assets at market value is economically equivalent to the government acquiring a proportional claim on the investor's holdings, sharing risk and return pro rata, and is therefore "orthogonal" to portfolio choice.

The authors employ a two-investor comparison approach, analyzing taxed and untaxed investors under geometric Brownian motion before generalizing results to any location-scale family distribution. They further examine implications under CAPM general equilibrium and a Modigliani-Miller framework.

The key findings are fourfold: the wealth tax does not alter return distributions per unit of asset, preserves the risk-reward profile (coefficient of variation), leaves optimal portfolio weights unchanged, and results in identical asset prices for taxed and untaxed investors. The tax operates purely as a multiplicative scaling factor that contracts both expected cash flows and discount rates by the same proportion, causing exact cancellation in valuation. Under CRRA preferences, these partial equilibrium results extend to general equilibrium. The paper also identifies pricing errors in prior literature and formalizes three channels through which neutrality breaks down: book-value taxation, liquidity frictions, and dividend extraction.

These results carry significant implications for wealth tax policy debates, challenging claims that proportional wealth taxes necessarily distort asset prices or investment decisions when applied universally at market value.
original_abstract: We analyse the effect of a proportional wealth tax on asset returns, portfolio choice, and asset pricing. The tax is levied annually on the market value of all holdings at a uniform rate. We show that such a tax is economically equivalent to the government acquiring a proportional stake in the investor's portfolio each period, a form of risk sharing in which expected wealth and risk are reduced by the same factor, while the return per share is unaffected. This multiplicative separability drives four main results: (i) the coefficient of variation of wealth is invariant to the tax rate; (ii) optimal portfolio weights are independent of the tax rate; (iii) the wealth tax is orthogonal to portfolio choice, inducing a homothetic contraction of the opportunity set that preserves the Sharpe ratio of every portfolio; (iv) taxed and untaxed investors price assets identically. Results are derived under geometric Brownian motion and generalised to the location-scale family. A Modigliani-Miller analysis confirms pricing neutrality and identifies an inconsistency in the literature regarding the discount rate for after-tax cash flows. Under CAPM with CRRA preferences, after-tax betas equal pre-tax betas and the security market line contracts by the tax factor; general-equilibrium prices are unchanged. This resolves an error in Fama (2021). The neutrality results depend on three conditions commonly violated in practice: universal taxation at market value, frictionless markets, and dividend consumption. We formalise three channels through which relaxing these conditions breaks neutrality: book-value taxation, liquidity frictions, and dividend extraction, and show they have opposing effects on asset prices.

title: Extreme Value Analysis for Finite, Multivariate and Correlated Systems with Finance as an Example
generated_summary:
This paper develops a framework for extreme value analysis of multivariate, correlated time series systems, using financial markets as a concrete application. The central methodological innovation is rotating multivariate return data into the eigenbasis of the Pearson correlation matrix, which decomposes the correlated system into interpretable modes—such as market-wide, sector-specific, and noise components—that can be analyzed using established univariate extreme value techniques.

The authors apply a threshold-based Peaks-over-Threshold approach combined with the Generalized Pareto Distribution, avoiding arbitrary block maxima methods. They analyze high-frequency intraday data (1-second resolution) from 479 stocks on the New York Stock Exchange for 2014. Crucially, the framework addresses nonstationarity by removing intraday volatility patterns through time-dependent rescaling, yielding residual series with substantially reduced autocorrelation in absolute values. The extremal index is estimated to account for remaining temporal clustering of extremes.

Key results show that the largest eigenmodes corresponding to collective market and sector movements exhibit heavy tails well-described by the Generalized Pareto Distribution, with positive shape parameters indicating power-law tail behavior. The nonstationary approach using local, time-dependent thresholds produces markedly improved fits compared to naive stationary estimation, as confirmed by quantile-quantile diagnostics.

The significance lies in providing a principled, practical method for extreme risk assessment in high-dimensional correlated systems that respects both cross-sectional dependencies and temporal nonstationarity, with broad applicability beyond finance to other complex systems.
original_abstract: Extreme values and the tail behavior of probability distributions are essential for quantifying and mitigating risk in complex systems of all kinds. In multivariate settings, accounting for correlations is crucial. Although extreme value analysis for infinite correlated systems remains an open challenge, we propose a practical framework for handling a large but finite number of correlated time series. We develop our approach for finance as a concrete example but emphasize its generality. We study the extremal behavior of high-frequency stock returns after rotating them into the eigenbasis of the correlation matrix. This separates and extracts various collective effects, including information on the correlated market as a whole and on correlated sectoral behavior from idiosyncratic features, while allowing us to use univariate tools of extreme value analysis. This holds even for high-frequency data where discretization effects normally complicate analysis. We employ a peaks-over-threshold approach and thereby fully avoid the analysis of block maxima. We estimate the tail shape of the rotated returns while explicitly accounting for nonstationarity, a key feature in finance and many other complex systems. Our framework facilitates tail risk estimation relative to larger trends and intraday seasonalities at both market and sectoral levels.

title: ICHOR: A Robust Representation Learning Approach for ASL CBF Maps with Self-Supervised Masked Autoencoders
generated_summary:
ICHOR is a self-supervised pre-training framework designed specifically for arterial spin labeling (ASL) cerebral blood flow (CBF) maps, addressing the lack of dedicated pre-trained models for this clinically important physiological imaging modality. The framework employs 3D masked autoencoders (MAEs) with Vision Transformers, where large fractions of input patches are randomly masked and the model learns to reconstruct missing content, thereby acquiring spatially coherent and semantically meaningful representations.

To support large-scale pre-training, the authors curate one of the largest ASL datasets assembled to date, comprising 11,405 CBF scans from 14 studies spanning diverse acquisition sites, protocols, and scanner platforms. This heterogeneous dataset enables the model to learn robust representations despite the substantial inter-site variability characteristic of ASL imaging. The pre-trained encoder is then adapted to downstream tasks using Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) and evaluated through nested five-fold cross-validation.

ICHOR is evaluated on four downstream tasks: three diagnostic classification tasks (cognitively unimpaired amyloid-negative versus cognitively impaired amyloid-positive, healthy older adults versus small vessel disease, and Alzheimer's disease versus behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia) and one ASL quality prediction task. Across these tasks, ICHOR achieves the best overall performance compared to existing neuroimaging self-supervised baselines that were pre-trained on structural MRI and adapted to ASL. The work demonstrates that modality-specific pre-training on ASL data yields superior transferable representations, establishing a foundation model approach for ASL-based neuroimaging analyses.
original_abstract: Arterial spin labeling (ASL) perfusion MRI allows direct quantification of regional cerebral blood flow (CBF) without exogenous contrast, enabling noninvasive measurements that can be repeated without constraints imposed by contrast injection. ASL is increasingly acquired in research studies and clinical MRI protocols. Building on successes in structural imaging, recent efforts have implemented deep learning based methods to improve image quality, enable automated quality control, and derive robust quantitative and predictive biomarkers with ASL derived CBF. However, progress has been limited by variable image quality, substantial inter-site, vendor and protocol differences, and limited availability of labeled datasets needed to train models that generalize across cohorts. To address these challenges, we introduce ICHOR, a self supervised pre-training approach for ASL CBF maps that learns transferable representations using 3D masked autoencoders. ICHOR is pretrained via masked image modeling using a Vision Transformer backbone and can be used as a general-purpose encoder for downstream ASL tasks. For pre-training, we curated one of the largest ASL datasets to date, comprising 11,405 ASL CBF scans from 14 studies spanning multiple sites and acquisition protocols. We evaluated the pre-trained ICHOR encoder on three downstream diagnostic classification tasks and one ASL CBF map quality prediction regression task. Across all evaluations, ICHOR outperformed existing neuroimaging self-supervised pre-training methods adapted to ASL. Pre-trained weights and code will be made publicly available.

title: The role of spatial scales in assessing urban mobility models
generated_summary:
This study systematically investigates how spatial scale affects the performance of three prominent urban mobility models—the gravity model, the radiation model, and the visitation law—using public transport flow data from Singapore. The authors construct spatial units at varying scales through two approaches: conventional administrative boundaries defined by urban planning authorities and data-driven distance-based clustering of transport nodes using Voronoi tessellation. Models are evaluated across these multiple scales to assess how aggregation choices influence comparative model performance.

The key results reveal that the visitation model consistently outperforms the gravity and radiation models at most spatial scales. However, at their respective optimal scales, all three models achieve comparable explanatory power, suggesting that scale selection matters as much as model choice. Notably, a window of intermediate spatial scales exists where all models perform poorly, with the visitation law suffering most—pointing to underlying urban organizational structures that constrain mobility dynamics. The analysis further demonstrates that distance-based clustering consistently yields superior model performance compared to administrative boundaries, which do not necessarily align with actual travel behavior patterns.

The study's significance is threefold: it provides empirical evidence that spatial scale fundamentally shapes mobility model evaluation, it demonstrates that data-driven spatial units better capture functional urban structures than imposed administrative boundaries, and it highlights how scale-dependent performance variations can serve as diagnostic tools for understanding urban organization. These findings carry practical implications for transport planning and urban policy, underscoring the need for scale-aware, data-driven analytical frameworks.
original_abstract: Urban mobility models are essential tools for understanding and forecasting how people and goods move within cities, which is vital for transportation planning. The spatial scale at which urban mobility is analysed is a crucial determinant of the insights gained from any model as it can affect models' performance. It is, therefore, important that urban mobility models should be assessed at appropriate spatial scales to reflect the underlying dynamics. In this study, we systematically evaluate the performance of three popular urban mobility models, namely gravity, radiation, and visitation models across spatial scales. The results show that while the visitation model consistently performs better than its gravity and radiation counterparts, their performance does not differ much when being assessed at some appropriate spatial scale common to all of them. Interestingly, at scales where all models perform badly, the visitation model suffers the most. Furthermore, results based on the conventional admin boundary may not perform so well as compared to distance-based clustering. The cross examination of urban mobility models across spatial scales also reveals the spatial organisation of the urban structure.

title: Self-organization of cavity solitons in Brillouin-Kerr ring resonators
generated_summary:
This paper investigates the self-organization of cavity solitons (CSs) in Brillouin-Kerr ring resonators, revealing how stimulated Brillouin scattering (SBS) mediates long-range interactions between solitons, leading to their spontaneous ordering into regular patterns. The main contribution is the identification and explanation of a novel mechanism by which acoustic waves generated through SBS create trailing tails behind each soliton, enabling deterministic soliton positioning and self-organization without external modulation.

The authors combine theoretical modeling with experimental observations in a fiber ring resonator. The methodology involves analyzing how a cavity soliton locally excites an acoustic wave through the Brillouin impulse response, which scatters the pump field and generates a decaying trailing wave pinned to the soliton. This trailing structure mediates interactions between successive solitons, creating preferred binding distances that lead to equidistant spacing. The theoretical framework incorporates coupled equations for the forward and backward fields along with the acoustic wave dynamics.

Key results demonstrate the spontaneous generation of stable, regularly spaced soliton patterns that persist over long timescales. The experiments confirm soliton oscillations induced by the beating between pump and backward-scattered fields, consistent with simulations. The solitons lock at positions determined by the weak intracavity modulation at twice the Brillouin frequency shift.

This work is significant because it establishes SBS-mediated interactions as a robust mechanism for soliton self-organization, offering a pathway toward controlled, deterministic generation of multi-soliton states in microresonator frequency combs without requiring complex external seeding or modulation techniques.
original_abstract: We report on the interaction between stimulated Brillouin scattering and temporal cavity solitons in doubly resonant ring resonators. Our experiments are performed in coherently driven passive optical-fibre resonators. We demonstrate that the interplay between four-wave mixing and cascade Brillouin lasing spontaneously generates patterns of CSs on a temporal grid at twice the Brillouin-shift. These patterns are shown to be highly stable owing to a long-range locking mechanism mediated by the acoustic oscillation generated by the solitons. We introduce a unified mean-field model of the cavity to describe the dynamics between the coupled forward and backward waves under coherent driving. This model reproduces very well the experiments and explains the paracrystalline structures of the soliton pattern. Our findings significantly advance the understanding of hybrid Brillouin-Kerr optical frequency combs.

title: Escaping the Hydrolysis Trap: An Agentic Workflow for Inverse Design of Durable Photocatalytic Covalent Organic Frameworks
generated_summary:
This paper introduces Ara, a large language model (LLM)-guided agent built on Google's Gemini model, designed for inverse design of hydrolytically stable covalent organic framework (COF) photocatalysts for water splitting. The central challenge addressed is the "hydrolysis trap," where COFs with promising band gaps degrade under aqueous photocatalytic conditions due to susceptible imine linkages.

The methodology combines an LLM-driven iterative reasoning loop with a fragment-based computational screening pipeline. Candidates from an 820-member combinatorial space (comprising varied nodes, linkers, linkage chemistries, and R-group substituents) are evaluated using GFN1-xTB semiempirical calculations calibrated against DFT band gaps (Spearman ρ = 0.91). A composite stability index integrating linkage chemistry, steric shielding, and hydrophobicity encodes hydrolytic durability. At each iteration, the agent receives quantitative feedback and proposes new candidates with explicit chemical justification.

Over 200 iterations across five seeds, Ara achieves a 52.7% hit rate—11.5 times that of random search (p < 0.001) and significantly outperforming Bayesian optimization in cumulative hits. Reasoning traces reveal interpretable strategies: convergence on non-hydrolyzable vinylene linkages, avoidance of excessively electron-withdrawing nodes, and systematic R-group tuning. Oracle analysis reveals complementary strengths, with the agent excelling at budget-constrained exploitation while Bayesian optimization provides broader exploration coverage. These results demonstrate that LLM-encoded chemical priors can substantially accelerate multi-criteria materials discovery.
original_abstract: Covalent organic frameworks (COFs) are promising photocatalysts for solar hydrogen production, yet the most electronically favorable linkages, imines, hydrolyze rapidly in water, creating a stability--activity trade-off that limits practical deployment. Navigating the combinatorial design space of nodes, linkers, linkages, and functional groups to identify candidates that are simultaneously active and durable remains a formidable challenge. Here we introduce Ara, a large-language-model (LLM) agent that leverages pretrained chemical knowledge, donor--acceptor theory, conjugation effects, and linkage stability hierarchies, to guide the search for photocatalytic COFs satisfying joint band-gap, band-edge, and hydrolytic-stability criteria. Evaluated against random search and Bayesian optimization (BO) over a space consisting of candidates with various nodes, linkers, linkages, and r-groups, screened with a GFN1-xTB fragment pipeline, Ara achieves a 52.7\% hit rate (11.5$\times$ random, p = 0.006), finds its first hit at iteration 12 versus 25 for random search, and significantly outperforms BO (p = 0.006). Inspection of the agent's reasoning traces reveals interpretable chemical logic: early convergence on vinylene and beta-ketoenamine linkages for stability, node selection informed by electron-withdrawing character, and systematic R-group optimization to center the band gap at 2.0 eV. Exhaustive evaluation of the full search space uncovers a complementary exploitation--exploration trade-off between the agent and BO, suggesting that hybrid strategies may combine the strengths of both approaches. These results demonstrate that LLM chemical priors can substantially accelerate multi-criteria materials discovery.

title: Waiting-time based entropy estimators in continuous space without Markovian events
generated_summary:
This paper presents a novel lower bound on the entropy production rate for continuous-space stochastic systems based on transition frequencies between coarse-grained spatial regions, eliminating the requirement of observing Markovian events—a significant limitation of previous waiting-time based entropy estimators.

The authors address a fundamental technical challenge: in continuous systems, waiting-time distributions between observable manifolds are ill-defined because a diffusing particle immediately recrosses any boundary it encounters. They resolve this by introducing two discretization schemes—discretizing the distance to manifolds and discretizing the manifolds themselves—and demonstrating that transition frequencies (the rate of transitions with specific transition times between spatial regions) remain well-defined in the continuum limit. The estimator leverages the log-sum inequality applied to a many-to-one coarse-graining of underlying infinitesimal Markovian transitions, extending previous results for blurred transitions in discrete Markov networks to overdamped Langevin dynamics in arbitrary dimensions.

The bound is demonstrated using simulated data from a simplified Brownian gyrator model, where its performance is compared against the finite-time thermodynamic uncertainty relation. The estimator captures the full information content of transition-time distributions between observable regions, making it applicable to higher-dimensional systems unlike previous one-dimensional approaches that required composite events.

This work expands the toolkit for thermodynamic inference from partial observations, which is particularly relevant for experiments where full microscopic resolution is unavailable. The authors suggest that the transition-frequency framework may generalize to other coarse-graining schemes, multi-particle systems, and underdamped dynamics.
original_abstract: Estimating entropy production in continuous systems that can only be observed with a limited resolution remains an open problem in stochastic thermodynamics. Extant estimators based on the measurement of waiting-time distributions require either the detection of Markovian events, which uniquely determine the state of the system, or assume a discrete underlying dynamics. We present a novel estimator that relies solely on the detection of a single particle leaving or entering regions, or crossing manifolds, in continuous space. This estimator is based on the frequency and the duration of transitions between such events. We derive this bound by introducing two kinds of discretization of space. Finally, we compare our novel bound to the TUR using simulations of a Brownian vortex and discuss its relation to other lower bounds to entropy production.

title: Equivalent Circuit Modeling of Mutually Resistively Coupled Microwave Cavities with Enhanced Phase Sensitivity Using Thin Metallic Foils
generated_summary:
This paper introduces and systematically investigates mutual resistive coupling between three-dimensional microwave cavity resonators, realized through thin metallic foils many skin depths thick. Unlike conventional coupling mechanisms based on reactive (inductive or capacitive) elements or apertures, this approach exploits purely dissipative interactions across continuous conductive interfaces to mediate energy and phase transfer between cavities.

The authors develop an equivalent circuit model representing a three-cavity microwave system, where each cavity is modeled as a lumped LCR resonator with mutual resistance terms describing the inter-cavity coupling through the foils. A first-principles derivation relates the electromagnetic properties of the foils to the measured coupling parameters. The model is validated against experimental data from a system in which two input cavities, driven with controlled relative phase and amplitude, excite a third output cavity through thin copper foils.

Key results demonstrate that the model accurately reproduces the observed interference phenomena and sharp anti-resonances in the system's frequency response. The derived coupling values agree with those extracted from fitted transfer functions. Notably, near balanced interference conditions, the phase sensitivity increases by nearly an order of magnitude compared to standard near-resonant operation.

The significance of this work lies in establishing resistive coupling as a deliberate, controllable mechanism for multi-resonator microwave systems. The enhanced phase sensitivity and sharp anti-resonances enabled by this approach hold promise for interferometric precision measurements and fundamental physics experiments, including tests of the scalar Electric Aharonov-Bohm effect.
original_abstract: We formulate and validate an equivalent circuit model describing mutual resistive coupling between three microwave cavity resonators interconnected via thin metallic foils. Each cavity is represented as a lumped LCR circuit, while the foils act as a dissipative interface that mediates energy exchange via mutual resistance. This coupling mechanism produces interference effects and a controllable anti-resonance when the input resonators are amplitude- and phase-balanced, a behavior not achievable with standard microwave antenna probes. All three resonators operated in the TM$_{010}$ mode, where two input resonators each excited the third via a thin copper foil. Analytical expressions are derived for the mutual resistance and coupling coefficient of these foils in this geometry. Under balanced conditions, a sharp anti-resonance emerges with a near order-of-magnitude enhanced phase sensitivity at the resonant frequency of the output cavity, consistent with model predictions. The experimentally extracted mutual coupling coefficients, $Δ_{13}=(5.00\pm0.01)\times10^{-6}$ and $Δ_{23}=(4.10\pm0.01)\times10^{-6}$, fall within the calculated range $Δ_{n3}\approx(1\text{--}48)\times10^{-6}$ derived from the foil's electromagnetic properties, where the spread is dominated by the estimated foil thickness uncertainty of $(9\pm1)\,μ\mathrm{m}$. These results confirm that resistive coupling can occur across a number of skin depths of a metallic interface, providing a new means of engineering controlled interference in multi-resonator systems. The approach offers potential applications in precision microwave experiments, phase-sensitive detection, and tests of fundamental electromagnetic interactions.

title: Particle-Guided Diffusion for Gas-Phase Reaction Kinetics
generated_summary:

title: HoloPASWIN: Robust Inline Holographic Reconstruction via Physics-Aware Swin Transformers

HoloPASWIN is a physics-aware deep learning framework for single-shot phase retrieval in inline digital holography that addresses the fundamental twin-image problem, where lost phase information during intensity-only recording creates conjugate image artifacts that obscure fine details in reconstructions.

The method employs a U-shaped encoder-decoder architecture built upon Swin Transformer blocks rather than conventional convolutional layers, enabling the capture of both local texture details and global diffraction patterns through hierarchical shifted-window attention mechanisms. The input hologram is first back-propagated using the Angular Spectrum Method to produce an initial "dirty" complex-field reconstruction, which the network then refines through residual learning—predicting a correction term rather than the full reconstruction. A key innovation is the physics-aware loss function combining supervised losses (amplitude, phase, complex field, and frequency domain terms) with an unsupervised physics-consistency loss that forward-propagates the predicted clean field and enforces agreement with the original recorded hologram, implicitly discouraging physically implausible conjugate components.

HoloPASWIN achieves strong quantitative performance with an average phase SSIM of 0.986 and phase PSNR of 46.55 dB on the test set. Ablation studies confirm the critical contributions of the physics-consistency constraint, frequency-domain loss, and residual learning strategy. The framework represents a principled, physics-integrated alternative to purely CNN-based approaches, designed to scale toward the complex entanglements encountered in real-world holographic imaging applications.
original_abstract: In-line digital holography (DIH) is a widely used lensless imaging technique, valued for its simplicity and capability to image samples at high throughput. However, capturing only intensity of the interference pattern during the recording process gives rise to some unwanted terms such as cross-term and twin-image. The cross-term can be suppressed by adjusting the intensity of reference wave, but the twin-image problem remains. The twin-image is a spectral artifact that superimposes a defocused conjugate wave onto the reconstructed object, severely degrading image quality. While deep learning has recently emerged as a powerful tool for phase retrieval, traditional Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are limited by their local receptive fields, making them less effective at capturing the global diffraction patterns inherent in holography. In this study, we introduce HoloPASWIN, a physics-aware deep learning framework based on the Swin Transformer architecture. By leveraging hierarchical shifted-window attention, our model efficiently captures both local details and long-range dependencies essential for accurate holographic reconstruction. We propose a comprehensive loss function that integrates frequency-domain constraints with physical consistency via a differentiable angular spectrum propagator, ensuring high spectral fidelity. Validated on a large-scale synthetic dataset of 25,000 samples with diverse noise configurations (speckle, shot, read, and dark noise), HoloPASWIN demonstrates effective twin-image suppression and robust reconstruction quality.

title: Spectral dynamics reservoir computing for high-speed hardware-efficient neuromorphic processing
generated_summary:
This paper introduces spectral dynamics reservoir computing (SDRC), a hardware-efficient neuromorphic computing framework that extracts computational information from the coarse frequency spectra of physical oscillatory systems using simple analog bandpass filters and envelope detectors. Unlike conventional time-multiplexed physical reservoir computing approaches that require complex, high-speed sampling circuits, SDRC leverages the rich nonlinear spectral dynamics inherently present in physical substrates, even when spectral resolution is limited by the time-frequency trade-off at high processing speeds.

The authors demonstrate SDRC using spin-wave dynamics in yttrium iron garnet (YIG) crystals, where microwave-frequency spin waves serve as the nonlinear physical medium. The system employs commercially available bandpass filters and diodes to decompose spin-wave responses into parallel spectral channels, with physics-guided optimization identifying computationally informative frequency bands corresponding to distinct spin-wave modes.

With only eight spectral nodes, the hardware-implemented SDRC achieves state-of-the-art-level performance on standard benchmark tasks including parity check and second-order nonlinear autoregressive moving average (NARMA-2), and demonstrates high accuracy on a real-world speaker recognition task using the TI-46 speech corpus. The results show that finely resolved spectral features are unnecessary—subtle inter-modal spectral dynamics from coarsely resolved spectra provide sufficient computational richness.

The significance of SDRC lies in its platform-agnostic, hardware-friendly architecture that dramatically reduces implementation complexity while enabling high-speed neuromorphic processing, with potential applicability to photonic, electromechanical, and superconducting systems.
original_abstract: Physical reservoir computing (PRC) is a promising brain-inspired computing architecture for overcoming the von Neumann bottleneck by utilizing the intrinsic dynamics of physical systems. However, a major obstacle to its real-world implementation lies in the tension between extracting sufficient information for high computational performance and maintaining a hardware-feasible, high-speed architecture. Here, we report spectral dynamics reservoir computing (SDRC), a broadly applicable framework based on analogue filtering and envelope detection that bridges this gap. SDRC effectively exploits the fast spectral dynamics embedded in short-time, coarse spectra of material responses to attain strong computational capability while maintaining high-speed processing and minimal hardware overhead. This approach circumvents the need for implementation-intensive, precision-sensitive integrated circuits required in high-speed time-multiplexing measurements, while enabling real-time use of the material's spectral manifold as a high-dimensional computational resource. We implement and experimentally demonstrate SDRC applied to spin waves that achieves state-of-the-art-level performance with only 56 nodes on benchmark tasks of parity-check and second-order nonlinear autoregressive moving average, as well as high accuracy of 98.0% on a real-world problem of speech recognition.

title: Global versus local internal-external field separation on the sphere: a Hardy-Hodge perspective
generated_summary:
This paper investigates whether the classical internal-external geomagnetic field separation, well-established for global spherical data, can be meaningfully extended to observations available only on a partial region (patch) of the observation sphere. The authors employ the Hardy-Hodge decomposition framework, which formulates the separation problem in terms of Hardy spaces representing internal-source and external-source contributions to vector fields on surfaces.

The methodology involves rigorous mathematical analysis of uniqueness and stability properties when restricting the decomposition from the full sphere to a spherical patch. The authors establish four principal results. First, localized measurements alone cannot uniquely determine internal and external contributions, as nontrivial canceling fields exist on any patch. Second, uniqueness can be restored by imposing a geophysically motivated condition requiring a source-free shell bordering the observation surface, equivalent to assuming external sources originate only above a fixed altitude. Third, even with this analyticity condition, the separation problem remains ill-posed, meaning arbitrarily small data perturbations can cause large changes in the separated components. Fourth, by assuming appropriate bounds on the contributions, a logarithmic conditional stability estimate is derived that quantifies how the thickness of the source-free shell influences stability.

These results are significant for ground-based and aeromagnetic geomagnetic studies where only regional data coverage is available, clarifying fundamental structural limitations of localized separation and providing theoretical guidance for practical geomagnetic field modeling from geographically incomplete observations.
original_abstract: Internal-external field separation is crucial for many aspects of geomagnetism, aiming at distinguishing contributions of the magnetic field generated within the Earth (or any other planet) from those produced in the exterior. When data is available on a full spherical observation surface, this separation is a standard, stable, and widely used procedure dating back to Gauss. However, when data is only available in a subdomain of the observation surface (as is the case for aeromagnetic and ground-based surveys), the situation changes. Here we show that, without prior assumptions, an internal-external field separation is not uniquely possible. Given the geophysically reasonable assumption that the exterior sources (e.g., ionospheric current systems) are located above a source-free spherical shell, we show that a unique separation becomes possible but that it is highly unstable. The results are based on a Hardy-Hodge decomposition of spherical vector fields and provide an explanation of the intrinsic difficulties of regional data-based internal-external field separation.

title: Compounding Vulnerability: Hub Removal Triggers Cascade Phase Transitions While Degrading Percolation Robustness in Scale-Free Networks
generated_summary:
This paper formalizes and investigates the concept of "compounding vulnerability" in scale-free networks, demonstrating that a common network intervention—hub removal—can simultaneously worsen resilience under two distinct failure models rather than improving overall robustness. The authors argue that resilience is not a scalar network property but a functional dependent on the specific stress model applied, and they formalize stress models as triples comprising perturbation sets, dynamical rules, and observables.

Using Barabási–Albert networks, the authors systematically study the joint effects of removing the top 10% highest-degree nodes on both bond percolation and Watts threshold cascade dynamics. They measure percolation thresholds and cascade sizes across parameter ranges, conduct controlled hub vulnerability experiments to decompose structural versus dynamical mechanisms, and derive a closed-form analytical expression for the post-removal cascade branching factor under a configuration-model approximation.

Key results show that hub removal raises the bond percolation threshold by approximately 68% while simultaneously expanding the cascade window, enabling global cascades at threshold values (notably φ = 0.22) that were previously subcritical. At this threshold, mean cascade size jumps from near zero to approximately 95% of the network. The hub vulnerability experiment reveals that cascade suppression by hubs is primarily dynamical (threshold-based) rather than structural, with 95% of cascades attributable to threshold modification alone versus 19% from connectivity changes.

These findings carry significant implications for infrastructure engineering, financial regulation, and public health, arguing that multi-stress-model resilience assessment should become standard practice before implementing topological interventions.
original_abstract: Hub removal in scale-free networks is known to degrade percolation robustness by raising the bond percolation threshold. We show that this same intervention simultaneously triggers a cascade phase transition under the Watts threshold model. In Barabási--Albert networks, removing the top 10\% of nodes by degree raises $p_c$ from 0.34 to 0.90, reducing robustness to random edge failure. Simultaneously, at cascade threshold $\varphi=0.22$, mean cascade size increases from $0.29\%$ to $20.6\%$, crossing from the subcritical to supercritical regime -- compounding, rather than trading off, the percolation degradation.   Using a controlled experiment that independently varies hub presence and hub activation threshold, we demonstrate that hub-mediated cascade suppression is primarily dynamical: making hubs vulnerable without removing them produces 95\% cascades versus 19\% with removal.   We operationalize Watts' (2002) stable-node mechanism as a quantitative condition $k > 1/\varphi$ and derive, under the configuration-model approximation, a closed-form expression for the post-removal cascade branching factor $z_1(\varphi, α, m)$. This predicts a newly opened interval where the pre-removal network is subcritical but the post-removal network is supercritical. We define $\varphi^*$ as the upper supercritical boundary, $\varphi^* = \sup\{\varphi : z_1(\varphi) \geq 1\}$. The $z_1$ derivation confirms that at $\varphi=0.22$, the pre-removal network is subcritical ($z_1=0.850$) while the post-removal network is supercritical ($z_1=1.195$). Our results establish that hub manipulation creates compounding vulnerability: both percolation and cascade metrics worsen simultaneously on static, unweighted networks. The effect vanishes in homogeneous networks (ER, WS).

title: Tree codes and sort-and-sweep algorithms for neighborhood computation: A cache-conscious comparison
generated_summary:
This paper presents a cache-conscious performance comparison of two update-oriented neighborhood detection algorithms for discrete element method (DEM) simulations: sort-and-sweep and tree codes (specifically, "minimal" quadtrees). Both algorithms update only changed particle neighborhoods rather than rebuilding contact lists from scratch each timestep, preserving stored contact information such as friction history.

The authors implement both algorithms within a two-dimensional DEM code simulating polygonal particles in a rotating drum configuration. They benchmark performance across multiple processors with different cache sizes and memory architectures, testing both MATLAB interpreter code and compiled C code generated via MATLAB Coder. They also analyze algorithmic complexity through cyclomatic complexity metrics and examine the effects of function inlining.

Key results demonstrate that both algorithms achieve linear O(N) time complexity for neighborhood updates, confirming theoretical predictions. Tree codes outperform sort-and-sweep by approximately 10%, with the updating portion being roughly ten times faster for tree codes. Performance ratios remain consistent across different processor architectures, suggesting the findings generalize beyond specific hardware. Compiled code provides speedups of 8–18× over interpreted code depending on system size.

The study concludes that tree codes offer superior performance for systems with significant particle motion and better parallelization prospects, though they come at the cost of substantially higher algorithmic complexity. Neither algorithm is recommended for highly penetrating particles or long-range force simulations where neighborhood changes are excessive.
original_abstract: Neighborhood algorithms may take a considerable percentage of computer time in discrete element methods (DEM). While the sort-and-sweep algorithm is ideal in some ways, as it only deal with particles whose relative positions change in one coordinate direction, the other directions must be processed too, for all particles. In contrast, tree-codes deal only with adjacent particles. We compare sort-and-sweep and tree-code neighborhood algorithms for two-dimensional DEM simulations of polygonal particles in a rotating drum with up to 12000 particles. We discuss the effects of system size and inlining on the performance with respect to the cache memory. For the tree code, the performance is slightly better, at the cost of significantly increased cyclomatic complexity. In particular, one benefit is improved possibilities for shared memory parallelization.

title: Wave interactions in a screeching jet
generated_summary:
This paper presents a comprehensive investigation of wave interactions in screeching supersonic jets using a hierarchy of linear and nonlinear analysis tools applied to experimental mean flow data. The study combines global stability analysis, resolvent analysis, harmonic resolvent analysis, and a novel nonlinear extension of harmonic resolvent analysis to systematically characterize the feedback mechanisms and energy redistribution processes underlying jet screech.

The global stability analysis identifies multiple lightly damped eigenmodes corresponding to interactions between Kelvin-Helmholtz wavepackets and different peaks in the shock-cell wavenumber spectrum—the first observation of modes stemming from multiple shock-cell wavenumbers in a global analysis. Resolvent analysis at the screech frequency produces modes closely matching experimental POD modes from particle image velocimetry data. A key methodological contribution is the bilinear formulation of harmonic resolvent analysis, which captures triadic interactions between the screech mode and fluctuations at harmonic frequencies. This analysis reveals energy redistribution from the screech frequency to its harmonics and predicts acoustic radiation patterns at harmonic frequencies that match experimental observations but had not been previously captured by linearized Navier-Stokes models. The nonlinear forcing analysis demonstrates that the screech mode's self-interaction alone, combined with triadic coupling, suffices to explain all observed harmonic features without requiring unknown turbulent forcing. These findings advance understanding of screech dynamics and provide a transferable framework for analyzing triadic interactions in other flows with strong harmonic components.
original_abstract: We use a series of global models to investigate the linear and nonlinear interactions between shock cells, Kelvin-Helmholtz waves, guided jet modes, and other fluctuations in a screeching jet. First, we identify a set of lightly damped global eigenmodes of the Navier-Stokes operator linearized about the mean flow and show that they result from interactions with different shock-cell wavenumbers. Second, we use resolvent analysis to study the linear input-output behavior of the jet and obtain a time-periodic representation of the screech mode, which compares favorably with experimental data. Third, we use harmonic resolvent analysis to study triadic interactions, including inter-frequency energy transfer, between the screech mode determined from resolvent analysis and other fluctuations in the jet. The components of the optimal harmonic resolvent mode at harmonics of the screech frequency match experimental observations that have not been previously predicted by global models. Fourth, we leverage a novel bilinear formulation of harmonic resolvent analysis to study the impact of the screech mode's nonlinear self-interaction on other fluctuations in the jet. We show that the forcing provided by this nonlinear self-interaction of the screech mode, along with its triadic interactions with other frequencies embedded within the harmonic resolvent operator, is sufficient to explain the redistribution of energy to other frequencies and the associated experimental observations. In aggregate, these findings underscore the critical role of triadic and nonlinear interactions in shaping screech dynamics and offer a promising workflow for studying similar interactions in other flows dominated by periodic motions.

title: Total Angular Momentum Coherent State Fields
generated_summary:
This paper introduces total angular momentum coherent state (TAMCS) fields, a new class of structured light beams that unify spin angular momentum (SAM) and orbital angular momentum (OAM) control through a single complex parameter. The work extends previous orbital angular momentum coherent state beams by incorporating polarization degrees of freedom within a rigorous angular momentum framework.

The methodology employs quantum angular momentum coupling theory, pairing circular polarization states (spin-1/2 representation for SAM) with Laguerre-Gaussian beams (spin-ℓ representation for OAM) to construct an orthonormal basis for structured light. Using Clebsch-Gordan coefficients, the authors build total angular momentum (TAM) fields as superpositions within fixed-TAM subspaces characterized by quantum numbers J and M. TAMCS fields are then defined as SU(2) coherent superpositions within each subspace, parameterized by a single complex variable.

Key results show that the amplitude of this parameter modulates both polarization and spatial structure with characteristic periodicity, while its phase induces rigid rotation around the optical axis. For specific subspaces, the framework naturally generates radially and azimuthally polarized modes as orthonormal pairs with identical intensity profiles. Importantly, these fields preserve both polarization and intensity distributions under paraxial propagation up to a scaling factor, and experimental results confirm the theoretical predictions.

The significance lies in enabling continuous, symmetry-preserving control over both polarization and spatial degrees of freedom simultaneously, with potential applications in optical trapping, high-resolution imaging, and classical and quantum communication.
original_abstract: Structured light fields exploit spin and orbital angular momentum for precision manipulation, advanced imaging, and high-capacity communication. Orbital angular momentum coherent state beams interpolate between Hermite- and Laguerre-Gaussian beams, enabling continuous spatial control. We introduce a symmetry-based framework for joint control of polarization and spatial structure under the shared \$su(2)\$ Lie algebra of spin and orbital angular momentum. Within this structure, we construct total angular momentum fields as superpositions of circular polarization and Laguerre-Gaussian beams, and define their \$su(2)\$ coherent states within fixed-angular-momentum subspaces. A single complex parameter controls both polarization and spatial degrees of freedom, enabling continuous, symmetry-preserving tuning.

title: A Rotation-Compensated Smartphone Accelerometer Application for Undergraduate Mechanics Experiments
generated_summary:
This paper presents a web-based smartphone application that measures acceleration with rotation compensation, transforming data from the device-fixed coordinate system into a stationary global frame using Euler angle rotations. The system, designed for undergraduate mechanics education, consists of a measurement app and a companion analysis app, both accessible through web browsers without requiring software installation, ensuring platform independence and ease of classroom deployment.

The methodology involves using smartphone accelerometer and gyroscope data to compensate for device orientation changes during motion, enabling physically meaningful acceleration measurements even when the phone rotates. The authors demonstrate the system through three representative experiments: sliding motion under kinetic friction, projectile motion, and uniform circular motion. For each case, acceleration data are numerically integrated to obtain velocity and position, with discussions of practical data-processing issues such as drift from sensor offsets and moving-average corrections.

Key results show that rotation-compensated acceleration data yield physically consistent velocity and position profiles across all three motion types. Classroom implementation in an undergraduate mechanics course, evaluated through Likert-scale questionnaires and open-ended responses from 102 students, indicated improved understanding of relationships among acceleration, velocity, and position, along with positive student engagement.

The significance of this work lies in lowering technical barriers to smartphone-based physics experiments, allowing students to focus on physical interpretation and kinematic concepts. The system provides a flexible, accessible tool for integrating hands-on experimental learning into physics and engineering curricula.
original_abstract: Smartphones equipped with sensors such as accelerometers, gyroscopes, and magnetometers offer valuable opportunities for physics education, allowing students to measure motion using their own devices. However, commonly used applications provide acceleration only in the device-fixed coordinate system, which makes it difficult to analyze two- or three-dimensional motion when the device rotates. To address this limitation, we developed a web-based accelerometer application that can provide acceleration in a stationary global coordinate system. This is achieved by simultaneously recording acceleration in the device-fixed coordinate system and Euler angles, and converting them to rotation-compensated acceleration in real time. We also built a companion web application for numerical integration, noise reduction, and visualization of the measured data. Both applications are installation-free and can be accessed directly through a smartphone browser.   We demonstrate the capabilities of the newly developed system through several representative types of motion, including sliding motion, projectile motion, and circular motion, by showing that rotation-compensated acceleration enables accurate reconstruction of velocity, displacement, and trajectories even when the smartphone changes its orientation. The applications were implemented in undergraduate mechanics classes, where students used them in group-based experiments. Classroom observations suggested that the use of these tools facilitated a deeper understanding of the relationships among acceleration, velocity, and position. These results suggest that rotation-compensated smartphone measurements provide a practical and effective tool for physics education.

title: Hollow toroidal rotation profiles in strongly electron heated H-mode plasmas in the ASDEX Upgrade tokamak
generated_summary:
This study investigates the formation of hollow toroidal rotation profiles in strongly electron-heated H-mode plasmas in the ASDEX Upgrade tokamak, addressing a critical concern for future fusion reactors that will rely less on neutral beam injection for plasma heating. Hollow rotation profiles, characterized by reversed core rotation gradients, are problematic because they increase susceptibility to MHD instabilities.

The authors employ a comprehensive momentum transport analysis framework combining NBI modulation experiments, Fourier decomposition of rotation profiles, and ASTRA transport modeling to separate diffusive, convective, and residual stress contributions to momentum transport. Linear gyrokinetic simulations using the GKW code complement the experimental analysis.

The key finding is the identification of a strong counter-current intrinsic torque during phases with significant electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH), attributed to a transition from ion-temperature-gradient-dominated turbulence to a mixed ITG–trapped-electron-mode regime. This intrinsic torque is the primary driver of hollow rotation profiles. Systematic parameter scans confirm that optimal solutions consistently favor inward convective momentum transport combined with counter-current intrinsic torque. Additional experiments at varying densities demonstrate that hollow profile formation depends critically on the balance between counter-current intrinsic torque and inward convective transport, with the pedestal-top rotation level playing a decisive role.

These results provide important constraints for predicting rotation behavior in future low-torque tokamak reactors, highlighting that strong inward convective momentum transport can mitigate hollow rotation profile formation.
original_abstract: This work investigates toroidal momentum transport in type-I ELMy H-mode plasmas in the ASDEX Upgrade tokamak, focusing on the formation of hollow rotation profiles under strong electron cyclotron resonance heating (ECRH). Applying the established momentum transport analysis framework to a neutral beam injection (NBI) modulation experiment, momentum transport coefficients were inferred self-consistently. This was done for phases with dominant NBI heating and with additional strong ECRH, during which the rotation profile severely collapsed without significant changes in the externally applied torque. The experimental rotation profiles were accurately reproduced, confirming the robustness of the inferred diffusive, convective, and residual-stress contributions. While the Prandtl number and inward Coriolis pinch remained comparable between phases, the NBI+ECRH phase exhibited a strong counter-current intrinsic torque. Linear gyrokinetic simulations indicate a transition from ion-temperature-gradient (ITG) turbulence to an ITG-trapped-electron-mode (TEM) mixed regime under strong ECRH, consistent with the observed counter-current intrinsic torque and particle pinch behavior. Additional high-ECRH discharges with modified density demonstrated that hollow rotation profiles emerge from a balance between counter-current intrinsic torque and inward convective momentum transport, strongly influenced by the pedestal-top rotation level, which is dominantly set by variations in the pedestal-top density. These findings highlight the importance of intrinsic torque and inward convection for maintaining favorable rotation profiles in future low-torque tokamak scenarios and motivate further exploration of edge torque generation mechanisms.

title: sFRC for assessing hallucinations in medical image restoration
generated_summary:
This paper introduces scanned Fourier Ring Correlation (sFRC), a novel metric for detecting hallucinations—false structures generated by AI-based image restoration methods—in medical imaging. The authors argue that existing evaluation approaches, including global fidelity metrics (PSNR, SSIM), physical image quality metrics, and task-based observer studies, are inadequate for comprehensively characterizing hallucinations in deep learning reconstructions.

sFRC operates by extracting local patches from AI-restored images and reference images (obtained via fully sampled analytical reconstruction), computing Fourier Ring Correlation for each patch pair, and comparing the frequency-domain similarity against a tunable hallucination threshold. This threshold is calibrated using expert-annotated or imaging-theory-identified hallucinated regions from a development dataset, then applied automatically to detect new hallucinations in test data.

The method is validated across three medical imaging applications: CT super-resolution using SRGAN, MRI subsampled restoration using U-Net and PLS-TV regularization, and CT sparse-view reconstruction using PAIL. Results demonstrate that sFRC consistently detects clinically significant hallucinations—including false plaques, tissue indentations, and air-mimicking artifacts—that global metrics like PSNR, SSIM, and Hellinger distance fail to capture. sFRC also correctly reflects increased hallucination rates for out-of-distribution data and greater subsampling factors.

The significance of sFRC lies in its modality-agnostic, objective, and locally sensitive framework for hallucination assessment, addressing a critical safety gap as AI-based medical image reconstruction devices increasingly seek regulatory approval.
original_abstract: Deep learning (DL) methods are currently being explored to restore images from sparse-view-, limited-data-, and undersampled-based acquisitions in medical applications. Although outputs from DL may appear visually appealing based on likability/subjective criteria (such as less noise, smooth features), they may also suffer from hallucinations. This issue is further exacerbated by a lack of easy-to-use techniques and robust metrics for the identification of hallucinations in DL outputs. In this work, we propose performing Fourier Ring Correlation (FRC) analysis over small patches and concomitantly (s)canning across DL outputs and their reference counterparts to detect hallucinations (termed as sFRC). We describe the rationale behind sFRC and provide its mathematical formulation. The parameters essential to sFRC may be set using predefined hallucinated features annotated by subject matter experts or using imaging theory-based hallucination maps. We use sFRC to detect hallucinations for three undersampled medical imaging problems: CT super-resolution, CT sparse view, and MRI subsampled restoration. In the testing phase, we demonstrate sFRC's effectiveness in detecting hallucinated features for the CT problem and sFRC's agreement with imaging theory-based outputs on hallucinated feature maps for the MR problem. Finally, we quantify the hallucination rates of DL methods on in-distribution versus out-of-distribution data and under increasing subsampling rates to characterize the robustness of DL methods. Beyond DL-based methods, sFRC's effectiveness in detecting hallucinations for a conventional regularization-based restoration method and a state-of-the-art unrolled method is also shown.

title: Strongly clustered random graphs via triadic closure: Degree correlations and clustering spectrum
generated_summary:
This paper provides a comprehensive analytical and numerical characterization of degree correlations and local clustering properties in the Static Triadic Closure (STC) random graph model, where a clustered network is constructed by closing triads in a backbone network with probability *f*. The authors derive exact expressions for the Pearson correlation coefficient as a function of the first four moments of the backbone degree distribution, and obtain analytical formulae for the local clustering spectrum, valid in the infinite-size limit.

The methodology leverages the separation of edges into backbone and triadic-closure-generated links, exploiting the uncorrelated nature of the backbone to obtain tractable results. The analysis covers random regular, Erdős-Rényi, and power-law backbone degree distributions.

Key findings reveal that triadic closure always introduces assortative (positive) degree correlations, with assortativity increasing with the fraction of closed triads and thus with transitivity. This provides a natural explanation for the positive correlation between assortativity and clustering commonly observed in social networks. For power-law backbones, sharp transitions in the Pearson coefficient emerge depending on the degree exponent. The clustering spectrum exhibits rich behavior: Erdős-Rényi backbones produce a striking apparent power-law decay with exponent near −1, while power-law backbones yield non-monotonic spectra with significant finite-size effects.

These results demonstrate that the STC model captures complex local structural properties analytically, establishing it as a valuable reference model that extends well beyond classical treelike random graph frameworks.
original_abstract: Real-world networks often exhibit strong transitivity with nontrivial local clustering spectra and degree correlations. Such features are not easily modelled in tractable network models, creating an obstacle to the theoretical understanding of such complex network structures. Here, we address this problem using a model for strongly clustered random graphs in which each triad of a random backbone is closed with a certain probability. Despite the intricate loopy local structure of the graphs obtained, we provide exact expressions for the local clustering spectrum and the degree correlations, filling the gap in the theoretical description of this model for random graphs. In particular, we find positive degree assortativity accompanies high transitivity, and non-trivial structure in the clustering spectrum. Exact asymptotic analytical results are complemented with extensive numerical characterization of finite size effects.

title: Photon statistics in waveguide QED: II Exact solutions in a thermodynamic limit
generated_summary:
This paper derives exact analytical solutions for photon statistics in waveguide quantum electrodynamics (WQED) in a thermodynamic limit where the atom number N → ∞ while the optical depth OD remains fixed. The authors study both chiral (unidirectional) and permutationally symmetric systems of two-level atoms coupled to a waveguide, starting from full inversion.

The methodology combines two approaches: an analytical 1/N expansion developed in a companion paper, whose coefficients simplify dramatically in the thermodynamic limit, and a second-order mean field (MF2) method formulated as continuum partial integro-differential equations. The authors demonstrate that MF2 becomes exact in this limit, yielding closed-form solutions expressed through generalized hypergeometric and modified Bessel functions.

Key results include: (1) the power emitted into the waveguide grows exponentially with optical depth for both system types; (2) the equal-time second-order coherence g⁽²⁾(0,t) → 2 for both systems; (3) shot-to-shot fluctuations in photon rates vanish for symmetric systems but persist with interesting features for chiral systems; and (4) a special time t_sp separates superradiant and subradiant emission regimes. The correlation structure reveals that downstream atoms develop stronger correlations due to cascaded irradiation from upstream atoms, with stretched exponential spatial dependence.

These results provide computationally efficient analytical predictions applicable to current experiments with large atom numbers, where exact simulation of the exponentially growing Hilbert space is intractable.
original_abstract: Waveguide quantum electrodynamics (WQED) offers a powerful framework for controlling light-matter interactions and realizing collective phenomena such as super- and subradiance. In general waveguide settings, the quantum dynamics spans the full Hilbert space, rendering exact theoretical treatments exponentially difficult and currently out of reach, and only a few models have exact, analytical solutions. Motivated by recent experiments, we treat the thermodynamic limit of the number of atoms, $N \rightarrow \infty$, while the homogeneous atom-waveguide coupling $β\rightarrow 0$ keeping the optical depth $4Nβ$ fixed. In this limit, a second order mean field method is exact, giving analytical solutions for the statistics of the photons emitted in the waveguide both for chiral and symmetric configurations starting from full inversion. As $N \rightarrow \infty$, the emission in freespace approaches that of an independent ensemble. However, until a special time, $\approx 1.59 \times$ the lifetime of a single-atom, we show an exponentially enhanced superradiance in the waveguide as the optical depth increases. After the special time, the emission into the waveguide exhibits subradiance. We also show that the initial shot-to-shot fluctuations in the rate of emission into the waveguide diminish in a chiral system and vanish in a symmetric system as $N$ approaches $\infty$. Additionally, the equal-time second-order correlation becomes trivial, showing that finite-size effects are essential to observe the emergence of second-order coherence. Finally, going beyond the thermodynamic limit requires higher order mean field methods. Our results illustrate finite- and infinite-body collective effects in symmetric and symmetry-lacking systems.

title: Stan: An LLM-based thermodynamics course assistant
generated_summary:
This paper presents Stan, a locally deployable large language model (LLM)-based learning assistant designed for a chemical engineering thermodynamics course. The main contribution is a system that provides both student-facing and instructor-facing tools, with particular emphasis on the latter—an area underrepresented in educational AI research. Rather than automating grading or content generation, Stan extends instructional capacity through analytic tools that examine classroom activity, enabling reflection, pattern recognition, and iterative course refinement.

Stan's architecture centers on local deployment, running on existing student and faculty hardware rather than cloud-based services. This approach addresses concerns around cost predictability, data governance, and privacy while avoiding usage-based pricing models. The system is built as a standard Python package following open-source principles, encouraging inspection and modification by instructors and students. It integrates lecture transcription, timestamped query systems, and a curated thermodynamics textbook as a grounding corpus for domain-specific reasoning through a natural language interface.

The authors identify important constraints, including hardware heterogeneity across student devices that limits model size—quantized 7B-class models are broadly accessible while larger models may exclude some students. They also note that local deployment may shift costs from subscriptions to instructional support time.

The significance of this work lies in demonstrating that locally deployable LLM systems can be meaningfully integrated into rigorous engineering curricula while preserving instructor agency, institutional autonomy, and pedagogical integrity, potentially reshaping communicative norms in technical instruction.
original_abstract: Discussions of AI in education focus predominantly on student-facing tools -- chatbots, tutors, and problem generators -- while the potential for the same infrastructure to support instructors remains largely unexplored. We describe Stan, a suite of tools for an undergraduate chemical engineering thermodynamics course built on a data pipeline that we develop and deploy in dual roles: serving students and supporting instructors from a shared foundation of lecture transcripts and a structured textbook index. On the student side, a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline answers natural-language queries by extracting technical terms, matching them against the textbook index, and synthesizing grounded responses with specific chapter and page references. On the instructor side, the same transcript corpus is processed through structured analysis pipelines that produce per-lecture summaries, identify student questions and moments of confusion, and catalog the anecdotes and analogies used to motivate difficult material -- providing a searchable, semester-scale record of teaching that supports course reflection, reminders, and improvement. title: PDE foundation model-accelerated inverse estimation of system parameters in inertial confinement fusion

title: Fundamental linewidth limit of electromagnetically induced transparency in a thermal Rydberg ladder

In this scheme, the energy resolution of the Rydberg state is set by the spectral linewidth of the EIT feature. While selection criteria for the two-photon resonance can narrow the linewidth to the order of the Rydberg state decay rate for a single atom, the Doppler shift from thermal velocity of the atoms broadens the ensemble linewidth to the order of the decay rate of the intermediate state. Here, we derive an analytic expression for the Doppler residual lineshape in the low-power limit and corroborate the results with experiment. For Rb, we find the full-width at half-maximum linewidth limit to be 1.84 MHz when scanning the coupling laser and measure an experimental linewidth of 2.04 MHz. These linewidths are around a factor of two narrower than previous theoretical estimates as well as previously reported measured linewidths. With this, we demonstrate the most precise two-photon energy resolution of a Rydberg state in thermal vapor to date. We then map out broadening mechanisms near this limit.

title: Photon statistics in chiral waveguide QED: I Mean field and perturbative expansions
