The notion of the characteristic function of the classical Sz.-Nagy--Foias Theory is extended to a commuting tuple of $\frac{1}{K}$-contraction where $K$ is an irreducible $\mathbb K$-invariant kernel. An explicit construction of the characteristic function of a $\frac{1}{K}$-contraction is provided. A characterization of a $\mathbb K$-invariant kernel with the complete Nevanlinna-Pick property is obtained via the existence of characteristic functions associated with $\frac{1}{K}$-contractions.

title: New Berry-Esseen bounds for parameter estimation of Gaussian processes observed at high frequency
generated_summary:
This paper establishes new Berry-Esseen bounds for parameter estimation of asymptotically stationary Gaussian processes observed at high frequency, where the discrete observation step size converges to zero. The work focuses on second moment estimators (SMEs) for the limiting variance of centered stationary Gaussian processes, as well as a general estimator constructed through a transformation function.

The authors employ Malliavin calculus on Wiener space combined with novel analytical tools to derive explicit rates of convergence in the central limit theorem for these estimators. A key methodological contribution involves developing new estimates for the Kolmogorov distance through two novel lemmas, which complement existing techniques for Wasserstein and total variation distances.

The main results provide bounds for the normal approximation of the SMEs in three probability metrics: total variation, Kolmogorov, and Wasserstein distances. For the general transformed estimator, bounds are obtained in Kolmogorov and Wasserstein distances. Notably, the Wasserstein and Kolmogorov bounds turn out to be identical, and the authors prove that most of their estimates are strictly sharper than those previously available in the literature, which relied on bounds from continuous-time versions of the estimators.

The theoretical framework is applied to derive explicit Kolmogorov and Wasserstein bounds for drift parameter estimators of fractional Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes of both the first and second kind, demonstrating the practical applicability of the improved convergence rates to important stochastic models used in statistical inference.
original_abstract: The purpose of this paper is to estimate the limiting variance of asymptotically stationary Gaussian processes observed at high frequency, using the second moment estimator (SME). We study rates of convergence of the central limit theorem for the SME in terms of the total variation, Kolmogorov and Wasserstein distances, using some novel techniques and sharp estimates for cumulants. We apply our approach to provide Berry-Esseen bounds in   Kolmogorov and Wasserstein distances for estimators of the drift parameters of Gaussian Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes.   Moreover, we prove that most of our estimates are strictly sharper than the ones obtained in the existing literature.

title: The Minkowski problem of $p$-affine dual curvature measures
generated_summary:
This paper introduces a new class of affine-invariant geometric measures called *p*-affine dual curvature measures, denoted $\widetilde{C}_p(K, \cdot)$, and studies the associated Minkowski problem. These measures arise from computing the variational formula of *p*-intersection bodies and generalize previously known affine-invariant measures: the affine-invariant measure of Cai-Leng-Wu-Xi emerges as a limit case when $p \to \infty$, and the classical cone-volume measure appears when both $p \to \infty$ and $q \to 0$.

The authors formulate the Minkowski problem for *p*-affine dual curvature measures, which asks for necessary and sufficient conditions on a finite Borel measure on the unit sphere to be realized as the *p*-affine dual curvature measure of a convex body. When the measure has a density function, this problem reduces to a Monge-Ampère type equation on the sphere involving the *p*-cosine transform.

The main results establish both existence and necessary conditions. For the existence theorem, the authors employ a variational approach, constructing a functional combining the volume of *p*-intersection bodies with an entropy integral. They prove that any non-zero even finite Borel measure satisfying a strict subspace concentration inequality can be realized as the *p*-affine dual curvature measure of an origin-symmetric convex body. Key technical ingredients include inequalities relating radial functions of *p*-intersection bodies to classical intersection bodies and careful estimates involving barrier convex bodies. Additionally, the authors establish a necessary subspace concentration condition that *p*-affine dual curvature measures of origin-symmetric convex bodies must satisfy, extending analogous results from the logarithmic Minkowski problem.
original_abstract: For $p\in (-\infty,0)\cup(0,1)$ and a convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ with the origin in its interior, we construct the family of $p$-affine dual curvature measures $\mathcal{I}_p(K,\cdot)$ with respect to $K$. The affine-invariant measure $\widetilde{C}_{n-1}^{\mathrm{a}}(K, \cdot)$ given in the paper [9] is the limit case of $\mathcal{I}_p(K,\cdot)$ as $p\rightarrow 1^-$. The classical cone-volume measure is the limit case of the affine measures $2|p|\mathcal{I}_p(K,\cdot)/(n^2V(\mathrm{I}_pK))$ when $p\rightarrow 0$ and $V(K)=2$, where $\mathrm{I}_pK$ denotes the $L_p$ intersection body of $K$. The Minkowski problems for the $p$-affine dual curvature measures are proposed and studied. Specifically, we give a sufficient condition for the existence of a solution to the even Minkowski problem for $p$-affine dual curvature measure. Moreover, a necessary condition is given when $p\in (0,1)$. The smooth case of this Minkowski problem is equivalent to solving a new type of partial differential equations with respect to $p$-cosine transforms.

title: The Complexity of the Constructive Master Modality
generated_summary:
This paper establishes the precise computational complexity of constructive modal logics equipped with the master modality, which captures the reflexive-transitive closure of the modal accessibility relation. The master modality enables reasoning about iterated modalities and has connections to temporal logic ("henceforth") and propositional dynamic logic.

The authors study the logics CK+ (constructive) and WK+ (Wijesekera variant), which extend basic constructive modal logics with master modalities for both box and diamond operators. The key methodological approach involves a series of embeddings: first, a translation from CK+ to WK+ that eliminates fallible models without loss of generality, and then a Gödel-Tarski translation from WK+ into classical propositional dynamic logic (PDL). This chain of translations allows the constructive logics to inherit known properties of PDL, including the exponential model property and ExpTime decidability.

The central result is that CK+, WK+, and the classical master modality logic GL are all ExpTime-complete. The lower bound follows from embedding GL into CK+, while the upper bound comes from the translation into PDL. As an application, the authors show that the constructive variant of PDL with a single atomic program (iCPDL) can be viewed as a fragment of WK+ and is therefore also decidable in ExpTime, improving upon a previously known NExpTime upper bound and confirming a conjecture from prior work.

These results advance the understanding of decidability and complexity for constructive modal logics relevant to the Curry-Howard correspondence and computational interpretations of modal reasoning.
original_abstract: We introduce the semantically-defined constructive master-modality logics $\sf CK^*$ and $\sf WK^*$, extending the basic constructive modal logic $\sf CK$ and the Wijesekera-style logic $\sf WK$ obtained by impossing infallibility. Using translations between our logics and fragments of $\sf PDL$, we show that both $\sf CK^*$ and $\sf WK^*$ are EXPTIME-complete and admit an exponential-size finite model property. In particular, for their diamond-free fragment, also studied by Afshari et al. and Celoni, we establish EXPTIME-completeness, thereby settling the conjecture of Afshari et al.   As an application, we embed $\sf CS4$ and $\sf WS4$ into the master-modality logics, showing that their validity problems are in EXPTIME.

title: Analysis of the Riemann Zeta Function via Recursive Taylor Expansions
generated_summary:
This paper presents a claimed proof of the Riemann Hypothesis through a recursive geometric approach based on Taylor series expansions of the Riemann zeta function. The main contribution is an attempt to demonstrate that non-trivial zeros of the zeta function cannot exist off the critical line Re(s) = 1/2, thereby establishing the hypothesis by contradiction.

The methodology begins by constructing an analytic continuation of the zeta function using recursive Taylor expansions. Starting from the point (2, 2) in the complex plane, the authors chain overlapping disks of radius 0.5, carefully avoiding the pole at s = 1, to cover the critical strip above Im(s) = 2. They then assume the existence of off-line zeros and consider symmetric pairs of points p1 and p2 equidistant from the critical line. The authors evaluate the real and imaginary parts of the difference between the zeta function values at these paired points, categorizing the resulting expressions into types (B, C, D) based on their graphical characteristics involving positivity and realness properties.

The key claimed result is that the required simultaneous vanishing of both the real and imaginary differences at symmetric off-line zeros is impossible, as the "positivity" and "realness" conditions cannot be perfectly balanced. The authors argue this creates a contradiction, proving no off-line zeros exist. If valid, this would resolve one of mathematics' most celebrated open problems, though such claimed proofs require extraordinary scrutiny from the mathematical community to verify their rigor and completeness.
original_abstract: We present an unconditional proof that non-trivial zeros of the Riemann Zeta function must lie strictly on the critical line $\text{Re}(s) = 0.5$. By defining a recursive path of Taylor expansions originating from the domain of absolute convergence, we translate the zeta function towards the critical region, which is an easy-to-understand form of the analytical continuation. We then assume the existence of off-critical-line (off-line) zeros, which exist in pairs symmetric by the critical line. If the pairs are zero in value, their real and imaginary components differences should be both zero. However, we derive a contradiction against the assumption via basic logical deduction, proving the non-existence of the off-line zeros.

title: Asymptotic Separability of Diffusion and Jump Components in High-Frequency CIR and CKLS Models
generated_summary:
This paper develops a unified framework for robust parameter estimation and jump detection in discretely observed Chan–Karolyi–Longstaff–Sanders (CKLS) jump-diffusion models, which encompass the Cox–Ingersoll–Ross (CIR) process as a special case, under high-frequency asymptotic regimes.

The methodology integrates two key components: a density power divergence-based estimator for drift parameters, which provides a tunable trade-off between statistical efficiency and robustness against jump contamination, and an extreme-value-theoretic jump detection rule based on locally normalized standardized residuals. The density power divergence framework continuously interpolates between maximum likelihood estimation and highly robust procedures through a tuning parameter that progressively bounds the influence of large, jump-induced increments while preserving contributions from diffusion-driven observations.

The authors establish consistency and asymptotic normality of the robust estimator under infill asymptotics and demonstrate that the residual normalization yields a detection statistic whose extremal behavior permits asymptotically valid separation of continuous and discontinuous components. Crucially, the robustness regularization does not alter the asymptotic classification boundary, preserving identifiability of the jump component.

Finite-sample simulation experiments corroborate the theoretical findings, showing that moderate robustness improves stability of both parameter estimation and jump identification, particularly when jump magnitudes are small or sample sizes are limited. As sampling frequency increases, detection performance converges to the asymptotic regime, confirming the theoretical scale separation between diffusion and jump increments. This framework advances robust inference for jump-diffusion models commonly used in interest rate and financial econometrics applications.
original_abstract: This paper develops a robust parametric framework for jump detection in discretely observed CKLS-type jump-diffusion processes with high-frequency asymptotics, based on the minimum density power divergence estimator (MDPDE). The methodology exploits the intrinsic asymptotic scale separation between diffusion increments, which decay at rate $\sqrt{Δ_n}$, and jump increments, which remain of non-vanishing stochastic magnitude. Using robust MDPDE-based estimators of the drift and diffusion coefficients, we construct standardized residuals whose extremal behavior provides a principled basis for statistical discrimination between continuous and discontinuous components. We establish that, over diffusion intervals, the maximum of the normalized residuals converges to the Gumbel extreme-value distribution, yielding an explicit and asymptotically valid detection threshold. Building on this result, we prove classification consistency of the proposed robust detection procedure: the probability of correctly identifying all jump and diffusion increments converges to one under proper asymptotics. The MDPDE-based normalization attenuates the influence of atypical increments and stabilizes the detection boundary in the presence of discontinuities. Simulation results confirm that robustness improves finite-sample stability and reduces spurious detections without compromising asymptotic validity. The proposed methodology provides a theoretically rigorous and practically resilient robust approach to jump identification in high-frequency stochastic systems.

title: Solution of a bilevel optimistic scheduling problem on parallel machines
generated_summary:
This paper addresses a bilevel optimistic scheduling problem on uniform parallel machines, where a leader minimizes the weighted number of tardy jobs by assigning jobs to machines, and a follower sequences jobs to minimize the total sum of completion times. In the optimistic setting, the follower returns the schedule most favorable to the leader among all its optimal solutions. The problem is motivated by Industry 4.0 contexts involving hierarchical interactions between a centralized manufacturing system and autonomous cyber-physical systems.

The authors establish that the problem is strongly NP-hard through a polynomial-time reduction from the Numerical 3-Dimensional Matching problem. They also present a mixed-integer programming (MIP) formulation with a polynomial number of variables and constraints, demonstrating the problem belongs to the first level of the polynomial hierarchy rather than the second. Three exact solution approaches are developed: a moderately exponential-time dynamic programming algorithm (primarily of theoretical interest), the MIP formulation, and a dedicated branch-and-bound algorithm incorporating column generation for lower bound computation and a memorization mechanism.

Experimental results show that the branch-and-bound algorithm generally outperforms the MIP formulation, though performance degrades with increasing numbers of machines. Both methods can solve instances with up to 40 jobs and 2 or 4 machines. The findings underscore the extreme computational difficulty of bilevel scheduling problems, even when the follower's subproblem alone is polynomially solvable, highlighting the need for future heuristic approaches to tackle larger instances.
original_abstract: We consider the uniform parallel machines scheduling problem in the context of optimistic bilevel optimization, where two speed options are considered. In this scenario, the leader aims to minimize the weighted number of tardy jobs, while the follower seeks to minimize the total completion time on a set of uniform machines. This problem has practical applications in Industry 4.0. We show that this problem is NP-hard in the strong sense by providing a reduction from the Numerical 3-Dimensional Matching problem and we provide a moderately exponential-time dynamic programming algorithm. The problem is solved by means of a concise MIP formulation and a branch-and-bound algorithm that embeds a column generation approach for the lower bound computation. Computational experiments are presented for instances with up to 80 jobs and 4 machines while larger problems are out of reach for the proposed approaches.

title: Bruhat-Tits group schemes over higher dimensional base-II
generated_summary:
This paper establishes the affineness and smoothness of Bruhat-Tits (BT) group schemes of types II and III over higher-dimensional bases, resolving a question left open in the authors' earlier work where these group schemes were constructed but could only be shown to be quasi-affine. The main theorem demonstrates that under mild tameness assumptions on the residue field characteristic, BT group schemes associated to arbitrary tuples of concave functions on root systems are smooth, affine, and have connected fibres. Importantly, the result is proven under more general hypotheses than previous work, requiring only that the generic group be split connected reductive rather than split, semi-simple, and simply connected.

The methodology employs a double inductive strategy. The first induction builds on the established existence of type I (parahoric) group schemes, extending results from the two-dimensional base case to arbitrary higher-dimensional bases. The second induction proves affineness for general concave group schemes by building inductively on the number of concave functions in the tuple. The approach draws on techniques developed by J.-K. Yu combined with methods from the authors' prior work, providing a new construction of types II and III BT group schemes that also reveals finer structural properties.

The significance lies in the importance of affineness for applications of BT group schemes in arithmetic geometry and the theory of algebraic groups over higher-dimensional bases, where quasi-affineness is insufficient for many purposes.
original_abstract: We prove that split reductive BT group schemes over a higher dimensional base are {\em affine}. Our method also gives a new construction of higher BT-group schemes more general than parahoric ones. The new ingredients are an extension of J.-K.Yu's construction in \cite{yu} to higher dimensional bases, Néron-Raynaud dilatations of subgroup schemes on divisors, combined with techniques from \cite{bt2} and the structure theory developed in \cite{bp}.

title: Minimal toughness in subclasses of weakly chordal graphs
generated_summary:
This paper investigates minimal toughness—the property that deleting any edge strictly reduces a graph's toughness—within several subclasses of weakly chordal graphs. The work is motivated by a conjecture of Dallard et al. that no minimally tough chordal graph exists with finite toughness exceeding 3/2, and extends the investigation to the broader class of weakly chordal graphs.

The authors provide complete classifications of minimally tough graphs in five subclasses: P₄-free graphs, complete multipartite graphs, co-chordal graphs with co-diameter at least 3, net-free co-chordal graphs, and complements of forests. A key methodological contribution is the "join condition," a necessary condition for the join of two graphs to be minimally tough, requiring that if one component contains a maximum-degree vertex of the join, the other must be regular. The authors also leverage dominating edges, matchings in bipartite graphs for local connectivity analysis, and a determination of toughness for all complete multipartite graphs, generalizing Chvátal's result for complete bipartite graphs.

A notable finding is that minimally tough weakly chordal graphs with arbitrarily large finite toughness exist, contrasting sharply with the chordal case. Specifically, certain complete multipartite graphs achieve this. All graphs appearing in the characterizations contain vertices of degree 2t (where t is the toughness), confirming the generalized Kriesell's conjecture for these graph classes. The results advance understanding of toughness structure in graph theory and relate to the longstanding Chvátal conjecture on Hamiltonicity.
original_abstract: The toughness of a graph $G$ is defined as the largest real number $t$ such that for any set $S\subseteq V(G)$ such that $G-S$ is disconnected, $S$ has at least $t$ times more elements than $G-S$ has components (unless $G$ is complete, in which case the toughness is defined to be infinite). A graph is said to be minimally tough if deleting any edge decreases the toughness. It is an open question whether there exists a minimally tough non-complete chordal graph with toughness exceeding $1$. We initiate the study of minimally tough graphs in the larger class of weakly chordal graphs. We obtain complete classifications of minimally tough graphs in the following subclasses of weakly chordal graphs: co-chordal graphs whose complement has diameter at least $3$, net-free co-chordal graphs, complements of forests, $P_4$-free graphs, and complete multipartite graphs. Our approach leads to simple proofs of two results on minimally tough graphs due to Dallard, Fernández, Katona, Milanič, and Varga.

title: Dispersion for the Schr{ö}dinger equation on the line with short-range array of delta potentials
generated_summary:
This paper establishes dispersive estimates for the Schrödinger operator on the real line perturbed by an infinite array of delta potentials, extending previous results that were limited to finitely many point interactions. The operator models electron interactions with crystal lattices and is relevant to nonlinear Schrödinger equation theory.

The main result proves that the standard dispersive estimate (the $L^1$ to $L^\infty$ bound with $t^{-1/2}$ decay) holds for the propagator projected onto the essential spectral subspace, provided the coupling constants satisfy a short-range summability condition and either a no-resonance-at-zero-energy hypothesis holds or stronger decay conditions on the coupling sequence are imposed.

The methodology employs a high/low energy decomposition following the Goldberg-Schlag approach. The high-energy contribution is handled through Born series analysis of the resolvent, requiring a limiting absorption principle established in weighted Sobolev spaces. A key technical challenge involves the resolvent identity between the free and perturbed operators, which is resolved by working with Friedrichs extensions since the operators have different domains. The low-energy analysis relies on constructing Jost solutions associated with the perturbed operator, deriving explicit formulas and bounds using techniques from Deift and Trubowitz, and representing the resolvent kernel through these solutions via a Stone formula.

The significance lies in providing the first dispersive estimate for Schrödinger operators with infinitely many point interactions, opening pathways to studying nonlinear extensions and scattering theory in periodic or quasi-periodic singular potential settings.
original_abstract: We study dispersive properties of the one-dimensional Schr{ö}dinger equation with a short-range array of delta interactions. More precisely, we consider the self-adjoint operator obtained by perturbing the free Laplacian on the line with a real-valued sequence of Dirac delta potentials and belonging to weighted ${\ell}$^1(Z) spaces. Under suitable decay assumptions on the coupling constants and in the absence of a zero-energy resonance, we establish the L^1 (R) $\rightarrow$ L^$\infty$ (R) dispersive estimate with decay rate |t|^{-1/2} for the associated Schr{ö}dinger group. The proof relies on a limiting absorption principle in weighted spaces, explicit representation of the resolvent kernel in terms of Jost solutions and Born series expansion of the Friedrichs extension of the perturbed operator.

title: Quantitative Error Estimates for Learning Macroscopic Mobilities from Microscopic Fluctuations
generated_summary:
This paper establishes quantitative error estimates relating microscopic fluctuation observables to their macroscopic counterparts encoded in gradient flow PDEs, focusing on the symmetric simple exclusion process (SSEP), independent Brownian particles, and fluctuating hydrodynamics SPDEs.

The authors develop a unified framework for bounding the discrepancy between the short-time quadratic variation of fluctuation fields and the corresponding macroscopic mobility operator. For the SSEP, the methodology exploits duality properties to derive Duhamel-type representations, combined with characterization of martingale quadratic variation through the carré-du-champ operator and uniform moment bounds. Similar techniques are applied to independent Brownian particles and regularized fluctuating hydrodynamics equations.

The key results provide explicit error bounds depending on both spatial discretization parameter and time discretization parameter. For the SSEP, the critical dimension d=1 emerges naturally, requiring a scaling relation between temporal and spatial parameters to control errors. For regularized SPDEs, analogous estimates are obtained with error terms depending on regularization and discretization parameters. For irregular (square-root coefficient) SPDEs, where mild formulations fail, the authors employ renormalized kinetic solutions to establish qualitative asymptotic fluctuation identities rather than quantitative bounds.

These results are significant for macroscopic fluctuation theory and non-equilibrium statistical mechanics, enabling rigorous, finite-size-controlled reconstruction of transport coefficients from particle data with quantified uncertainty, thereby providing a principled approach to integrating microscopic fluctuations into macroscopic predictions.
original_abstract: We develop quantitative error estimates connecting microscopic fluctuation of interacting particle systems with the mobilities of their hydrodynamic limits. Focusing on the Symmetric Simple Exclusion Process and systems of independent Brownian particles, we provide explicit bounds for the discrepancy between the quadratic variation of fluctuation fields and the corresponding mobilities, in terms of time and spatial discretization parameters. In addition, we establish analogous error estimates for a class of fluctuating hydrodynamic stochastic PDEs with regularized coefficients. For stochastic PDEs with irregular square-root type coefficients, including Dean-Kawasaki type equations, we further identify the asymptotic behavior of the associated fluctuation structures within the framework of renormalized kinetic solutions. Our results provide quantitative insights into the relationship between microscopic fluctuation mechanisms and macroscopic mobilities, and contribute to a structured comparison between discrete particle systems and continuum fluctuating hydrodynamic descriptions.

title: Boundary stabilization of flows in networks of open channels modeled by Saint-Venant equations
generated_summary:
This paper addresses the boundary stabilization of Saint-Venant equations modeling shallow water flow in divergent star-shaped and tree-shaped networks of open channels, accounting for friction source terms that produce spatially varying steady-states.

The main contribution is demonstrating that exponential stabilization in the H² norm of entire tree-shaped channel networks can be achieved using only one feedback control at each terminal node of the tree, with no controls required at internal nodes or at the root of the network. This is a surprising result because the relative number of available controls can be quite small for large trees, yet stabilization is still attained. The conditions on control tuning parameters are explicit and depend only on the values of the target steady-states at the boundaries of terminal branches.

The methodology relies on constructing a novel explicit Lyapunov function for the H² norm that is compatible with the physical coupling conditions imposed at network junctions—a key challenge since previously known Lyapunov functions are incompatible with these network constraints. This Lyapunov function works for arbitrary channel lengths, a property that is unusual for hyperbolic systems. The authors first establish results for the linearized system and then extend them to the nonlinear case.

As a secondary contribution, the approach yields new explicit sufficient conditions for single-channel stabilization that improve upon existing results. Since Saint-Venant equations belong to the broader class of density-velocity systems, the methodology is expected to extend to other networked hyperbolic systems, such as isentropic Euler equations for gas pipeline networks.
original_abstract: This work investigates the boundary stabilization of flows in star-shaped and tree-shaped networks of open channels governed by the Saint-Venant equations with a friction term. Due to the existence of the friction term, the steady-states are non-uniform. We show that any such network can be stabilized with only controls at the terminal nodes of the network, even when there are no controls at the nodes inside the network. The number of control is optimal. The main tool we use is the Lyapunov approach, and the main challenge is that the state-of-the-art Lyapunov functions developed for Saint-Venant equations with source terms cannot be used. In this work, we manage to construct a new efficient and explicit Lyapunov function and, in turn, we give explicit ranges of the control tuning parameters that depend only on the values of the given non-uniform steady-states at the ends of the branches. Moreover, this Lyapunov function also improves the existing conditions found in the last decade for a single channel modelled by Saint-Venant equations.

title: Brunnian spanning 3-disks for the 2-unlink in the 4-sphere
generated_summary:
This paper constructs infinitely many pairs of non-isotopic Brunnian spanning 3-disks for the standard 2-component unlink in the 4-sphere. The key novelty lies in the "Brunnian" property: while each pair of spanning disks is collectively non-standard, each individual disk is isotopically standard when considered alone—the non-triviality arises only from their mutual interaction.

The author's methodology centers on barbell diffeomorphisms of the complement of the unlink, which is diffeomorphic to a connected sum of two copies of S¹ × D³. To detect these diffeomorphisms, the author develops an induced invariant derived from the generalized Dax invariant, which maps into homotopy groups modulo hexagon relations. A crucial technical step involves constructing coefficient functionals on the target of the Dax invariant that vanish on an "admissible span" (corresponding to trivial contributions) but detect the barbell diffeomorphism family, thereby proving non-triviality.

The main results establish that for each positive integer k, the barbell diffeomorphisms are non-trivial and pairwise non-isotopic, yielding infinitely many pairwise non-isotopic collections of Brunnian spanning disks. The Brunnian property is verified by showing that capping off either component produces barbells that are trivial in the single-component setting. The spanning disks become isotopically standard when viewed in the full 4-sphere, consistent with prior results.

This work extends the application of generalized Dax invariants beyond boundary-connected sums to internal connected sums, opening new avenues for studying exotic phenomena in 4-dimensional topology.
original_abstract: We show that the $2$-component unlink in $S^4$ admits infinitely many isotopy classes of spanning $3$-disks that are Brunnian.

title: Modal Fragments
generated_summary:
This survey article unifies two largely independent research traditions on syntactic fragments of modal logic. The first tradition, initiated by Kuznetsov and Rașcu in the 1970s, defines fragments through arbitrary modal formulas as connectives and studies the lattice structure of resulting modal clones. The second, inspired by Schaefer's theorem and Post's lattice classification of Boolean functions, restricts attention to "simple" modal fragments parameterized by Boolean function bases combined with specified subsets of modal operators.

The authors survey key results from both traditions, revealing a fundamental trade-off: the general modal-clone framework is algebraically natural but often yields undecidability for meta-problems such as expressive containment, whereas simple modal fragments retain enough structure to leverage Post's lattice, enabling systematic complexity classifications for problems including satisfiability, equivalence, and model checking across modal, temporal, hybrid, and description logics. The paper also contributes new results on the learnability and teachability of formulas from examples across propositional and modal fragments.

Several open problems are identified, including the decidability of modal clone containment for non-transitive logics, persistent classification gaps at affine Boolean clones, possible extensions of positive results to shallow uniform-depth fragments beyond simple ones, and the development of a general Boolean-basis-parameterized notion of bisimulation. The work provides a valuable conceptual bridge between algebraic and complexity-theoretic perspectives on modal logic fragments, offering a unified framework for future research.
original_abstract: We survey systematic approaches to basis-restricted fragments of propositional logic and modal logics, with an emphasis on how expressive power and computational complexity depend on the allowed operators. The propositional case is well-established and serves as a conceptual template: Post's lattice organizes fragments via Boolean clones and supports complexity classifications for standard reasoning tasks. For modal fragments, we then bring together two historically independent lines of investigation: a general framework where modal fragments are parameterized by a basis of "connectives" defined by arbitrary modal formulas (initially proposed and studied by logicians such as Kuznetsov and Ratsa in the 1970s), and the more tractable class of what we call simple modal fragments parameterized by Boolean functions plus selected modal operators, where Post-lattice methods enable systematic decidability and dichotomy results. Along the way, we collect and extend results on teachability and exact learnability from examples for both propositional fragments and simple modal fragments, and we conclude by identifying several open problems.

title: Bloch and Landau constants for meromorphic functions
generated_summary:
This paper investigates Bloch and Landau constants for classes of meromorphic functions defined on the unit disk with prescribed simple poles, addressing a conjecture posed by Bhowmik and Sen. The Bloch constant measures the radius of the largest schlicht (univalent) disk in the image of a function, while the Landau constant measures the radius of the largest disk contained in the image, with both constants taken as infima over a given function class.

The main contribution is twofold. First, the authors establish that the Bloch constant and Landau constant for the class of meromorphic functions with a simple pole at the origin are infinite, thereby disproving the conjecture of Bhowmik and Sen, who had proposed specific finite values as the exact Bloch and Landau constants for this class. The key insight is that allowing the pole position to approach the boundary of the unit disk causes these constants to grow without bound. This result demonstrates that the previously established upper bounds in the literature do not represent sharp values, contrary to what was conjectured.

Second, the authors extend the investigation to meromorphic functions with two prescribed simple poles in the unit disk, establishing bounds for the corresponding Bloch and Landau constants in this broader setting. The work contributes to the rich tradition of determining exact values or sharp estimates for Bloch-type constants, a longstanding theme in geometric function theory, and highlights the fundamental differences between the analytic and meromorphic settings.
original_abstract: Let $\mathcal{M}_1(λ)$ be the class of all meromorphic functions $f$ in the unit disk $\mathbb{D}=\{z\in\mathbb{C}\}: |z|<1$ having a simple pole at $λ\in \overline{\mathbb{D}} \setminus \{0\}$ and satisfying the normalization $f'(0)=1$. Let $B(λ)$ and $L(λ)$ denote the Bloch and Landau constants, respectively, for this class. In this article, we first show that the Bloch constant $B(1)$ and the Landau constant $L(1)$ are infinite. Using these results and a conformal mapping technique, we establish that $B(p)$ and $L(p)$ are likewise infinite for any $p \in (0,1)$, thereby refuting a recent conjecture. Finally, we extend our study to the class of meromorphic functions having two simple poles and prove that their associated Bloch and Landau constants also remain infinite.

title: A stabilizer interpretation of the (extended) linearized double shuffle Lie algebra
generated_summary:
This paper provides a novel stabilizer interpretation of two important Lie algebras arising in the study of multiple zeta values and multiple q-zeta values: the linearized double shuffle Lie algebra and the linearized balanced Lie algebra. These Lie algebras encode the depth-graded algebraic relations among multiple zeta values and balanced multiple q-zeta values, respectively.

The authors' methodology involves interpreting these Lie algebras as stabilizers of specific algebraic structures under natural Lie algebra actions. For the linearized double shuffle Lie algebra, the authors show it is isomorphic to the stabilizer of a bialgebra coproduct (dual to a shuffle product) under the action of primitive elements associated with another bialgebra coproduct. For the linearized balanced Lie algebra associated with multiple q-zeta values, they demonstrate it is isomorphic to the stabilizer of an involution map under an analogous Lie algebra action.

The key results establish bigraded isomorphisms between these Lie algebras and their corresponding stabilizers, and show that a known injective Lie algebra morphism between the two linearized Lie algebras extends naturally to their stabilizer descriptions, yielding a commutative diagram of injective Lie algebra morphisms. A significant consequence is that the stabilizer construction inherently carries a Lie algebra structure, providing alternative proofs that both spaces are indeed Lie algebras—results originally established through different methods. This stabilizer perspective offers a unified and conceptually transparent framework for understanding the algebraic structures governing relations among multiple zeta values and their q-analogues.
original_abstract: The linearized double shuffle Lie algebra introduced by Brown reflects the depth-graded structure of multiple zeta values. In a previous paper, the first author introduced an extension of this Lie algebra that accommodates multiple q-zeta values and multiple Eisenstein series. Inspired by the stabilizer interpretation of the double shuffle Lie algebra given by Enriquez and Furusho, we provide in this paper a stabilizer interpretation of both Lie algebras and show that the stabilizers preserve the extension from the first linearized Lie algebra to the second one.

title: Robust adaptive NMPC using ellipsoidal tubes
generated_summary:
This paper presents a robust adaptive nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) algorithm that uses ellipsoidal tubes to handle both additive and parametric model uncertainties while maintaining computational tractability. The main contribution is extending ellipsoidal tube MPC theory to incorporate online parameter adaptation through set membership estimation, yielding a framework with recursive feasibility, robust stability guarantees, and favorable computational scaling.

The methodology employs sequential convex approximation, where the nonlinear MPC optimization is convexified through linearization around nominal state and control trajectories. Approximation errors from linearization are bounded within ellipsoidal tubes that contain predicted state trajectories, while perturbations around linearization points are confined to polytopic sets. The resulting online optimization is formulated as a second-order cone program. A line search procedure is integrated to ensure recursive feasibility and performance guarantees even when only a single optimization iteration is performed per time step. Set membership parameter estimation enables online learning and reduction of conservatism as parameter uncertainty decreases.

Key results demonstrate that the algorithm achieves input-to-state practical stability and converges at least linearly, consistent with sequential convex programming for smooth problems. Numerical analysis shows that ellipsoidal tubes scale more favorably with problem dimensions compared to polytopic tube approaches, offering an improved balance between computational cost and control performance.

The significance lies in providing a practically implementable robust adaptive NMPC framework that avoids the nonconvex online problems or restrictive offline design requirements of existing nonlinear approaches.
original_abstract: We propose a computationally efficient nonlinear Model Predictive Control (NMPC) algorithm for safe, learning-based control. The system model is represented as an affine combination of basis functions with unknown parameters, and is subject to additive set-bounded disturbances. Our algorithm employs successive linearization around nominal predicted trajectories and accounts for uncertainties in predicted states due to linearization, model errors, and disturbances using ellipsoidal sets. The ellipsoidal tube-based approach ensures that constraints on control inputs and system states are satisfied. Robustness to uncertainty is ensured using bounds on linearization errors and a backtracking line search. We show that the ellipsoidal embedding of model uncertainty scales favourably with system dimensions in numerical simulations. The algorithm incorporates set membership parameter estimation, and provides guarantees of recursive feasibility and input-to-state practical stability.

title: A Second-Order Algorithm Based on Affine Scaling Interior-Point Methods for nonlinear minimization with bound constraints
generated_summary:
This paper proposes a Second-Order Algorithm Based on Affine Scaling Interior-Point Methods (SOBASIP) for solving nonlinear minimization problems with bound constraints. The main contribution is extending the Homogeneous Second-Order Descent Method (HSODM), originally designed for unconstrained optimization, to handle bound-constrained problems by incorporating an affine scaling interior-point framework.

The methodology involves introducing a suitable affine scaling matrix derived from the optimality conditions of the bound-constrained problem, which is combined with the Newton step to construct an affine scaling subproblem. A homogenization technique then transforms this subproblem into an Ordinary Homogeneous Model (OHM), which can be solved as an eigenvalue problem—specifically by computing the leftmost eigenvector of an aggregated matrix. In this paper, we extend HSODM to solve nonlinear optimization problems with bound constraints and propose a second-order algorithm based on affine scaling interior-point methods (SOBASIP). In each iteration, an appropriate affine matrix is introduced to construct an affine scaling subproblem based on the optimality conditions of the problem. To obtain a valid descent direction similar to HSODM, we utilize the homogenization technique to transform the scaling subproblem into an Ordinary Homogeneous Model (OHM), which is essentially an eigenvalue problem that can be solved efficiently. The descent direction is constructed from the optimal solution to the OHM, and then backtracking line search is used to determine the new iteration point. Theoretical analysis establishes that SOBASIP achieves a global iteration complexity of O(epsilon^(-3/2)) for finding an epsilon-approximate second-order stationary point and converges locally at a superlinear rate under certain conditions. title: Formal Entropy-Regularized Control of Stochastic Systems

original_abstract: Analyzing and controlling system entropy is a powerful tool for regulating predictability of control systems. However, these results do not extend to entropy-based performance measures. We solve this problem by first obtaining bounds on the entropy of system discretizations using traditional formal-abstractions results, and then obtaining an additional bound on the difference between the entropy of a continuous distribution and that of its discretization. The resulting theory enables formal entropy-aware controller synthesis that trades predictability against control performance while preserving formal guarantees for the original continuous system. More specifically, we focus on minimizing the linear combination of the KL divergence of the system trajectory distribution to uniform -- our system entropy metric -- and a generic cumulative cost. We note that the bound we derive on the difference between the KL divergence to uniform of a given continuous distribution and its discretization can also be relevant in more general information-theoretic contexts. A set of case studies illustrates the effectiveness of the method.

original_abstract: The Rayleigh expansion is widely used as a formal radiation condition in the analysis and numerical treatment of grating diffraction problems for incoming plane waves. However, the Rayleigh expansion does not always lead to uniqueness of open waveguide scattering problems, due to the existence of surface/guided waves (in other words, Bound States in the Continuum (BICs)) which exponentially decay in the direction perpendicular to the periodicity. In this paper we suppose that a bi-periodic inhomogeneous medium supports BICs at some real-valued incident wavenumber. Based on singular perturbation arguments, we justify the Limiting Absorption Principle (LAP) for both time-harmonic acoustic and electromagnetic scattering of plane waves from bi-periodic structures. Replacing the wavenumber $k$ with $k+iε$, we prove that the unique solution with $ε>0$ converges to a solution of the original diffraction problem that additionally satisfies an orthogonal identity. This constraint condition together with the classical Rayleigh expansion leads to a sharp radiation condition to ensure uniqueness of time-harmonic scattering of plane waves by BIC-supporting bi-periodic materials.

title: Nitsche methods for constrained problems in mechanics

original_abstract: We present guidelines for deriving new Nitsche Finite Element Methods to enforce equality and inequality constraints that act on the value of the unknown mechanical quality. We first formulate the problem as a stabilized finite element method for the saddle point formulation where a Lagrange multiplier enforces the underlying constraint. The Nitsche method is then presented in a general minimization form, suitable for nonlinear finite element methods and allowing straightforward computational implementation with automatic differentation. To validate these ideas, we present Nitsche formulations for a range of problems in solid mechanics and give numerical evidence of the convergence rates of the Nitsche method.

title: Positional s-of-k games

original_abstract: We introduce a general framework for positional games in which players score points by claiming a prescribed portion of each winning set, extending the notion of scoring Maker-Breaker games. In the scoring variant, Maker gains a point by fully claiming a winning set, while Breaker aims to minimize Maker's total score. In this paper, we generalize these models for all k-uniform positional games by fixing an integer threshold s in {1,2,..., k} so that a player scores a point whenever she claims at least s elements of a winning set of size k. We refer to this class as s-of-k games. Such formulation allows for a flexible description of scoring objectives that appear in both theoretical models and real-life board games.   We further investigate the impact of strategy restrictions on the achievable score. In particular, we analyze s-of-k games both under optimal play, where the score is denoted by SC, and under the additional constraint that Maker is restricted to a pairing strategy. The corresponding score in this setting is denoted by SC_2. While the unrestricted score captures the standard notion of optimal play in scoring positional games, the pairing-restricted score allows us to observe Maker's loss incurred by limiting her to these standard strategies.   We comprehensively study s-of-k games played on regular grids, which provide a natural and uniform setting for illustrating the general framework. After developing several general tools for the analysis of both scores, we complement them by a number of ad-hoc strategies tailored for particular cases of these games, to obtain both upper and lower bounds for the two scores on triangular, square, rhombus and hexagonal grids.

title: Non-Euclidean Gradient Descent Operates at the Edge of Stability

The authors introduce **directional smoothness**, an average curvature measure between consecutive iterates, as a key intermediary quantity governing EoS dynamics. Through a simple identity, they show that monotonic loss decrease requires directional smoothness below 2/η, while loss oscillation forces directional smoothness to oscillate around this threshold. original_abstract: The Edge of Stability (EoS) is a phenomenon where the sharpness (largest eigenvalue) of the Hessian converges to $2/η$ during training with gradient descent (GD) with a step-size $η$. Despite (apparently) violating classical smoothness assumptions, EoS has been widely observed in deep learning, but its theoretical foundations remain incomplete. We provide an interpretation of EoS through the lens of Directional Smoothness Mishkin et al. [2024]. This interpretation naturally extends to non-Euclidean norms, which we use to define generalized sharpness under an arbitrary norm. Our generalized sharpness measure includes previously studied vanilla GD and preconditioned GD as special cases, as well as methods for which EoS has not been studied, such as $\ell_{\infty}$-descent, Block CD, Spectral GD, and Muon without momentum. Through experiments on neural networks, we show that non-Euclidean GD with our generalized sharpness also exhibits progressive sharpening followed by oscillations around or above the threshold $2/η$. Practically, our framework provides a single, geometry-aware spectral measure that works across optimizers.

title: Stochastic Optimal Feedforward-Feedback Control for Partially Observable Sensorimotor Systems

The significance of this work is twofold: it provides a principled theoretical reconciliation of the feedforward impedance control versus optimal feedback control debate in motor neuroscience, and it offers a practical, interpretable computational tool with approximation guarantees applicable to both biological modeling and robotic systems with variable impedance actuators.
original_abstract: Robust control of complex engineered and biological systems hinges on the integration of feedforward and feedback mechanisms. This is exemplified in neural motor control, where feedforward muscle co-contraction complements sensory-driven feedback corrections to ensure stable behaviors. However, deriving a general continuous-time framework to determine such optimal control policies for partially observable, stochastic, nonlinear, and high-dimensional systems remains a formidable computational challenge. Here, we introduce a framework that extends neighboring optimal control by enabling the feedforward plan to explicitly account for feedback uncertainties and latencies. Using statistical linearization, we transform the stochastic problem into an approximately equivalent deterministic optimization within a tractable, augmented state space that retains critical nonlinearities, offering both mechanistic interpretability and theoretical guarantees on approximation fidelity. We apply this framework to human neuromechanics, demonstrating that muscle co-contraction emerges as an optimal adaptation to task demands, given the characteristics of our sensorimotor system. Our results provide a computational foundation for neuromotor control and a generalizable tool for the control of nonlinear stochastic systems.

title: $\mathrm{L}^{2}$--convergence of the time-splitting scheme for nonlinear Dirac equation in 1+1 dimensions

The key result demonstrates that time-splitting solutions converge strongly in L² to the unique strong solution of the NLDE as the mesh size tends to zero, for initial data in L². The authors establish local L² stability bounds via uniformly bounded Glimm-type functionals, extend these to global stability estimates by decomposing the solution domain into characteristic triangular subdomains, and prove precompactness of the solution family. original_abstract: We study the time-splitting scheme for approximating solutions to the Cauchy problem of the nonlinear Dirac equation in 1+1 dimensions. Under the assumption that the initial data for the scheme are convergent in $\mathrm{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R})$, we prove that the approximate solutions constructed by the corresponding time-splitting scheme are strongly convergent in $\mathrm{C}([0,\infty);\mathrm{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}))$ to the global strong solution of the nonlinear Dirac equation. To achieve this, we first establish the pointwise estimates for time-splitting solutions. Based on these estimates, a modified Glimm-type functional is carefully designed to show that it is uniformly bounded in time, which yields $\mathrm{L}^2$ stability estimates for the scheme. Furthermore, we prove that the set of time-splitting solutions is precompact in $\mathrm{C}([0,T];\mathrm{L}^{2}(\mathbb{R}))$ for any $T>0$. Finally, we show that the limit of any subsequence of the time-splitting solutions is the unique strong solution to the Cauchy problem of the nonlinear Dirac equation.

title: Lagrangian structures on the derived moduli of constructible sheaves

Key results include shifted Poisson structures on moduli of constructible and perverse sheaves, and the identification of shifted symplectic leaves obtained by fixing monodromy data. A concrete application is given for knots in 3-manifolds, where the moduli of perverse sheaves with prescribed monodromy around the knot carries a 0-shifted symplectic structure.

original_abstract: Given a compact oriented manifold of dimension $n$ with a conically smooth stratification, we show that the moduli of $\mathcal{D}(k)$-valued constructible sheaves and the moduli of perverse sheaves are $(2-n)$-shifted Lagrangian. The former statement follows from the construction of a relative left $n$-Calabi--Yau structure on the stable $\infty$-category of $\mathcal{D}(k)$-valued constructible sheaves. This is achieved via a lax gluing result for categorical cubes equipped with cubical Calabi--Yau structures. Given a codimension $2$ submanifold, we further identify symplectic leaves corresponding to perverse sheaves with prescribed monodromy.

title: Analytic structure of $q$-pseudoconcave subsets of continuous graphs

A key technical result establishes that the upper closed limit of a net of local maximum sets remains a local maximum set. A reduction lemma is employed to obtain foliations on lower-dimensional sets, which are then lifted using the graph-defining function.

The principal result shows that any q-pseudoconcave subset that is locally the graph of a continuous function over a closed subset admits a foliation by complex manifolds of appropriate dimension. As an application, the paper obtains foliations on q-pseudoconcave sets contained in graphs of differentiable functions. These results deepen the understanding of the relationship between complex analytic structure and the behavior of plurisubharmonic functions, while requiring only minimal regularity assumptions.
original_abstract: Let $Γ(g)$ be the graph of a continuous function $g:D\subset\mathbb{C}^n\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{C}^p$ (for $n\geq 1$ and $p\geq 0$). We prove that any $n$-pseudoconcave subset $Z$ of $Γ(g)$ can be realised as the disjoint union of $n$-dimensional complex manifolds. Moreover, we show that the same conclusion can be made for any $n$-pseudoconcave subset $Z$ of $\mathbb{C}^N$ (for $1\leq n<N$), which is locally the graph of a continuous function over a closed subset of $\mathbb{C}^n\times\mathbb{R}$.

title: Quadratic form estimations for Hessian matrices of resistance distance and Kirchhoff index of positive-weighted graphs

From this foundation, they obtain explicit formulas for resistance distance and Kirchhoff index in this extended setting. original_abstract: Let $G^{w}=(V,E,w)$ be a positive-weighted graph with the weight $w(e)>0$ for all $e\in E$. The weighted graph $G^{\widetilde{w}}=(V,E,\widetilde{w})$ is called a hyper-dual number weighted graph, where the weight $\widetilde{w}(e)=w(e)+Δw(e)(\varepsilon+\varepsilon^{*})$ is a hyper dual number, $Δw(e)$ is a real number, $\varepsilon$ and $\varepsilon^{*}$ are two dual units, $e\in E$. In this paper, we give a representation for the Moore-Penrose inverse of the Laplacian matrix, and calculation formulas for the resistance distance and Kirchhoff index of $G^{\widetilde{w}}$, respectively. We establish quadratic forms of the Hessian matrices for the resistance distance and Kirchhoff index of $G^{w}$ via generalized matrix inverses. We further derive explicit bounds on the eigenvalues of the Hessian matrices for the resistance distance and the Kirchhoff index of $G^{w}$ in terms of graph parameters. title: An Efficient Stochastic First-Order Algorithm for Nonconvex-Strongly Concave Minimax Optimization beyond Lipschitz Smoothness

original_abstract: In recent years, nonconvex minimax problems have attracted significant attention due to their broad applications in machine learning, including generative adversarial networks, robust optimization and adversarial training. Most existing algorithms for nonconvex stochastic minimax problems are developed under the standard Lipschitz smoothness assumption. In this paper, we study stochastic minimax problems under a generalized smoothness condition and propose an algorithm, NSGDA-M, which simultaneously updates the inner variable by stochastic gradient ascent and updates the outer variable by normalized stochastic gradient descent with momentum. When the objective function is nonconvex-strongly concave, we show that NSGDA-M finds an $ε$-stationary point of the primal function within $\mathcal{O}(ε^{-4})$ stochastic gradient evaluations in expectation, and $\mathcal{O}\left(ε^{-4}(\log(\frac{1}δ))^{3/2}\right)$ stochastic gradient evaluations in high probability, where $δ\in (0,1)$ is the failure probability. We verify the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm through numerical experiments on a distributionally robust optimization problem.

title: Geodesic-transitive graphs with large diameter

These findings advance understanding of symmetry hierarchies in algebraic graph theory and contribute to the broader classification program for distance-transitive graphs by identifying geodesic-transitivity as a natural refinement.
original_abstract: We review the nearly complete classification project for finite distance-transitive graphs and compile a list of all known graphs. Interestingly, we find that those graphs with diameter larger than 4, apart from a small finite number of exceptions, are geodesic-transitive. Their geodesics exhibit a clear (often geometric) structure. On the other hand, we provide examples of graphs that are distance-transitive but not geodesic-transitive, including two infinite families with diameter 3 and a few sporadic ones with diameter 3, 4 or 7. In the last section, we extend our investigation to polar Grassmann graphs and provide an explicit description of their geodesics.

title: Multi-Species Keller--Segel Systems: Analysis, Pattern Formation, and Emerging Mathematical Structures

This work bridges theory and computation to elucidate mechanisms underlying microbial self-organization, with potential applications in microbial ecology, tissue engineering, and biofilm modeling, while demonstrating that numerical method selection critically influences the accuracy and richness of captured emergent patterns.
original_abstract: Chemotaxis systems of Keller--Segel type constitute one of the central mathematical frameworks for understanding aggregation phenomena in biological and ecological systems. Over the past decades, the theory has evolved from the classical single-species model to increasingly sophisticated multi-species and multi-signal formulations that capture competition, cooperation, antagonistic chemotaxis, and interactions with fluid environments.   This article provides a comprehensive exposition of multi-species Keller--Segel systems and their mathematical structure. We review fundamental analytical results concerning local and global well-posedness, mechanisms of finite-time blow-up, and the role of critical mass and dimensionality. Particular emphasis is placed on how cross-diffusion, antagonistic interactions, logistic effects, and nonlinear production terms alter the qualitative behavior of solutions.   We further examine the mathematical mechanisms underlying pattern formation, including diffusion-driven instabilities, bifurcation phenomena, and the emergence of spatial and spatiotemporal structures. Connections between analytical thresholds and observed nonlinear dynamics are highlighted, and the interplay between reaction kinetics, chemotactic sensitivity, and diffusion is discussed from a unifying perspective.   By synthesizing classical results with recent developments, this survey aims to clarify the structural principles governing multi-species chemotaxis systems, identify common analytical techniques, and outline open problems that remain central to the field. The exposition is intended to serve both specialists and researchers entering the area of nonlinear partial differential equations and mathematical biology.

title: Horospherical splittings of $\mathfrak g$ and related Poisson commutative subalgebras of $\mathcal S(\mathfrak g)$

original_abstract: The density matrix is a positive semidefinite operator of trace 1 characterizing the state of a quantum system. We consider the inverse problem to reconstruct such density matrices from indirect measurements, also known as quantum state tomography. To solve such inverse problems in high or infinite dimensional settings, we study variational regularization using the quantum relative entropy as penalty functional. Quantum relative entropy is an analog of the well-known maximum entropy functional with compositions of functions replaced by the spectral functional calculus. The main aim of this paper is to establish the regularizing property of this scheme. As a crucial intermediate step, we establish lower semi-compactness of the penalty functional with respect to the weak-$*$-topology. Moreover, we compute the subgradient, proximal operator, and conjugate functional of the quantum relative entropy on finite dimensional spaces. This enables us to apply iterative algorithms from convex optimization to solve the regularized problems numerically. To show the validity and practical value of our results, we apply our theory to the examples of Photon-Induced Near-field Electron Microscopy (PINEM) and to optical homodyne tomography.

title: U-OBCA: Uncertainty-Aware Optimization-Based Collision Avoidance via Wasserstein Distributionally Robust Chance Constraints

These chance constraints are further transformed into deterministic nonlinear constraints, eliminating the need for integer variables and enabling efficient numerical optimization. The framework is validated through simulations and real-world experiments on a smart wheelchair platform in narrow corridor navigation and parking scenarios. Results demonstrate that U-OBCA achieves the lowest conservatism among compared methods, with the smallest minimum distance to obstacles while maintaining a full success rate. Notably, in the parking scenario, U-OBCA is the only method that successfully completes the task, as all baselines using elliptical approximations render the tight parking space infeasible. original_abstract: Uncertainties arising from localization error, trajectory prediction errors of the moving obstacles and environmental disturbances pose significant challenges to robot's safe navigation. Existing uncertainty-aware planners often approximate polygon-shaped robots and obstacles using simple geometric primitives such as circles or ellipses. Though computationally convenient, these approximations substantially shrink the feasible space, leading to overly conservative trajectories and even planning failure in narrow environments. In addition, many such methods rely on specific assumptions about noise distributions, which may not hold in practice and thus limit their performance guarantees. To address these limitations, we extend the Optimization-Based Collision Avoidance (OBCA) framework to an uncertainty-aware formulation, termed \emph{U-OBCA}. The proposed method explicitly accounts for the collision risk between polygon-shaped robots and obstacles by formulating OBCA-based chance constraints, and hence avoiding geometric simplifications and reducing unnecessary conservatism. These probabilistic constraints are further tightened into deterministic nonlinear constraints under mild distributional assumptions, which can be solved efficiently by standard numerical optimization solvers. The proposed approach is validated through theoretical analysis, numerical simulations and real-world experiments. The results demonstrate that U-OBCA significantly mitigates the conservatism in trajectory planning and achieves higher navigation efficiency compared to existing baseline methods, particularly in narrow and cluttered environments.

title: Biquadratic SOS Rank and Double Zarankiewicz Number
generated_summary:
This paper introduces the **double Zarankiewicz number**, a novel extension of the classical Zarankiewicz problem that bridges extremal graph theory and sum-of-squares (SOS) representations of biquadratic forms. The authors define a generalized cycle-free condition incorporating both edge types and prove that graphs attaining the double Zarankiewicz number yield irreducible doubly simple biquadratic forms, establishing the fundamental inequality that the maximum SOS rank of biquadratic forms is bounded below by the double Zarankiewicz number.

The methodology combines combinatorial graph theory with linear-algebraic arguments. The authors systematically analyze small parameter cases, determining exact values for several configurations. For the 3×3 case, they establish that the double Zarankiewicz number equals 7, matching the classical value. For the 4×4 case, they prove the value is 10, strictly exceeding the classical Zarankiewicz number of 8, achieved through a construction using eight ordinary edges and two double edges. For the 4×5 case, they establish bounds between 10 and 11, conjecturing the true value is 11.

The significance of this work is twofold: it explains previously observed gaps between SOS ranks and classical Zarankiewicz numbers, and it establishes a productive new connection between extremal combinatorics and algebraic optimization, opening numerous directions for future research in both fields.
original_abstract: The maximum sum-of-squares (SOS) rank of an $m\times n$ biquadratic form, denoted $\operatorname{BSR}(m,n)$, has recently been shown to be bounded below by the classical Zarankiewicz number $z(m,n)$, the maximum number of edges in a $C_4$-free bipartite graph. However, a gap was discovered for the $4\times3$ case: $\operatorname{BSR}(4,3)\ge 8 > z(4,3)=7$, arising from a construction that adds a square of a bilinear form $(x_4y_2+x_1y_3)^2$ to a $C_4$-free simple biquadratic form. This paper introduces the double Zarankiewicz number $z_2(m,n)$ to capture such phenomena. We define a new class of bipartite graphs that may contain both ordinary edges (1-edges) and ``double edges'' (2-edges), the latter corresponding to squares of simple two-term bilinear forms. A graph $G$ of this type yields a doubly simple biquadratic form $P_G$, and we prove that if $G$ contains no \emph{generalised $C_4$-cycle} then $\operatorname{sos}(P_G)=|E_1|+|E_2|$; consequently $\operatorname{BSR}(m,n)\ge z_2(m,n)$. We determine the exact value of $z_2(m,n)$ for several small parameters: $z_2(m,2)=m+1$, $z_2(2,n)=n+1$, $z_2(3,3)=6$, $z_2(4,3)=8$, and $z_2(5,3)=9$. For the $4\times4$ case we establish $10\le z_2(4,4)\le 11$, leaving the exact value as an open problem. These results improve the known lower bounds for $\operatorname{BSR}(4,4)$ and $\operatorname{BSR}(5,3)$. The paper concludes with a discussion of open questions and connections between extremal graph theory and the study of SOS representations.

title: Hat guessing with proper colorings
generated_summary:
This paper introduces and studies a novel variant of the hat guessing game on graphs, where the adversary is restricted to assigning hat colors that form a proper coloring of the graph—meaning no two adjacent vertices receive the same color. The proper hat guessing number, denoted HG_p(G), is defined as the largest number of colors for which players can guarantee at least one correct guess under this constraint, and it is always at least as large as the standard hat guessing number.

The authors establish results for several graph families. For complete graphs K_n, they prove that HG_p(K_n) = 2n − 2, significantly exceeding the standard hat guessing number of n. The lower bound relies on a strategy constructed using perfect matchings between subsets of different sizes, while the upper bound follows from a general result showing HG_p(G) ≤ 2n − 2 for any n-vertex graph, with equality if and only if G is a complete graph. For trees on at least two vertices, the proper hat guessing number equals exactly 3, proved through an inductive argument starting from the unique two-vertex tree. For book graphs B_{s,t} (a clique of size s connected to an independent set of size t), the number is determined to be 2s − 1 when t is sufficiently large. The authors also provide bounds in terms of chromatic number and maximum degree, and compute exact values for all graphs on at most five vertices.

This work opens a new direction in combinatorial hat guessing problems, demonstrating that structural constraints on the adversary can substantially increase players' guessing power.
original_abstract: We initiate the study of the hat guessing number of a graph where the adversary is only allowed to provide a proper coloring of the graph. This is the largest number $q$ for which there is a guessing strategy on each vertex that only depends on its neighborhood, such that for every proper coloring of the graph with $q$ colors at least one vertex guesses its color correctly. In this variation, we prove that the hat guessing number of the complete graphs on $n$ vertices is $2n - 1$, which is roughly twice the classical hat guessing number of the complete graph. Our winning strategy is related to finding perfect matchings between the middle layers of the boolean poset of dimension $2n - 1$. We prove that the hat guessing number of all trees on $n \geq 3$ vertices is equal to $4$. We derive some general upper and lower bounds for all graphs and give improved estimates for book graphs. Using our results and an ILP formulation of the problem, we determine the exact hat guessing number for all graphs on at most $4$ vertices, give bounds on graphs on $5$ vertices, and propose general conjectures.

title: Non-Runge Fatou-Bieberbach Domains in Stein Manifolds with the Density Property

The central question is whether non-Runge examples, where holomorphic functions on the subdomain cannot be approximated by global holomorphic functions, also exist in this broader geometric setting.

The authors establish two main theorems providing sufficient conditions for the existence of non-Runge Fatou-Bieberbach domains of two kinds: the first kind arises from basins of attraction of automorphisms with attracting fixed points, while the second kind comes from the push-out method producing biholomorphic copies of the manifold within itself. The methodology builds upon the Andersén-Lempert theory and its relative versions, which underpin the density property framework. The authors also introduce a new notion of weak density property as part of their theoretical development.

For both types of non-Runge Fatou-Bieberbach domains, the authors provide concrete examples where their sufficient conditions are satisfied, though they note that examples of the second kind are considerably harder to construct. This work significantly broadens understanding of the Poincaré-Fatou-Bieberbach phenomenon beyond Euclidean spaces, demonstrating that the rich function-theoretic complexity captured by non-Runge domains persists in the general setting of Stein manifolds with large automorphism groups.
original_abstract: Let $X$ be a Stein manifold with the density property. We present methods of constructing two kinds of non-Runge Fatou-Bieberbach domains in $X$, which by definition are proper open subsets of $X$ biholomorphic either to $\mathbb{C}^n$ or to $X$. For both kinds, we provide examples where our methods apply.

title: How Does the ReLU Activation Affect the Implicit Bias of Gradient Descent on High-dimensional Neural Network Regression?
generated_summary:

The authors address the gap between prior work showing that gradient descent converges to the minimum-ℓ₂-norm solution under exact orthogonality of features and worst-case results suggesting implicit bias is uncharacterizable.

The methodology centers on a novel primal-dual framework for analyzing gradient descent dynamics, where primal variables represent predictions on training examples and dual variables capture coefficients in the data span. This formulation naturally handles the ReLU nonlinearity, as the sign of primal variables determines activation patterns. The framework enables simultaneous tracking of both active and inactive examples, overcoming a key limitation of prior approaches.

For single-ReLU and two-ReLU models with sufficiently high-dimensional data, the authors completely characterize the implicit bias, showing that gradient descent converges to solutions where each neuron fits only the examples matching its sign. They establish that the distance between the gradient descent limit and the minimum-ℓ₂-norm solution scales as Θ(Σᵢλᵢ²/n²), where n is the number of training examples and λᵢ are eigenvalues of the data covariance matrix. This demonstrates the solutions are close but not identical in high dimensions.

A key insight is that, unlike linear models which interpolate all training examples, ReLU networks interpolate only data-dependent subsets, revealing an intrinsic example-selection mechanism that fundamentally distinguishes nonlinear from linear implicit bias.
original_abstract: Overparameterized ML models, including neural networks, typically induce underdetermined training objectives with multiple global minima. The implicit bias refers to the limiting global minimum that is attained by a common optimization algorithm, such as gradient descent (GD). In this paper, we characterize the implicit bias of GD for training a shallow ReLU model with the squared loss on high-dimensional random features. Prior work showed that the implicit bias does not exist in the worst-case (Vardi and Shamir, 2021), or corresponds exactly to the minimum-l2-norm solution among all global minima under exactly orthogonal data (Boursier et al., 2022). Our work interpolates between these two extremes and shows that, for sufficiently high-dimensional random data, the implicit bias approximates the minimum-l2-norm solution with high probability with a gap on the order $Θ(\sqrt{n/d})$, where n is the number of training examples and d is the feature dimension. Our results are obtained through a novel primal-dual analysis, which carefully tracks the evolution of predictions, data-span coefficients, as well as their interactions, and shows that the ReLU activation pattern quickly stabilizes with high probability over the random data.

title: Construction of higher Chow cycles on cyclic coverings of $\mathbb{P}^1 \times \mathbb{P}^1$, Part II
